22242-the-youth-s-companion-volume-lii-n:
The Youth's Companion was America's best-loved family weekly for a hundred years. This number, volume 52 number 11, is dated Thursday, March 13, 1879. J. T. Trowbridge, a regular contributor, supplies the lead story. In it a one-eyed hostler leans on a bar and lectures on bears. Let them alone, he says, and they will mostly let you alone. A vicious one turns up now and then.

Stories, poems, household pages, and a children's corner fill the issue. The Companion reached more American homes than any magazine of its century. Mark Twain and a dozen presidents wrote for it. One surviving number shows the wholesome, story-rich mixture that made it a fixture by the fireside.
813: 813, Maurice Leblanc's Arsène Lupin mystery. The numbered puzzle. This book preserves that detective tale. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
arxiv-2511-20313:
Zhou, Dacier, and Konstantinou deliver a reality check on software supply chain scanning. Their 2025 paper audits SBOM-based vulnerability management empirically. A software bill of materials lists every dependency inside a product. Scanners match that list against known flaws. The practice is promoted as supply chain hygiene.

The study covered 2,414 open-source repositories at scale. Lock files plus strong package managers produce accurate SBOMs. Generators like Syft and Trivy then agree consistently. The downstream scanners are the real problem. Their false positive rate hit a staggering 97.5 percent. Most flags point at flaws in unreachable code. A vulnerable function may sit in a package unused. Function call analysis prunes the noise effectively. It cut sixty-three percent of the false alarms. Developers drown in alerts that mean nothing today. The two-stage fix restores trust in the reports. Accurate lists plus reachability checks make alerts actionable.
arxiv-2511-20513:
Peng, Bigham, and Wu show design taste refuses to be merged. Their 2025 paper presents DesignPref, a dataset of personal design preferences. AI generators increasingly produce interfaces and slides for users. Training them usually pools human preference labels together. Personal taste varies too much for that pooling to work.

Twenty pro designers judged twelve thousand pairwise UI comparisons. Each judgment carried strength ratings and written reasons. Agreement between trained designers was strikingly low. Krippendorff's alpha for binary choices measured only 0.25 in the data. Designers weighted aspects like layout and type differently. Majority-vote judge models failed to mirror personal preferences. Per-designer models did far better. They won even with twenty times fewer examples each. Those reasons reveal disagreement stems from differing priorities. The dataset is the first for personalized design scoring.
arxiv-2511-20613:
Danassis and Goel pit AI-written code against graduate students in a strategy tournament. Their 2025 paper benchmarks coding agents on a logistics game. The Auction, Pickup, and Delivery Problem couples bidding with routing. Agents must bid under uncertainty and plan profitable deliveries. Unit-test benchmarks never measure such strategic depth.

Forty LLM-coded agents entered from many top models. Prompting styles varied, including free-form vibe coding. Seventeen human agents were written before LLMs existed. Twelve double round-robin tournaments ran about forty thousand matches. Human agents took all top five spots consistently. Thirty-three of forty machine agents lost to simple baselines. Handing the best human solution to the best model backfired. The model made that strong solution significantly worse. Long-horizon planning and opponent reasoning remain human strengths. The authors call for benchmarks where code must compete, not just compile.
arxiv-2511-20713:
Minhui Zhang and colleagues at the University of Waterloo formalise in 2025 a cheaper way to find where a language model keeps making the same mistake. Such failure groups are called error slices: GPT-5 answered Montreal when asked which of London or Montreal is further north, hinting at a wider cold-means-northern bias. Finding slices normally means paying human annotators to label huge piles.

Their approach, Active Slice Discovery, groups likely slice members automatically and asks an annotator to check only a small subset. The team tested it on toxicity classification, hunting human-defined slices in the Jigsaw dataset with a Llama 3.1 model. Uncertainty-based methods, which ask about the cases the system is least sure of, worked best across the representations and algorithms tried. On several slices they matched full-data accuracy while using only 2 to 10 percent of the slice membership labels, well ahead of random sampling.
arxiv-2511-20813:
Simon Hacks maps in 2025 the requirements for militaries adopting train-while-you-fight. The old maxim was train like you fight, rehearsing in peacetime; modern operations change too fast, with new weapons and procedures arriving mid-mission, as Ukraine's wartime learning showed. Train While You Fight demands continuous learning during operations, delivered by remote learning platforms working across allies under denied, degraded, or patchy connectivity.

Using design science, Hacks derives challenges from Partnership for Peace and NATO documents and identifies seven: modularity, interoperability, resilience, multilingual support, scalability, platform independence, and data security and privacy. He then maps each challenge to software engineering patterns. One strategy is a reach-back workflow, where field users send observations to a 24/7 triage cell that curates and injects updated content. The German armed forces' virtual learning environment, merging Moodle and ILIAS with access controls by clearance level, illustrates how the patterns combine nationally.
arxiv-2511-21013:
Ryosuke Kadono uses 2025 simulations to reinterpret a puzzling pattern in muon studies of battery materials. Muon spin relaxation probes how ions hop inside battery cathodes: implanted muons feel the ions' magnetic fields, and the signal's wobble rate is read as the ion jump rate. Many studies see an odd peak in that rate near some temperature, with the linewidth dropping above it.

He simulated spectra with an extended Kubo-Toyabe function that accounts for ion jumps, across 10 to 400 kelvin, then re-analysed them with the conventional function, mimicking earlier practice. The re-analysis reproduced the anomaly: it arises when the ion jump rate shoots up past the muon's jump rate as temperature climbs. The effect emerged with a linewidth of 0.3 megahertz and a correlation parameter of 0.8 in his runs. His advice: reanalyse vintage data with the extended function, and treat results showing no anomaly as silent about ion diffusion.
arxiv-2511-21413:
Tim Trappen, Robert Keßler, Roland Pabel, Viktor Achter, and Stefan Wesner retrofit a supercomputer for chatty AI workloads in 2025. Universities want to serve large language models to students and staff, and high-performance computing centers have the hardware, but classic supercomputer scheduling assumes batch jobs, not synchronous users waiting on replies. Their system runs the open-source vLLM inference engine on the supercomputer RAMSES, stitching together Slurm scheduling with Kubernetes orchestration.

Trappen and his coauthors add HPC-native pieces like Apptainer containers plus Prometheus and Grafana monitoring around custom microservices. Benchmarks on two hardware configurations show the architecture scaling efficiently at 100, 500, and 1000 concurrent requests. The integration costs only about 500 milliseconds of added end-to-end latency. The team presents the design as a production-ready, modular template for other centers facing the same demand.
arxiv-2511-21613:
Dongyang Fan, Diba Hashemi, Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, and Martin Jaggi show that the labels attached to training documents can teach language models faster, in 2025. Earlier work found that prepending a document's URL during pretraining accelerates learning, but nobody had mapped which other metadata helps. The team tested a wider range, from quality indicators to domain labels, varying both content and placement.

Fine-grained metadata won consistently: detailed quality scores and domain information sped training more than coarse signals, and the shared trait of every effective type was finer granularity, more specific information per document. Placement matters too. Appending metadata at the end, so the model must predict it as an auxiliary task, also accelerates pretraining, with the largest gains for fine-grained domain information. Even learnable meta-tokens trained with a masked loss recovered part of the speedup. Probing the model's internals, the authors distill practical guidelines for metadata design.
arxiv-2512-00113:
Neuromorphic processors copy some design ideas from the brain to run AI with very little power. Amirreza Yousefzadeh offers a tutorial on building scalable digital versions of them in 2025. The tutorial starts from RISC-V cores and moves toward arrays of neuromorphic units.

Digital neuromorphic chips suit low-power, always-on edge applications, such as sensors that must react without waking a larger system. The author lays out the main architectural design principles and illustrates them with the SENECA platform as a running example. New engineers entering the field get a guided path through the design choices involved. Tutorials like this one lower the entry barrier for a fast-moving hardware field.
arxiv-2512-00213:
Random connection models scatter points in space and link nearby pairs, forming clusters that can suddenly span the whole system. Mikhail Chebunin and Günter Last study the sharp phase transition in such a model in 2025. The points come from a Poisson process with a given intensity.

The authors derive exponential moment bounds for an arbitrary cluster when the intensity stays below a critical value. Strong bounds of this kind prove the transition is genuinely sharp, not gradual. These models describe wireless networks and material structures, so knowing exactly where giant clusters appear has practical as well as theoretical value. Exponential bounds are strong evidence, ruling out slowly growing giant clusters below threshold.
arxiv-2512-00613:
The Hubbard model is the simplest model that still captures how electron interactions create magnets and insulators. Fahad Equbal and Ahsan study the Mott crossover in the half-filled Hubbard model in 2025, resolved by spin. They use exact diagonalization on a small square cluster.

The crossover runs from a correlated metallic state to a Mott-insulating state as interaction strength grows. The authors examine both spin sectors and the entanglement between electrons. Even small clusters, solved exactly, benchmark the approximations used for real materials where no exact solution exists. Exact diagonalization is exact but tiny, which is why the small square cluster matters as a benchmark. Entanglement tracks how inseparable the electrons' states become across the crossover.
arxiv-2512-00813:
Savitha K S, Sandi Klavžar, and Tijo James study a two-player graph game in a 2025 paper. In the Maker-Breaker resolving game, two players take turns claiming unplayed vertices of a graph. One player, Resolver, wants to claim every vertex of some resolving set. A resolving set pins down all vertices by their distances to it.

The other player, Spoiler, wants to grab at least one vertex from every resolving set, blocking Resolver. The authors study the game on lexicographic products, a way of building big graphs from smaller ones. Knowing who wins helps judge how robust location schemes on networks can be.
arxiv-2512-01113:
Dongyue Li and four coauthors teach branching networks for multitask reasoning in a 2025 paper. Algorithmic reasoning, following step-by-step logical procedures, is a core benchmark for graph neural networks and large language models. Ideally one model would handle many algorithmic tasks at once, rather than a separate model per task.

Learning many procedures together is hard, since tasks interfere and need different steps at different times. Their branching networks learn to route computation so one model can perform well across tasks. Efficient multitask reasoning would cut the cost of serving many narrow models, and test whether machines can share skills across procedures.
arxiv-2512-01213:
Yangbangyan Jiang and co-authors work on a score used to judge sorting models. The full score counts how well a model ranks good cases above bad ones. A partial score looks at just one slice of that rank. That slice matters when false alarms must stay very low.

Two ways to train for the partial score had a gap between them. The team works to close that gap. Closing it means the score seen in training matches the score that counts in use. Gains here help fields like disease tests and fraud checks, where low false alarm rates are key.
arxiv-2512-02013:
Robots guided by vision-language-action models can understand scenes and act, yet long jobs with a defined end state, like assembling LEGO or rearranging objects, still defeat them. Chenyang Gu and co-authors present ManualVLA in 2025, a single model that both writes a step-by-step manual and carries it out.

The model uses chain-of-thought reasoning to generate the manual, then follows it during manipulation, joining high-level planning with precise hand control. Splitting the two abilities across separate systems is what earlier approaches did, and the seams showed on long tasks. A unified model that plans in words and then acts offers a cleaner path to dependable robot helpers.
arxiv-2512-02213:
Chatbots serve low-resource languages poorly, largely because good instruction datasets for training them are scarce and hard to build. Mamadou Keita and three co-authors present InstructLR in 2025, a scalable approach to creating such datasets, aimed at languages spoken across Africa and other underserved regions.

Effective text generation needs many examples of instructions paired with good responses, in the language itself. Curating those by hand for hundreds of languages does not scale, so a systematic generation approach is required. Better instruction data is the most direct route to language technology that works for the majority of the world's speakers.
arxiv-2512-02413:
Turning a flat floor plan into a 3D model starts with finding the walls, thin lines that segmentation models easily miss or blur. Dmitriy Parashchuk, Alexey Kapshitskiy, and Yuriy Karyakin introduce MitUNet in 2025, a hybrid network for precise wall segmentation in floor plan recognition.

The design pairs a Mix-Transformer encoder with a U-Net decoder, reinforced by spatial and channel attention blocks. That combination targets both thin structures and geometric precision, the two known weak points. Accurate automatic reconstruction of indoor spaces feeds renovation planning, real estate tools, and robot navigation maps.
arxiv-2512-02513:
Krishnendu S. Tharakan and Carlo Fischione tackle the hard task of streaming virtual reality over wireless links. Wireless VR frees users to move anywhere, but the video must stay sharp, smooth, and nearly instant. Headsets also have limited computing power, which tightens every design choice.

Their 2025 study uses federated learning, where devices train a shared model without sending raw data away. The design is decentralized and fairness aware, so weaker devices are not left behind. Multi task training lets one model serve several VR needs at once, saving bandwidth and battery. Fair shares keep small headsets in the loop, not locked out by weak links or low charge.
arxiv-2512-02713:
Theodoros Aivalis and three co-authors trace which training images shaped what an image generator produces. As generative models grow stronger, questions of credit, transparency, and copyright grow sharper. Knowing which data drove an output is central to answering them fairly.

Their framework builds ontology aligned knowledge graphs automatically to interpret generated outputs. Concepts in the graph link an image back to the data and ideas behind it. Such traceability could help artists seek credit, help auditors check datasets, and help builders explain their models to regulators and users. Graphs of this kind can be read by staff who know no code, which broadens who can audit a tool.
arxiv-2512-02913:
Underwater optical links promise fast data through the sea, but turbulence in the water fights the beam. A Gaussian light beam crossing a turbulent underwater channel suffers fading and scattering. Even weak turbulence can severely degrade communication quality, the study notes.

The analysis covers multi wavelength channels, comparing how several colors of light perform at once. Knowing which wavelengths hold up best guides design of links for divers, submarines, and ocean sensors. Reliable underwater optics would ease inspection, science, and rescue work where radio fails quickly. More than one hue at once gives a link a spare path when one hue fades, a cheap form of back up for sea gear.
arxiv-2512-03113:
Water flow through soil and rock is hard to predict fast. Zhenglong Chen and five co-authors offer a learning-based shortcut in this 2025 work. The flow, called Darcy flow, changes over time and depends on random traits of the porous material.

Their method blends time coding, operator learning, and a U-shaped network. It learns to map random inputs to flow fields across space and time. A fast stand-in model can replace slow simulations in design and planning. That speed helps in groundwater, oil, and carbon storage studies. For flow modelers, adaptive sampling focuses effort where the field changes fastest.
arxiv-2512-03213:
Fake projective planes look like a classic surface but are not. Lev Borisov and Bojue Wang find explicit equations for a new pair in this 2025 work. The pair is labeled in the Cartwright-Steger classification of these rare surfaces.

Explicit equations let other mathematicians compute with the surfaces directly. Fake projective planes are scarce and hard to construct, so each new pair matters. Their equations can test ideas in complex geometry and number theory. The work adds concrete examples to a field that has few of them. Each new fake plane tests the classification scheme that predicts which types can exist.
arxiv-2512-03313:
A famous counterexample in dynamics leaves an open question. Yi Liu and Lin Wang revisit Herman's converse KAM mechanism in this 2025 work. Herman built a perturbation of an integrable system from two parts: a hyperbolic term and a bump function.

Herman himself noted it was unclear whether the bump function was truly needed. Liu and Wang return to that remark and examine the mechanism again. KAM theory concerns which motions survive small disturbances. Settling Herman's question sharpens the border between stable and chaotic dynamics. Bump functions look minor, yet they can decide whether a counterexample truly works.
arxiv-2512-03913:
Robot training data is gathered by human operators, and their failed attempts are usually thrown away as useless. Jeongeun Park and colleagues argue that waste is a mistake in a 2025 robotics preprint. Failures record where a policy is fragile, and their model, VINE, learns from successes and failures together in a hierarchical vision-language-action system.

VINE splits the work between a high-level reasoner and a low-level controller. The reasoner searches a tree of possible subgoals over a scene-graph sketch, scoring each branch with success probabilities learned from both good and bad demonstrations. Brittle branches are pruned before anything moves. The controller then executes the chosen sequence with its skills unchanged. Trained only on offline teleoperation data, VINE improved success rates across challenging manipulation tasks. The authors conclude that failure data is an essential resource, not noise, for dependable robot behaviour.
arxiv-2512-04113:
Short-answer questions make students generate understanding rather than recognise it, but grading hundreds of written responses eats instructor time. Shyam Agarwal, Ali Moghimi, and Kevin C. Haudek propose a grading framework built on near-domain data in a 2025 preprint on computers and society. The raw material is answers to similar questions from previous years, already labelled by humans.

The method grades new responses by leaning on that archive, and it needs no pre-written rubric. In the authors' tests it beat state-of-the-art machine learning models and large language models, including the GPT family. Margins reached ten to twenty percent in some cases. That held even when those models were handed reference answers. The paper also names two advantages of labelled near-domain data, in accuracy and data efficiency. The authors describe the work as the first to formalise grading around such data.
arxiv-2512-04313:
Haolin Xiong and seven co-authors present Mind-to-Face, a system that turns brain wave readings into lifelike moving faces, in work posted on arXiv in 2025. Most avatar tools copy what a camera sees, so they fail when a face is covered or when a feeling stays hidden inside. Brain signals offer a direct path past the camera, if they can be read well enough.

The team recorded brain waves and multi-angle face video at the same time while people watched clips meant to stir feelings. A neural network then learned to map the signals onto dense three-dimensional face shapes with tens of thousands of points, and a graphics method drew those shapes as photo-like video. Tests showed brain waves alone could rebuild a person's changing face, even faint feelings, which suggests the signals carry far more about the face than was once assumed.
arxiv-2512-04613:
Torsten Hoge and Gerhard Roehrle settle a question about hyperplane arrangements: whether a property called MAT-freeness is fixed by combinatorics alone. Arrangements are finite sets of flat walls through a space, studied in algebra and geometry. Each arrangement has a combinatorial skeleton that records how the walls cross. A property is combinatorial if that skeleton alone decides it. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows MAT-freeness fails that test.

The authors show the property depends on the underlying field, the number system over which the arrangement is defined. Two arrangements can share one skeleton yet differ in MAT-freeness when the field changes. That split proves the property is not combinatorial. Negative results like this one map the border of what counting and crossing data can decide. They warn researchers to track field choice in freeness studies, and they close an open line in the theory of arrangements.
arxiv-2512-04813:
Huanqian Wang, Chi Bene Chen, Yang Yue, and co-authors present MOVE, a simple data collection habit that teaches robot arms to handle objects wherever they sit. Imitation learning trains robots on human demonstrations, but data are scarce. Worse, most demonstration sets record each task from one fixed layout: objects, targets, and cameras never move. A robot trained on such data fails when the cup sits two inches left. Their 2025 arXiv paper names that bottleneck and fixes the collection, not the model.

MOVE, short for Motion-Based Variability Enhancement, keeps the scene in motion while demonstrations are recorded. Objects and targets shift, and viewpoints change, so each trajectory carries rich spatial variety. The habit is cheap: no new hardware, just moving setups during collection. Robots trained on MOVE data generalized across space far better in team tests. Data habits may matter as much as model size for real-world robots.
arxiv-2512-05113:
Hao-Jen Chien and four co-authors present Splannequin, a method for freezing time in Mannequin Challenge videos. In those clips, people hold statue-still while a single camera moves through the scene. The goal here is a crisp three-dimensional model of that frozen moment for viewers to explore, with a whisper of motion kept on demand. Ordinary reconstruction tools built for moving scenes do not aim at this frozen result.

The authors model the scene with dynamic Gaussian splatting, which keeps nearby moments of variation, then render stills by pinning the model's clock. The catch is artifacts: elements unobserved at weakly supervised moments turn ghostly or blurred. Splannequin detects two troubled states of the model's building blocks, hidden and defective, and anchors each to better-observed moments. It drops into existing pipelines as simple extra loss terms, and viewers preferred its results overwhelmingly in tests.
arxiv-2512-05213:
Gareth Jones and fourteen co-authors take a fresh look at DLA0817g1, a galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young, already spinning like a settled disk. Few such rotators are confirmed at this distance, making each one precious. The team adds new infrared spectroscopy from the Webb telescope and combines it with archival radio data on the same galaxy.

Line ratios paint a distinctive portrait. The gas is unusually rich in heavy elements for its epoch, and much of its star formation is hidden by dust. Ionization is gentler than in its peers, and there is no sign of an active nucleus. Modelling shows the hydrogen and carbon gas rotate almost identically, though the hydrogen is more stirred up. A revised gas mass eases a previous strain in the galaxy's budget. The authors call it a smouldering galaxy, enriched by past star formation but currently quiet.
arxiv-2512-05513:
Chinthani Sugandhika, Chen Li, Deepu Rajan, and Basura Fernando benchmark whether video-language models can show what they know. These models answer questions about videos impressively, but their reasoning is often ungrounded — right answers without the evidence located in space or time. Their benchmark, Know-Show, unifies reasoning and localization in five scenario families. These span spatial relations among people, objects, and hands, plus a temporal dimension. The benchmark is built from established video datasets with thousands of human-written questions.

Current models, open and closed alike, fall well short of human grounded reasoning on it. To close the gap the authors add GRAM, a training-free plug-in that selects video tokens by attention and stamps them with timestamps, giving models grounding without retraining. Know-Show is offered as a standard for a capability multimodal systems claim but rarely demonstrate: pointing at the evidence for what they say.
arxiv-2512-05613:
Pasquale De Marinis and five co-authors address a hard task in images: marking out objects of a new kind, in a new setting, from only a few labeled examples. Older methods are shaky here, need the examples present at test time, and cost much computing. Their 2025 paper offers DistillFSS, a framework that bakes what the examples teach into the model's own settings, through a teacher and student setup.

Once that knowledge sits in a dedicated layer of the student network, no support images are needed at run time. That makes inference fast and light. New classes can be added through quick, teacher led tuning, and the method scales to large example sets. To test it fairly, the team built a fresh benchmark spanning medical scans, factory inspection, and satellite views. On it, DistillFSS matched or beat leading rivals, most clearly when several classes or several examples were in play.
arxiv-2512-05713:
Chenxu Li, Shengfan Liu, and Xiongfeng Ma ask how much randomness a quantum random number generator based on spontaneous emission really produces. Atoms shedding light at random are a natural random source. Yet older security claims rested on loose, case by case reasoning. The role of quantum coherence, the wave-like overlap behind true unpredictability, was not pinned down. Their 2025 paper gives the problem a full information theoretic treatment.

They model two eavesdroppers: one who can reach the atoms themselves, and one who touches only its purifying partner system. Devices that draw bits from single photon timing prove vulnerable to the stronger attacker, though they still guarantee a floor of randomness against the weaker one. Devices based on where photons land, or on phase fluctuations, stand up to both attackers. The team computes the intrinsic randomness of these schemes. Builders of such hardware now have numbers, not hopeful estimates.
arxiv-2512-06113:
Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta rebuild a core computation of digital twins for speed, on reconfigurable hardware. Model recovery runs constantly inside real time twins. On graphics processors it runs badly, choked by dependencies and data movement. MERINDA moves the work onto an FPGA as a streaming dataflow pipeline.

On chip tiling keeps data local; fixed point arithmetic trims cost. The old bottlenecks vanish. On representative workloads MERINDA needed up to six times fewer cycles than a comparable FPGA baseline. A lagging twin is a history book. Hardware software co-design of this kind is how the twin keeps up with the machine it mirrors.
arxiv-2512-06213:
Kathryn Devine, Grace Wolf-Chase, and their co authors describe MIRION, a catalog of young star forming regions built from a citizen science project. Volunteers with the Milky Way Project marked thousands of glowing spots in space images, nicknamed yellowballs for their color in false color views. Most of these spots are dense gas clouds lit and carved by young stars still buried in dust.

The catalog gathers more than six thousand of these objects into five linked tables. They hold light measures in the mid and far infrared, the speeds and distances of the gas clouds tied to each spot, and facts about the star forming clumps themselves. Early study finds links between the colors of the spots and the age and traits of their clumps. The catalog greatly widens the list of mid weight star forming sites open to study.
arxiv-2512-06513:
S Agaev, K Azizi, and H Sundu study two hypothetical particles built from four heavy quarks. Each is a molecule like pairing of two known heavy mesons, one built from bottom quarks and one mixing bottom and charm. Their shared quark content makes them axial vector states, a class defined by how they behave under spin and reflection. Such exotic states, if real, would stretch the standard picture of how quarks bind.

Using QCD sum rules, which tie quark level physics to particle traits, the team computes both masses. They come out equal, and both states prove unstable, falling apart into ordinary heavy mesons. The authors then work out one state's width, taken as equal for its twin, from its main decay routes into heavy meson pairs, plus smaller routes where a quark pair annihilates.
arxiv-2512-06613:
Yueying Ke builds a classifier that names microscopic algae the way a taxonomist would, level by level. Diatoms, glass shelled algae, are telltales for the health of water, but naming them takes scarce experts. Most automated tools guess only the species, a flat call that can be wrong in ways that mislead. Ke's network, DiatomCascadeNet, predicts five ranks in a cascade: class, order, family, genus, and species.

Each level reads the shared image features plus the calls made above it, and masks block any call that is not a valid descendant of the rank above. On a filtered set of over a thousand images across many species, the cascade matched flat rivals at the species level and beat them at every rank above. When the species call failed, the genus call was still usually right, and errors stayed taxonomically close.
arxiv-2512-06713:
Donghang Duan and five co authors anonymize text locally, without sending private words to a cloud service. Current tools lean on powerful remote models, which creates a paradox: to protect your data you must first hand it over. Moving the job to small local models seems safer, but the usual greedy strategies strip so much that the text loses its use.

Their framework, RLAA, runs a contest on the user's own machine, with no training. An attacker model tries to infer who or what the text hides, an anonymizer rewrites to block it, and an arbitrator referees. The arbitrator weighs each edit by privacy gained against utility lost, and filters out ghost leaks, inferences that were never real. That rational gate allows early stopping before the text is gutted. Across benchmarks the method struck a better privacy utility balance than the greedy state of the art.
arxiv-2512-07313:
Bosun Kang, Hyejun Park, and Chenglin Fan revisit the ski rental problem, the classic puzzle of deciding when to stop renting and buy, given that the season's length is unknown. Traditional algorithms guard against the worst case while assuming nothing. Newer learning-augmented methods accept a forecast and promise not to stray too far if it is wrong. The authors merge both instincts in a Bayesian frame that keeps an exact probability distribution over how long the season might run.

That machinery lets the algorithm reason about uncertainty honestly and absorb expert prior beliefs without special casing. Its guarantees scale with the quality of the prior, sliding smoothly between worst-case protection and fully informed play. Experiments across varied scenarios show near-optimal results when priors are good and sturdy worst-case behavior when they are not.
arxiv-2512-07613:
Arthur Fleig wrote this 2025 retrospective on feeling virtual touch in mid-air. In 2013, a system called UltraHaptics showed that focused ultrasound can create touch sensations on bare skin. No gloves or held devices are needed, since the pressure lands in empty air.

Fleig looks back at that formative work and the research paths it opened. Ultrasound mid-air haptics grew from earlier studies of airborne sound as a touch medium. The 2013 system set the technical and perceptual base for the field. Later work used the sense of touch to enrich screens, stories, and shared virtual spaces. It also helped users who cannot rely on sight or sound alone. Fleig stresses how much the field owes to teamwork across disciplines. Engineers, psychologists, and designers each shaped what the technology became. The piece serves as a short history and a map of open ground.
arxiv-2512-07713:
Krzysztof Sobucki and Paweł Gruszecki wrote this 2025 physics paper on spin waves in ultrathin magnetic films. The films carry perpendicular anisotropy and a chiral interaction called DMI. Changing the field in time can bend spin waves much like a lens bends light.

The authors study such temporal interfaces with simulations and theory. How waves refract and reflect in time turns on precession ellipticity. That ellipticity acts as a kind of magnonic impedance for the interface. Smooth field ramps, they find, suppress unwanted temporal reflections. Near the stripe-domain transition, the story grows stranger. Critical fields divide the film into damping, slow-instability, and strong-instability regimes. In the slow window, damping itself drives spin-wave growth. The growth rate rises in direct proportion to the damping strength. A temporal-slab protocol turns that oddity into huge, frequency-preserving amplification.
arxiv-2512-07813:
Hari Prakash Thanabalan, Lars Bengtsson, Ugo Lafont, and Giovanni Volpe wrote this 2025 robotics paper. Soft robots struggle to steer through rough and tangled terrain. Adding actuators for steering makes them complex, hungry, and hard to control.

Their robot borrows its gait from the inchworm, arching and stretching along. A single rolled dielectric elastomer actuator supplies all of its motion. Direction needs no extra motors at all in their design. Grooves printed into the floor do the steering instead. The patterned substrate passively guides the robot's alignment and path. By varying the groove angle, the team steers with precision in experiments. Control systems stay simple, and energy use drops with the complexity. The approach suits soft robots that must stay light and cheap. Search and rescue, pipe inspection, and planetary exploration are named targets. Passive guidance, they show, can replace active steering hardware.
arxiv-2512-08213:
Md Nazmul Haque, Elizabeth Lin, Lawrence Arkoh, Biruk Tadesse, and Bowen Xu, software engineering researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is a quiet risk in code generating language models: they invent software package names that do not exist, or suggest packages with known security flaws. The team asks what happens to those risks when models are quantized, shrunk to fewer bits to run cheaply on small machines.

They tested five sizes of the Qwen family at full, eight bit, and four bit precision, across three datasets of Go tasks. Quantization raised the rate of invented packages sharply, with four bit models degrading most. Even among real packages, the share carrying known flaws rose as precision fell. Most invented names mimicked realistic Go module paths, pointing at fake repositories. The findings warn that cheaper, smaller models can quietly weaken the software supply chain.
arxiv-2512-08313:
Gabriele Ravizza, Julian Villegas, Christer P Volk, and colleagues, audio researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their task is finding the headphone frequency response that listeners prefer, a target curve that makers tune products against. Preference is personal and listeners are untrained, so extracting it with ordinary listening tests is slow and noisy.

The team adapts an algorithm called interactive differential evolution to sound, driven by an adaptive paired rating test. Listeners compare pairs of tunings on a scale, and the algorithm evolves toward each person preferred response. Data from three listening experiments with more than twenty consumers let the authors judge convergence with two measures. The method did converge, even with untrained participants. They suggest it could ease the job of drawing out reliable frequency response preferences from ordinary consumers. That would help headphone designers tune products to real tastes rather than expert guesses.
arxiv-2512-08613:
Manzi Kevin Maxime, a computer scientist, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 on predicting protein structure from sequence. Knowing where a protein chain folds into helices, sheets, and coils is a basic step toward understanding what the protein does. Sequence alone is cheap to obtain, so predicting those local structures computationally is a long standing goal.

His model is a transformer, the attention based architecture behind modern language models. Attention lets it weigh both nearby residues and distant ones, since a fold can depend on far apart positions. To enlarge the training data, a sliding window augmentation cuts the standard CB513 benchmark into more training samples. The transformer generalized well across proteins of varying length, capturing local patterns and long range interactions together. Attention models, fed with augmented windows, look like a practical route to the task.
arxiv-2512-09013:
Paul Garnier and coauthors present a graph neural network model that simulates blood flow in brain aneurysms far faster than standard methods. Aneurysm rupture risk is tied closely to local flow measures such as wall shear stress and its oscillation over the cardiac cycle. Classic fluid simulations are accurate but very slow and need specialist expertise, while imaging methods lack the resolution to capture fine shear patterns.

Their surrogate model reproduces full field flow directly from vessel geometry in under a minute per cardiac cycle. It is trained on high fidelity simulations of patient specific aneurysms and joins graph transformers with autoregressive prediction. The model generalizes to unseen patient geometries and inflow conditions without mesh specific tuning. Predictions can be produced within minutes of patient imaging and compared with hospital assessments. The authors frame the system as a step toward real time, bedside aneurysm analysis.
arxiv-2512-09113:
Mahmoud Abdelgalil and Jorge Poveda introduce event triggered extremum seeking algorithms for model free optimization. Extremum seeking finds an optimum by probing a system,. In practice, exploration and exploitation are tightly coupled, which makes event triggered design delicate, since updates should fire only when needed.

Their controllers are cast as well posed hybrid dynamical systems with multiple time scales, using recent Lie bracket averaging tools for such systems. A low pass filter is added, and flow and jump sets are designed carefully to secure regularity, stability, and robustness. The optimal point is rendered stable in a semi global practical sense, with a uniform dwell time between events. A variant with two tunable parameters allows analysis by classic averaging tools instead. Simulations validate the theory and illustrate the behavior. The work gives a rigorous base for resource aware optimization that updates only at meaningful events.
arxiv-2512-09413:
Evgeny Korotyaev and Zongfeng Zhang study inverse problems for ZS-operators, the operators behind the Zakharov-Shabat system used in soliton theory. An inverse problem asks whether an operator can be recovered from its spectral data, the fingerprints left by its vibrations or scattering. The authors consider two such problems on the unit interval, each producing a mapping from a space of potentials into spectral data.

The central question is whether the two inverse problems are isomorphic, meaning one mapping can be obtained from the other by composing with an isomorphism of the potential space itself. They treat the problems under basic boundary conditions and on the circle. The proof rests on nonlinear analysis and on properties of a four-spectra mapping developed in their earlier work. Results of this kind clarify how much information different spectral measurements really carry about the underlying operator.
arxiv-2512-09913:
Sander Riisøen Jyhne and colleagues release NordFKB, a benchmark dataset for teaching computers to read Norwegian maps from the air. The data comes from Norway's authoritative national map database, known for high accuracy. It pairs high resolution aerial photographs with detailed labels for thirty-six classes of features. Labels come as segmentation masks in GeoTIFF format and as bounding boxes in the popular COCO style. Material comes from seven areas chosen for varied climate, terrain, and settlement.

Only image tiles containing at least one labeled object are included. Training and validation sets were sampled across all areas, keeping class mixes representative. Human experts reviewed the annotations for quality. The team also releases standard evaluation tools for segmentation and object detection, so results can be compared fairly. The dataset supports research in automated mapping, land administration, and spatial planning, with room to grow in coverage, time span, and data types.
arxiv-2512-10613:
L Balkenhol and a large collaboration take stock of cosmic inflation using the freshest sky data. Inflation, a burst of rapid expansion in the universe's first moments, sets the initial conditions of cosmology and solves several classic puzzles at once. Models are judged mainly by two numbers: the spectral index of the first density ripples and the ratio of gravitational wave power to those ripples.

Combining Planck, South Pole Telescope, Atacama Cosmology Telescope, and BICEP/Keck data, the team finds the spectral index sits just below one. While the gravitational wave ratio is capped at a few percent. Adding DESI's distance measurements nudges the index upward, which favours simple monomial potentials over the popular Starobinsky and Higgs models. A family of polynomial attractor models can fit both readings, and the data and plotting tools are public.
arxiv-2512-10713:
Itay Dreyfuss and co-authors build PACIFIC, a machine for generating benchmarks that test whether language models can follow code instructions exactly. Coding assistants must obey sequences of user instructions and mentally dry-run code, predicting what it does without executing it. Hand-written tests for that skill are scarce, fixed, and prone to leaking into training data.

PACIFIC generates fresh benchmark variants automatically, with difficulty under the designer's control and expected outputs defined sharply enough that grading is a simple comparison. That sidesteps both the tool-use distractions of agent-style tests and the contamination problem, since new variants can be minted at will. The authors generated a ladder of suites and ran leading models through them. Even advanced systems separate clearly as difficulty rises, showing the generator can keep producing tests hard enough to discriminate among top performers.
arxiv-2512-10913:
Mohammad Rezoanul Hoque, Md Meftahul Ferdaus, and M Kabir Hassan review what reinforcement learning has done for finance. Learning by trial and reward promises tailor-made strategies where classical methods fail, and the papers have exploded. The authors screened one hundred and sixty-seven papers from 2017 to 2025, concentrating on market making, portfolio optimisation, and trading systems.

On balance, reinforcement learning beat traditional methods, most clearly in market making. The review catalogues recurring performance problems and proposes one framework for the field's shared worries: explainability, robustness, and whether a system can be deployed at all. Evidence from synthetic data carries a practical moral, that implementation quality and domain knowledge often matter more than fancy algorithms. The authors call for clear designs that regulators can accept, sturdier behaviour in shifting markets, and standard benchmarks, and advise firms to invest in microstructure and risk knowledge over fancier algorithms.
arxiv-2512-11013:
Pawel Batorski and Paul Swoboda present PIAST, a fast method for building good prompts for large language models when training examples are scarce. Models react strongly to prompt design, yet hand crafting few shot examples takes skill and time. PIAST grows a small set of examples automatically from human instructions.

The method repeatedly keeps, drops, or swaps examples, judging each one's value with a Monte Carlo estimate of its contribution. Aggressive subsampling and a replay buffer keep those judgements fast, and users can spend different amounts of compute time. On a small budget it beat other automatic prompting methods on text simplification and grade school maths. With more time it set new best results among automatic methods on several tasks.
arxiv-2512-11113:
K. S. Babu, Sumit Biswas, and Shaikh Saad build a model that unifies quarks and leptons at energies within reach of today's colliders. Their framework is a Pati Salam model, which treats leptons as a fourth colour of quark, extended with a particle spectrum inspired by a larger unifying theory. It naturally contains a leptoquark gauge boson, a particle that links quarks and leptons directly.

A softly broken symmetry shapes the model so the new boson couples ordinary matter only to new heavy fermions, except in one quark sector. That structure suppresses the flavour changing decays that usually force such bosons to be extremely heavy. The boson could be quite light by unification standards, though linked limits on companion particles push the realistic floor higher. The authors detail collider signatures, including unusual heavy quarks, plus tests through rare muon processes, and show neutrino masses arise from higher dimensional interactions.
arxiv-2512-11213:
Dongwon Jung, Peng Shi, Muhao Chen, and Yi Zhang present FutureWeaver, a framework for spending a fixed computing budget wisely across a team of AI agents. Giving language models more time to think improves their answers, but multi agent systems lack a principled way to divide that extra compute among collaborators. Ad hoc setups waste budget or starve the steps that matter most.

FutureWeaver first packages recurring collaboration patterns into reusable modules, discovered automatically by reflecting on self play interactions. A two level planner then chooses immediate actions while also looking ahead in abstract terms, steering the whole run within budget. On complex agent benchmarks the framework beat baseline systems across many budget levels. The authors present it as a step toward planned, budget aware teamwork at inference time.
arxiv-2512-11313:
The Simons Observatory team built a pipeline to catch fast astrophysical flashes directly in the raw data stream of a cosmic microwave background telescope. Such telescopes scan the sky to map faint ancient light, and brief events lasting from milliseconds to minutes are usually searched for only after maps are made. Working with the time ordered data preserves sensitivity to the quickest signals.

The team tested the pipeline by injecting fake stellar flare shaped events into simulated observations. For half second flares it recovered most events above band dependent brightness thresholds, and longer flares were detectable at much lower brightness. Positions of detected events could be pinned down in each observing band. The approach readies microwave surveys to double as monitors for flaring stars and other rapid transients.
arxiv-2512-11513:
Yi Zhang and fellow authors refine the theory of quantum droplets, tiny self bound puddles of ultracold gas held jointly by quantum swings. Standard droplet theory adds the famous Lee Huang Yang correction, which assumes atoms interact only at zero range. Real interactions have finite reach, and connecting droplet physics to systems like superfluid helium demands those details.

Using a self steady effective field theory, the team derives an equation of state for 3D mixtures of bosonic atoms at zero temperature with finite range forces. Attraction between components encourages pairing, and the fluctuation correction becomes nonuniversal: it encodes the short range interaction explicitly, while shrinking to the known universal result when the range is sent to zero. Extending the fluid equations predicts fractional shifts in the droplets' breathing frequencies. Measuring those shifts would reveal droplet motion and the underlying atomic potentials.
arxiv-2601-06713:
Christian Bar proves an upper bound for total mean curvature of spin fill-ins in 2026. Gromov conjectured such an estimate for compact Riemannian manifolds. The bound should depend only on the boundary metric, Gromov proposed.

It should also depend on a lower bound for the fill-in's scalar curvature. Bar proves Gromov's conjecture when the manifolds are spin. He also assumes the mean curvature H is non-negative throughout. Total mean curvature measures how the boundary bends on average everywhere. Bounding it from boundary data alone is a strong rigidity statement. geometers working on scalar curvature will use this result directly. Spin geometry here delivers what general methods could not yet. The proof closes a named conjecture in a natural class.
arxiv-2601-07113:
Natham Aguirre wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on the long-run values of a math model of training. The model comes from discrimination training, where a subject learns to tell two cues apart. Its core is a periodic linear difference equation. A difference equation gives the next value from past values, step by step.

The trait here is written w of t. The key term is w at a whole count of steps, each of length T. Aguirre asks what that term tends to as the count grows with no bound. The change in w at each step is set by two time-based terms. One is a drive term, F of t. The other is a loss term, A of t times w. The paper works out the end values the trait can reach. They tell what the model says a trained subject does in the long run.
arxiv-2601-07713:
Jules Linden, Cathal O'Donoghue, and Denisa Sologon review what is known about who bears the cost of carbon taxes. Carbon taxes are popular with policymakers but politically contentious. The central dispute is distributional: burdens differ across population groups. Poorer households often spend a larger share of income on energy. The authors' 2026 preprint is a systematic review and meta-analysis of modeling studies.

Most studies assess the impact in advance using microsimulation models. A meta-analysis pools their results to find consistent patterns. Knowing which groups lose, and by how much, shapes compensation design. Revenue recycling can offset burdens if it is aimed well. The review serves policymakers and economists who must judge fairness claims with evidence rather than slogans.
arxiv-2601-07913:
Dmitry Shishkin and Amir Michaelis measure symmetry in pictures of exploded stars and glowing gas shells. They present a pipeline based on Transformation Information, an information measure of self-similarity under geometric changes. The measure compares an image with its rotated or reflected copy on their overlap. The comparison uses a Kullback-Leibler divergence, expressed as cross-entropy. Their 2026 preprint applies the method to planetary nebulae and supernova remnants.

Symmetry in these objects records how the explosion or outflow was shaped. Eyeball judgments of symmetry are hard to reproduce. A number lets astronomers compare many objects on one scale. The pipeline is released as code, built on standard scientific Python tools. The paper serves astronomers studying stellar deaths. It turns a qualitative impression into a measurement.
arxiv-2601-08113: Nardos Belay Abera and Yize Chen study how to run AI data centers with less energy and carbon cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such centers are being built at large scale for large language models. Training and serving these models demand huge computation, and cooling adds a second heavy load. The authors treat cooling and compute as one joint management problem. Coordinating both sides at once may cut total energy use more than tuning each alone. The work speaks to operators facing power and emissions limits.
arxiv-2601-08413: Hanxiang Yang and co-authors describe high-power free-electron laser light beyond the extreme ultraviolet at SHINE. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that linac-based free-electron lasers offer high brightness and narrow bandwidth. They also give controllable polarization and wide wavelength tuning. Superconducting radio-frequency advances now allow megahertz repetition rates in linacs. That enables lasers with both high repetition rate and high average power. Flexible polarization at SHINE would serve experiments that probe magnetism and chiral materials with intense short-wavelength light.
arxiv-2601-08713: Naren Medarametla and Sreejon Mondal of Vellore Institute of Technology in Chennai present a robot localization framework. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets autonomous basketball robots that must know their position in real time. Localization is a fundamental capability for autonomous robots in dynamic environments. A basketball court adds moving players and fast play, which strain standard methods. A real-time framework built for this setting could transfer to other fast indoor robots. The work serves student robotics teams and researchers in robot navigation.
arxiv-2601-08913:
Ambuj and four co-authors show a gain when a noisy plain link and a pure quantum link are used as a pair. Each link on its own can send a fixed count of notes with no flaw at all. One would guess the pair can send at most the product of those counts. The team shows that guess is wrong, in a good way.

Used as a pair, the links can send more flaw free notes than the product allows. The gain is called superadditivity. It means joint use beats the sum of parts in a strict sense. A reader in comms work gets a clean proof of that gain. It hints that mixed plain and quantum links may carry more than we thought.
arxiv-2601-09013:
James Wheeler couples a spin field to a broad form of gravity where the grid itself can twist and stretch. In that form, space is set by a frame that need not stay square or fixed in length. Twist is called torsion. Stretch of the grid is called nonmetricity. Both need a source, just as mass sources plain gravity.

Wheeler uses a Dirac field, the field for spin half bits like electrons, as that source. He ties the grid group to known spin groups by a clean map. That map lets the spin field drive twist in a direct way. A reader in gravity theory gets a neat source plan for two hard to source traits.
arxiv-2601-09813:
James W. G. Doran and four co-authors simulate tuberculosis spread in Uganda, person by person. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses agent-based modelling to study how gender shapes transmission. Tuberculosis is an airborne disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

In 2023, TB again became the world's leading killer among infectious diseases, passing COVID-19. More than ten million people are diagnosed each year. Men and women differ in exposure, care seeking, and risk, and a population average hides those gaps. An agent model can test which gender-linked factors drive the burden, guiding fairer control programs.
arxiv-2601-10013:
Ce Zheng, Shiyao Ma, Ke Zhang, Chen Sun, and Wenqi Zhang pick which users train a shared model. In shared training, phones train one model with no raw data sent. But tests of this work often split data in ways no real net would see.

Phone data also link to each other in real nets. Past picks for who trains next tend to miss those links. The team made a pick plan that uses side facts about users. It groups users by those facts first. The plan is built for real phone nets run to 3GPP rules. It aims for picks that match how data truly splits.
arxiv-2601-10313:
Peng-Fei Zhang and Zi Huang build attacks that can fool many sight and text models at once. A small change to an image can flip a model's call. Such tests show how frail a model is. Past attacks were made for one case at a time. That makes them slow to run at scale.

A broad attack works on new cases with no fresh build. The team refine such attacks in stages. Each stage hones the change for a wider set of cases. The aim is a cheap, broad test of model frailty. Labs can then rank models by how well they stand up.
arxiv-2601-10413:
Haiyue Yuan, Nikolay Matyunin, Ali Raza, and Shujun Li map how firms move user data, from their own privacy texts. Such texts state what data is took, kept, and shared. But they are long and dense with law terms. Few users can read them in full. Firms also phrase like facts in unlike ways.

The team built LADFA to read these texts at scale. It pairs a large language model with fetched facts. It pulls out the flow of user data: what, to whom, and why. The map can then be checked by pros. It makes a firm's true flow clear to see.
arxiv-2601-10513:
Xuan Luo and co authors test how well large omni models show empathy. Such models take in text, sound, and sight at once. To judge them on their own is a key need. But empathy is a feel trait. It is hard to score by a fixed rule.

The team built AEQ-Bench for this task. It grades how a model reads and meets the moods of a user. Cues may come in words, tone, or face. The bench joins all three. It gives a shared scale for a trait that past tests split by mode. That helps labs rank omni models on care, not just facts.
arxiv-2601-10813:
Srivathsan Poyyapakkam Sundar, Vibin Abraham, Bo Peng, and Ayush Asthana set out benchmarks meant to be decisive for quantum chemistry. Progress toward quantum utility needs more than better algorithms. It needs chemical problems whose electronic structure truly strains classical methods. Only then can a quantum machine prove its worth on a task that matters.

The authors curate a hierarchy of such benchmark systems. The sets probe distinct regimes of electron correlation. They span molecular, bioinorganic, and heavy-element chemistry. A shared ladder of hard cases lets teams compare machines and methods fairly. It also keeps the field honest about where quantum advantage is real and where it is still a hope.
arxiv-2601-10913:
Santiago Martínez Novoa, María Catalina Ibáñez, Lina Gómez Mesa, and Jeremias Kramer survey methods for classifying chest X-ray diseases. Chest X-rays are among the most common scans used to diagnose diseases of the thorax. Reading them at scale is slow, skilled work. The authors review several image processing and analysis techniques for the multi-class task.

Among the methods covered is DenseNet121, a deep network widely used for medical images. The team also deploys an open-source web application that puts the classifier to use. A browser tool can bring automated reading to clinics without local AI hardware. The work serves both researchers comparing methods and practitioners who need working tools.
arxiv-2601-11113:
Lele Zheng and co-authors fine-tune large language models in a subspace under differential privacy. Fine-tuning adapts a model to a task, often on sensitive data. Differential privacy gives strict guarantees, but adding noise across the full parameter space creates huge perturbations. Training wobbles and quality drops. The authors confine the noise to a subspace instead.

Working in a lower-dimensional subspace shrinks the noise's total size. Privacy guarantees can hold while the model still learns. The balance matters for hospitals, law firms, and banks that fine-tune on private records. The work offers a steadier path to private adaptation than naive noise over billions of parameters.
arxiv-2601-11713:
Rodney Martinez Alonso and four coauthors reject interference with wireless autoencoders. Their 2026 preprint works in the Walsh domain for ultrawideband links. Inter-cell interference can swamp a receiver in dense networks. Partial in-band interference is the specific foe here.

Narrower-band 5G base stations coexist with the UWB system. Their signals leak into the band and jam reception. The team designs an end-to-end wireless autoencoder. Transmitter and receiver are jointly optimized as one net. The encoding and decoding run in the Walsh domain. Walsh structure can spread signals away from the jammer. The method aims to keep links live amid interference.
arxiv-2601-12013:
Hollis Williams runs a numeric study of Hawking mass for closed surfaces moved by expanding flows. The surfaces sit in flat Minkowski spacetime and are not spheres. Under smooth flow, Hawking mass should rise in a set way in the curved case.

Less is known when that flow is run by discrete code on set shapes far from round. His tests check if the rise still holds in such code. That check matters for numeric work in gravity, where code must track theory. It shows where discrete flows can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-12213:
Hongyang R. Zhang, Zhenshuo Zhang, Huy L. Nguyen, and Guanghui Lan revisit matrix completion when samples are ultra-sparse. Matrix completion fills a table from a few seen cells. In their case, each cell is seen with low chance. The chance is C over d, for a fixed whole number C of at least two.

That is far fewer samples than most past work assumes. The team ask what can still be recovered in that regime. Ultra-sparse results matter for surveys and sensor nets where each cell is costly. The work sets new limits for the task.
arxiv-2601-12413:
Shihong Liu and nine co authors work on how to measure oxygen in far off galaxies. Telescopes like JWST now let us probe galaxies at high redshift. A key value is oxygen abundance, which tracks how enriched a galaxy is. Common tools for this task use strong spectral lines, with names like O3N2 and R23.

The team show that these tools lose precision at high redshift. At a fixed oxygen level, galaxies span a wide range in other traits. Ionization level and nitrogen enrichment both shift a lot from galaxy to galaxy. That spread blurs the line based estimates. Their work updates the diagnostics to deal with this spread and give sharper values.
arxiv-2601-12513:
Barbara Siljeg and six co authors image a galaxy that was thought to be dark. Dark galaxies hold lots of neutral hydrogen gas but no stars, or so the label claims. Models and simulations predict such systems should be common. Yet firm cases in hydrogen surveys have been hard to pin down, since a starless cloud is easy to doubt.

The team take high resolution hydrogen images of one candidate, J0139+4328. Their title gives the twist: the galaxy is not so dark after all. They identify an optical counterpart, faint starlight at the same spot. A case like this sharpens the hunt for truly dark galaxies. It shows how deep imaging can reclassify a supposed dark system.
arxiv-2601-12613:
Nathan Lindzey proves an Eventown style result for permutations. Eventown problems ask how large a family can be when all its members meet each other in a set way. Here the family consists of permutations of n elements. The meeting rule is that the ratio of any two members must contain an even cycle.

That rule is called even cycle intersecting in the work. Lindzey finds how large such a family can be, in the spirit of the classic Eventown theorem. Extremal results like this are gems of combinatorics. They often come with rigid structure for the largest families. The permutation setting links the problem to the symmetric group, a hub of algebra.
arxiv-2601-12813:
Keyin Wang and six co authors present a formally verified procedure for width inference in FIRRTL. FIRRTL is an intermediate language for register transfer level hardware designs. Bit widths of many components are not stated explicitly in FIRRTL programs. Compilers must infer those widths during compilation, a step called InferWidths.

The official compiler pass can fail even for simple FIRRTL programs. A verified procedure would rule out such failures by proof, not by testing. Formal verification checks the inference logic against a precise specification. Hardware bugs are costly, so compiler correctness matters from the first pass. The work was supported by Chinese research programs.
arxiv-2601-12913:
Pietro Barbiero and six co authors argue that the study of AI interpretability needs a new base. In their view, the field is ill posed as it now stands. The word itself has no test that can say if a method works. A term that cannot be tested cannot guide design, they argue.

They hold that a useful sense of the word must rest on symmetries. A symmetry is a change that leaves the key facts the same. Such rules can shape how a model is built and can be checked. Theirs is a position paper, a call to reset the terms of a field. It speaks to teams who build and judge tools that explain AI.
arxiv-2601-13013:
Xiaohui Zhao, Xinjian Zhao, and co-authors tackle a key task for news feed ads at Baidu. The task is to guess the long term worth of each user to the firm. Good guesses help set bids and split funds for growth over time, not just quick clicks.

The team names two blocks in the way. First, ads aimed by age or group traits give worth values that swing a lot across groups. Second, fast shifts in ad plans make user act chains uneven, and tastes change fast. Their answer is a graph based net that tracks both links and time. The name joins hyper graph links with time steps to catch both effects at once.
arxiv-2601-13113:
Di Wang and Fa-Yin Wang model what happens when a giant star strays near a huge black hole. As the star nears, tides shake it and drain energy from its orbit. That drain can trap the star in orbit around the hole, a path called tidal capture.

If the star strays closer still, tides can tear off part of it. Such a partial tear can then repeat on later passes. The pair model how capture and repeat tears link to each other. Their work helps read brief bright flares seen in far galaxy cores. It also helps guess how often such repeat events should turn up in sky surveys.
arxiv-2601-13513:
Noriyuki Tonami and co-authors sort sound events when many mics in a spread array are marred. Spread multi channel sound sense can tag events at large scale, from street noise to faults. Its score drops when many channels are worn. It drops too when the test layout parts from the train layout.

Their front end paints in the lost parts by physics, with no learn step. It uses reverse time migration, a wave back track tool from geophysics. That paint step feeds a stock event tagger. A learn free front end can be set on a new array with no re teach. For sound teams, that ease is the gain.
arxiv-2601-13713:
Aditya Bharat Soni and co-authors train open models to write tests that replay reported bugs in 2026. A good reproduction test shows a bug in code from a plain-language issue report. Such tests help devs find the root cause fast. They also back test-first work, where the test comes before the fix.

Their system, SWE-Tester, trains open-source language models for this task. It works on real-world code stores, not toy examples. Better bug replay tests can also make coding agents more effective. The work targets a slow, manual step in daily software work.
arxiv-2601-14413:
Matheus Curado Ferreira, F. T. Falciano, and Guilherme L. Pimentel mix two inflation ideas in this 2026 paper. Ghost inflation is a known framework where cosmological fluctuations can generate enhanced primordial non-Gaussianity, mostly of the equilateral type. In its original form, it clashes with current observational constraints. The team tries a distinct setup.

In their model, a standard inflaton drives the background expansion. Excitations of a ghost condensate act as spectator fields that interact with the inflaton. The title calls this amplifying the cosmological collider. That phrase names the hunt for particle marks in the pattern of primordial fluctuations. The work is pure theory. It adds no new sky data, but it does add a new test for old data. Readers get a new route to strong signals that past ghost models could not keep.
arxiv-2601-14813:
Jule Schindler and Emil Wiedemann study a fluid model in this 2026 math paper. The inviscid Leray-alpha equations are an inviscid nonlocal regularisation of the Euler equations. They smooth the flow over a length set by alpha, which tames the wildest small scales. The paper studies the nonlocal-to-local limit: what happens as alpha shrinks to zero.

In the first part, the authors prove convergence of strong solutions. Solutions of the Leray-alpha equations converge to strong solutions of the Euler equations. The result holds in Sobolev spaces for dimensions two and three, for a large class of regularising kernels. Readers get proof that the smoothed model honestly returns the true Euler flow.
arxiv-2601-14913:
Nijin J. Thykkathu, Matt J. Jarvis, and the MIGHTEE team ask how the rate of star birth has changed over cosmic time. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses radio waves to trace that history. Radio light is not blocked by dust, unlike much visible light.

Radio views can also be sharp enough to pick out single galaxies. The team works out radio luminosity functions for galaxies that form stars. These functions count how many galaxies shine at each radio brightness. They trace the count out to a redshift near 4.5, deep into the past.
arxiv-2601-15013:
Michael Feil and Julius Lipp speed up a repeated step inside transformer models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with batch inference, where many text sequences run through the model at once. Those sequences often share a common prefix, such as a system prompt.

Standard engines treat each sequence on its own. They recompute the same MLP activations for each copy of the shared prefix. The authors present RadixMLP, which deduplicates that work inside the batch. Shared prefix work is done once, and the savings in time and compute grow with the batch.
arxiv-2601-15413:
Tatiana Pavlidou, Aleks Scholz, and Koraljka Muzic date the young star clusters of the Perseus cloud. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a basic need in astronomy: knowing a cluster's age. Ages let astronomers track how a region formed its stars over time.

The authors test a new way to estimate those ages. It rests on a well-founded assumption: the initial mass function is the same across a star-forming cloud. That means the mix of stellar masses at birth is fixed. From a cluster's mass distribution, its age can then be read off.
arxiv-2601-15613:
Jianxiong Yao and five co-authors build a framework for energy flow in plasmas in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is capacitively coupled plasmas, widely used in industry and research. Electron energy in such plasmas is absorbed, converted, moved, and lost. Grasping each step is essential for reading discharge physics. It also matters for the processes these plasmas run, like etching and coating.

The authors propose a kinetic-moment framework. It rests on particle-in-cell simulations with Monte Carlo collisions. Those simulations track huge numbers of particles and their crashes. Moment methods then summarize the energy story in usable form. Bridging raw simulation and clear physics is the aim. Process engineers rely on such understanding to tune plasma tools.
arxiv-2601-15713:
Jordi José and Margarita Hernanz simulate an exploding star system in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is T Coronae Borealis, a recurrent nova. Recurrent novae erupt more than once. Some are identified by vast super-shells left by past eruptions. Their recurrence times are short, from about one year to a century. That pace sets them apart from ordinary novae.

The authors run hydrodynamic simulations of the system. The goal is to predict nucleosynthesis: which elements the blasts forge. Novae seed space with fresh isotopes. Predicting those yields tests the physics inside the model. T Coronae Borealis draws public interest because its next eruption is awaited. Simulations like these tell observers what chemical signs to look for when it blows.
arxiv-2601-15813:
Clare Chemery, Hendrik Edelhoff, and Ludwig Bothmann build a machine learning pipeline for ecologists in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ecologists increasingly work with image data, from camera traps to field photos. Off-the-shelf models rarely fit local needs. A species mix or habitat can be unique to one study site. The authors offer a lightweight experimentation pipeline instead. It lowers the barrier to applying learning methods on image data.

With it, ecologists can experiment on their own. They can move past generic models and tune to local datasets. Target variables can match the actual research question. The paper targets working scientists, not ML specialists. Tools that hand control to domain experts tend to produce insights that generic pipelines miss. That independence is the point of the design.
arxiv-2601-15913:
Lei Chen, Alice Devillers, Luke Morgan, and Friedrich Rober count colorings that break symmetry in a 2026 arXiv paper. The distinguishing number of a permutation group is defined plainly. It is the fewest colors needed to color the underlying set. The coloring must leave the identity as the only color-preserving group element. Any nontrivial symmetry must disturb some color. The authors compute this number for two graph families.

Complete bipartite graphs and crown graphs are their targets. Both are highly symmetric, so breaking all symmetry with few colors is a puzzle. The fewer the colors, the stronger the result. Distinguishing numbers connect group theory with graph coloring. They also model real tasks, like tagging items so that only the true arrangement looks unchanged.
arxiv-2601-16013:
Ziemowit Kostana, Jarosław Swaczyna, and Agnieszka Widz study infinite random graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some countable graphs arise from a random process with probability one. Up to isomorphism, the outcome is essentially unique. The Rado graph is the classical example. In that case, each pair of points gets an equal chance of an edge. The authors drop that equal-probability rule. Their graphs allow varied probabilities across pairs.

Unequal chances make the random construction richer. The question is which graphs still arise almost surely. Such universal graphs serve as limits and test cases in logic and combinatorics. A broader construction widens the family of known examples. The paper is in pure mathematics, where clean existence results anchor whole theories.
arxiv-2601-16313:
Sandra Glotzer, Jeong Rae Kim and Joseph Falson grow NbO films by a heat led growth window. Their 2026 preprint deals with films of niobium oxide, NbO. The team finds a growth mode that turns on past a high heat. Films grown that way beat past films in build and flow. The good mode holds through a range of oxygen push in the growth gas.

Good films form again and again in that range. The team maps the traits that mark the best films. A firm growth window eases work by other labs. It gives a clear recipe for high grade NbO films. Such films serve tests of charge flow in oxides.
arxiv-2601-17113:
J. Sarrato-Alós and a team of five co-authors ask if star birth past shapes dark cores. Dark cores in galaxies can be dense cusps or soft cores. Star birth bursts can stir gas and shift that core. Their 2026 preprint tests that link in fake galaxies. Two famed sim sets, NIHAO and FIRE-2, give the test beds. All galaxies get one same read path.

The team sorts birth past by burst strength and spread. It then sets that sort next to core slope. A firm link would tie bright past to dark shape. Such ties help scopes read real galaxy cores. They test tales of how small galaxies grew.
arxiv-2601-17213:
Asmaa AlMellah, Faeq Abed, and Gaber Faisel study a rare particle process in the scotogenic model. That model links dark matter made of fermions to new scalar particles. The authors look at electron and positron beams that collide. The crash can make a pair of charged scalars, one plus and one minus.

They trace how the pair forms at the lowest order. Paths include exchange of a photon and exchange of a Z boson. A third path swaps new heavy fermions in a side channel. Work like this tells collider teams what signals to hunt for. It also shows how dark matter ideas can be tested in lab crashes.
arxiv-2601-17313:
Briceyda B. Delgado proves a uniqueness result for Calderón's inverse problem. The problem asks what can be learned about the inside of a body from edge measures. It is the math base of electrical impedance tomography. That method sends small currents through a body and reads voltages to map inner conductivity.

Delgado uses integral formulas for solutions of the Vekua equation. The work sits inside Clifford analysis. Links to the conductivity and Schrödinger equations frame the proof. A uniqueness proof says the edge data can pin down one inner state. That ground matters for medical imaging. It tells builders that the map they seek is not a guess among many.
arxiv-2601-17613:
Jingxu Wu, Jie Shi, Chenjia Li, and Yuwei Yin link matter traits to black hole images. They build an explicit linear map for that link. Inputs are compact, conserved changes to the stress-energy tensor. The map gives the metric response in static, spherical spacetimes. From there it yields geometric observables. Key outputs are the shadow radius and photon-sphere frequency.

Those outputs are what horizon-scale imaging measures. A direct map lets teams test matter ideas against photos. It skips long nonlinear solves for small changes. Black hole imaging is now a data-rich field. Fast links from matter to image sharpen its tests. The work serves both gravity theory and observation.
arxiv-2601-18013:
Fei Wan examines whether a matching method lives up to its sales pitch. His 2026 preprint compares coarsened exact matching with propensity score matching.
