Both methods pair treated and untreated cases to estimate effects fairly. Coarsened exact matching is often sold as the better choice on imbalance, model dependence, bias, and efficiency. Wan argues that the claim is still uncertain, and he gives reasons for doubt.

One reason is a common misreading of the method's name. The matching is not exact on the raw variables; it is exact only after the variables are coarsened into bins. That detail changes what the method can promise. The paper helps applied researchers pick matching tools with open eyes.
arxiv-2601-18213:
Chengkai Huang and co-authors model the whole path of a user's future behavior, not just the next click. Their 2026 preprint presents Generative Chain of Behavior, or GCB. Long-term trajectories matter for understanding how tastes evolve and for timely recommendations. Most sequential recommenders aim only at the next item. That narrow aim misses how one action sets up the next across a long chain. GCB treats user interactions as an autoregressive chain, generating step after step.

A chain view can plan offers and content over weeks, not moments. It can also show where a user's path is likely to fork. The work serves platforms that think in journeys. Predicting the path, not the step, is the shift.
arxiv-2601-18513:
Kai Hu, Haoqi Hu, and Matt Fredrikson build a new net that can prove its own strength in the face of tricks. Some nets come with a bound that shows no small shift in a shot can flip their call. Past nets with that proof were small, slow to train, or weak on big shot sets. Their net drops two common parts to break that trade.

The net has no folds of the classic kind and no hard caps that slow its growth. It trains by steps that keep its weights on a curved space where the bound holds by form. A new part shifts the shot to catch form with no folds at all. The team bill it as the first net of its kind to reach huge scale. Such nets could serve fields where a proof of strength is a must, not a plus.
arxiv-2601-18813:
Matthias Gehnen and Julius Stannat study a chess form in which each side sees just part of the board. In that form, called Fog of War chess, a player knows where their own men stand but not where the foe's men hide. A move can land on a hid foe and take it, or walk in-to a trap. The form is played a lot on-line, but its maths was bare.

The pair give the first strict study of its end phase, when few men are left. With few men, the fog thins and the game turns on what each side can work out of past takes and checks. Their work maps which end states are wins, which are draws, and how the fog shifts the worth of each man. A strict base could guide both play and the bots that learn the form.
arxiv-2601-18913:
Mohammad Elayan and Wissam Kontar learn the trade-offs of self-drive cars straight from real road data. A self-drive car must weigh three aims at once. It must stay safe, it must not waste time, and it must deal well with the cars and folk near it. A gain in one aim can cost in the next. Past work set those weights by hand or by a plan, not by how cars truly drive.

The team score each tick of real drives on all three aims. Those scores chart the space of trades that real drives make. A car can then be set to a point in that space by choice, with eyes open. The chart is built in parts, so each aim's score can be checked on its own. Such a chart could help firms set drive style with care.
arxiv-2601-19013:
Zeyi Xu and Long Chen build a faster downhill method for convex problems that adapts as it goes. Gradient descent steps against the slope to find a low point, and speed ups exist, but they need true values for smoothness and convexity. Wrong values can slow or break the run.

Their method, A2GD, updates those values as it runs, guided by a Lyapunov style check. Borrowing from the study of steppers for differential equations, it runs a line search only when built up error turns positive. Fewer slope checks, kept guarantees, and no hand tuning make the method handy for large smooth problems.
arxiv-2601-19213:
Weiming Hu and a large team add metadata to tiny number formats so big models lose less accuracy. Low bit microscaling formats store blocks of numbers with one shared power of two scale. That blunt sharing is a main cause of the accuracy drop seen in formats like MXFP4.

Their format, M2XFP, augments the blocks with extra metadata to guide the scaling. Better scales mean each small block hugs its true values more closely. Formats like this decide how cheaply the largest models can be served, since memory and bandwidth rule their cost.
arxiv-2601-19313:
Hetong Wang and three co-authors cancel interference between data streams by shaping waves in the air itself. Stacked intelligent metasurfaces are layers of tunable sheets that bend radio waves as they pass. The team uses them to build a multi stream transmission scheme that aims to be free of interference by design.

Their angle is fresh: instead of fighting interference at the receiver, they exploit it in the wave domain. Constructive interference can add signal rather than noise when the waves are shaped right. Such schemes could lift the capacity of dense wireless links without more spectrum.
arxiv-2601-19413:
Michele Martinelli and a large team design the interconnects that will wire tomorrow's supercomputers and AI clusters. High performance computing blends many cutting edge technologies that must work as one. The wires between nodes, the interconnect, often decide how much of a machine's power real jobs can use.

Their project, NET4EXA, lays out a path for interconnects built for exascale loads and AI traffic. AI training moves vast data between chips, so yesterday's networks strain. A fresh interconnect design is a bet on what the next decade of computing will ask of its plumbing.
arxiv-2601-19513:
Haixu Xi, Heng Zhang, and Chengzhi Zhang address a daily strain on researchers: too many papers to read. Journals and preprint servers now publish at a pace no scholar can follow. A good recommendation system can point each reader to papers that match their needs. That help can raise research efficiency and spark new ideas.

The authors improve recommendations by describing each paper in finer detail. They pull out fine-grained knowledge entities, the specific concepts and terms a paper is built from. They also build document embeddings, numeric summaries of a paper, from several facets at once. Matching readers to papers on these richer signals should beat plain keyword overlap. The work speaks to anyone building search and alert tools for science.
arxiv-2601-19713:
Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, and Mathias B. M. Svendsen study how to move quantum states along a chain of atoms. Rydberg atoms interact over long distances through dipole forces. Those interactions extend two classic models that host topologically protected edge states. Topological protection promises transfer that resists small errors.

The authors build a theoretical framework for state transfer that is fast, robust, and high-fidelity. Speed matters because quantum states decay. Robustness matters because real arrays are imperfect. Long-range couplings complicate the physics but also offer new control. A reliable transfer protocol is a building block for quantum networks and simulators. The work shows how topology can protect information in transit.
arxiv-2601-19913:
Shinwoo Park and Yo-Sub Han ask whether experts can learn to spot machine-written Korean. Even linguistically trained readers struggle to tell human text from fluent model output. They tend to over-trust surface correctness. The authors treat expert detection as a learnable skill that structured training can improve.

They introduce LREAD, a rubric drawn from national Korean writing standards. The rubric targets micro-level artifacts, the tiny tells that separate human from generated text. Readers calibrate their judgement against the rubric. Better detection supports education, publishing, and platform integrity in Korean. The study reframes detection from gut feeling to a trainable craft.
arxiv-2601-20313:
Yiwei Bao, Andrea Addazi, and Shuai Zha build an exact framework for neutrino decoherence in turbulent matter, as found in core-collapse supernovae. Neutrinos streaming through this churning matter lose their quantum coherence, which changes the flavors that detectors later see. The authors use the Nakajima-Zwanzig projection method to derive an exact master equation for the neutrino state.

For turbulence with a red power-law spectrum, the memory term in that equation follows a power law in time. This leads naturally to a fractional calculus description. The framework gives supernova modelers a firmer handle on how flavor signals are reshaped on their way out. The math is hard, but the aim is plain to state.
arxiv-2601-20413:
Nouar Aldahoul and six colleagues study schadenfreude, the pleasure people take in others' misfortune, in Facebook news engagement. Online, this feeling has become a visible, performative part of how news spreads. Yet little is known about how common it is, how it changes, or how it patterns across societies.

The authors analyze ten years of engagement with nine major news publishers. The outlets span the United States, the United Kingdom, and India, with left, right, and centrist papers. A decade-scale map of schadenfreude can show platforms and editors how misfortune-driven engagement shapes public discourse.
arxiv-2601-20613:
The xbench team presents AgentIF-OneDay, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents follow instructions in daily-life tasks. Agent capability on long, complex work keeps growing, with strong results in coding, deep research, and hard problem solving. Yet general users rarely feel those gains in everyday scenarios.

The benchmark works at task level, scoring how well agents carry out ordinary instructions. Daily tasks involve messy context and small steps that lab tests skip. A shared yardstick for them could steer agent design toward usefulness that people notice in normal life, not only in demos.
arxiv-2601-20813:
Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, and Jose Medel construct new solutions to a system from geometry and physics. Their 2026 paper concerns the Hull-Strominger system with G2 symmetry. They build the solutions as torus fibrations over K3 orbifolds. A fibration stacks copies of a torus over each point of a base space. Here the base is a singular K3 surface.

The construction starts with three chosen divisors on that surface. They must be primitive with respect to a particular Kähler metric. The stable bundle then comes from an adapted Serre construction, moved into the singular setting. The total spaces are principal torus bundles over the K3 surfaces. The result adds fresh examples to a system that links complex geometry with string theory. Such examples help test what the theory can produce.
arxiv-2601-21013:
Chinmay Kulkarni and a large team of co-authors assemble a twenty-seven-year record of young stars flickering. Their 2026 paper surveys large-amplitude variability in young stellar objects. Infrared light can probe this variability across the full range of youth. The span runs from deeply embedded protostars to pre-main-sequence stars with dusty disks. The team built light curves from 1997 to 2024.

Three space telescopes supply the record. They are ISO, Spitzer, and WISE with its NEOWISE phase. All observed in the infrared, between three and eight microns. Stitching their archives gives one long, uniform view. Big brightness swings can signal bursts of accretion or clearing dust. The survey lets astronomers count how common such drama is. It is a legacy dataset for the study of how stars grow.
arxiv-2601-21213:
Gaofeng Wang, Weike Wang, and Tianfang Wu study the Boltzmann equation for gas mixtures whose molecules have different masses. The equation tracks how the spread of molecule speeds changes over time and space. Most past work treats a single kind of gas.

Mixtures with unequal masses behave in richer ways, since light and heavy molecules trade energy at different rates. The authors prove that classic smooth solutions exist for this harder case. Their result fills a gap in the theory of gases. It also supports models of real mixtures, from air to industrial gas flows, where mass gaps are the norm.
arxiv-2601-21613:
Hugo Morvan, Jonas Agholme, and co-authors present a software package for filling gaps in very large datasets. Missing data are common in big medical registries, where they can bias results if handled badly. Multiple imputation fills each gap several times to reflect the doubt around it.

Their package, bigMICE, scales that process to data too large for standard tools. It was built with Swedish health quality registries in mind. Registries guide real care decisions, so honest handling of missing values matters. The tool lets analysts keep the rigor of imputation without shrinking their data to fit old software.
arxiv-2601-22313:
Yavuz Bakman, Duygu Nur Yaldiz, Salman Avestimehr, and Sai Praneeth Karimireddy warn that a clean test today may not keep a model safe tomorrow. Their 2026 preprint notes that large models are updated often in real use. Past work shows updates can strip safety traits or revive facts meant to be erased.

They call the risk hair-trigger alignment: a small update flips the model back. Checks done from outside, with no view of the weights, cannot rule it out. The claim presses teams to test after each update, not just at launch. It reshapes how release gates should work.
arxiv-2601-22413:
Carlos Segovia links the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famed open claim in math, to a grid of number partitions. The hypothesis concerns where a key function hits zero, and it governs how primes spread. His 2026 preprint uses a known equivalent form of the claim.

That form rests on a threshold for how large a divisor-sum can grow. Segovia builds a direct bridge from that form to the Young lattice, a grid that sorts box diagrams. A new bridge gives attackers of the claim a fresh path. It may also reveal why the threshold takes its odd value. The work is a link, not a proof.
arxiv-2601-22713:
D. Vincenzi reports a beam test of a hybrid photon detector that reads single photons with fine timing. The device pairs a microchannel plate tube with a CMOS chip sealed inside. His 2026 preprint describes its run in a high-energy hadron beam at CERN, in a Cherenkov setup.

The detector ran at high gain and timed photons to a few hundred picoseconds. Fast, sure photon timing serves particle physics and imaging alike. A sealed, chip-read design could scale to large detectors. The test shows the concept works in a real beam. That proof is the paper's core.
arxiv-2601-23013:
Ernesto Benitez-Walz and four co-authors characterize faint stellar streams with self-supervised learning. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from galaxies and clusters, glowing very dimly. Studying them reveals how the Milky Way grew by swallowing smaller systems.

They apply a nearest-neighbor contrastive method to a curated part of the Dark Energy Survey's second data release. The method learns from the images themselves, without hand labels. Automated stream-finding could survey far more sky than manual inspection allows. Low surface brightness features are the target, the faint tidal debris that wide-field surveys record but rarely catalog well.
arxiv-2601-23213:
Roberto Rubboli, Erkka Haapasalo, and Marco Tomamichel characterize all valid forms of conditional entropy. Entropies measure uncertainty, with central roles in information theory, statistics, and the quantitative sciences. Under natural operational axioms, the most general entropy is the Rényi family, indexed by one real parameter.

Conditional entropy, uncertainty given side information, needed its own full characterization. The authors supply it, showing exactly which functions can serve. A complete axiomatic map prevents ad hoc measures and anchors quantum and classical information theory alike. The Rényi family, parameterized by a single real number, frames the conditional characterization the authors complete.
arxiv-2603-02013:
Matthias Aschenbrenner, Lou van den Dries, and Joris van der Hoeven revisit a class of equations in this 2026 mathematics paper. The equations are second-order linear ones with rates of change as terms. Their input functions come from Hardy fields, which force very calm long-term growth. Such inputs cannot wiggle wildly, yet solutions can still swing up and down.

The authors prove a guess made by Boshernitzan in 1982 about those swinging solutions. Each swing can be split into a size part and a phase part. Both parts live in a larger Hardy field, so the swings stay highly regular. They give sharp rules for when those parts are unique. They also trace the swings' long-term path, zeros, and peak points.
arxiv-2603-02913:
Julianna Piskorz, Katarzyna Kobalczyk, and Mihaela van der Schaar ask whether a language model's number forecasts can be read from its insides. Language models now tackle regression tasks like forecasting, but sampling their word-by-word output many times to build a distribution is slow and costly. Their 2026 paper looks for a shortcut.

Small probes trained on the model's internal signals predict summary values of its output distribution directly, such as the mean, median, and quantiles. The signals carried real information about those summaries, including the model's own uncertainty. The finding suggests cheap, sampling-free uncertainty estimates may be feasible for numerical predictions. It also raises fresh questions about how models quietly encode doubt about numbers.
arxiv-2603-03313:
Minghua Wu and three colleagues probe a weakness of large language models called the embodiment gap. Models learn from text, so their sense of how words feel, move, or sound often drifts from human bodily experience. The 2026 study asks whether focused fine-tuning with human ratings can pull those internal representations closer to human ones.

Using similarity analysis across concepts, the team finds fine-tuning reorganizes the model's semantic space in a targeted way rather than lifting everything evenly. Which base model started best barely predicts which tuned model ends best. Gains carry across languages and related senses, yet fail to transfer when the task format changes sharply. The results show model representations stay surprisingly flexible under the right supervision.
arxiv-2603-03413:
Giorgio Ottaviani's lecture notes tour classical invariant theory from musical ratios to tilings. Expanded from lectures at a 2025 summer school in Tromsø, Norway, the notes connect binary quartics and ternary cubics through their harmonic and equianharmonic invariants. They then carry the analogy onward to modular forms. Harmonic quadruples, the opening topic, reach back to Pythagorean tuning and the cross-ratio.

Triangle groups appear in both elliptic and hyperbolic settings, together with their associated tilings. A short Hilbert paper on polynomials that are powers gets a full discussion, originally set as work for the school's participants. The appendix collects exercises with sketched solutions, plus a section on Pfaffians edited by Vincenzo Galgano. The notes serve readers meeting invariant theory's classical roots with modern eyes.
arxiv-2603-03813:
Aaron L Galper and seven colleagues study the flaws in a crystal made of beads squeezed between plates. Confined to a gap barely wider than one particle, colloids buckle into up or down states, and neighbors prefer opposite states, like antiferromagnetic spins. On the nearly triangular lattice, trios of neighbors frustrate each other: no arrangement satisfies everyone. Their 2026 paper catalogs the topological defects of this two-level order.

Two orders coexist, the positions of the triangular lattice and the up-down spin pattern above it, and each grows its own defects. Both kinds shape grain boundaries and the coarsening of spin domains. The team classifies the spin defects, writes basic rules for their motion, watches dislocations interact with spin defects, and maps which defects drive the coarsening dynamics. The buckled monolayer becomes a laboratory for frustrated, self-assembled matter.

austen-pride-and-prejudice-1813:
Jane Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813, in the first edition text used here. The novel of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy became her most beloved work. Austen wrote it in her twenties and reworked it before it reached print at last.

Elizabeth, sharp and poor, must find a husband or face a bleak future. Darcy seems proud and cold, and first talks between them spark and clash. Letters, visits, and a scandal with Wickham slowly show both their true worth. Pride falls on one side and prejudice on the other, in fine balance. Austen's wit and craft make the courtship plot feel fresh each time.
avalon-tantra-great-liberation-1913:
Arthur Avalon was the pen name of Sir John Woodroffe, a judge in India. His Tantra of the Great Liberation came out in 1913. The work turns the Mahanirvana Tantra into English. It brought Tantra to the English world for the first time in full.

Rites, hymns, and rules for the life of the faith fill the text. The work dates from a late age of the Tantra line. Woodroffe adds long notes to clear hard points for new readers. The book is the root work of all Tantra study in the West since.
averroes-horten-texte-glauben-wissen-191:
Max Horten published this German volume in 1913, gathering texts on the clash between faith and knowledge in Islam. Horten, a scholar of Islamic philosophy, translated writings by al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Averroes. The book's title means texts on the dispute between belief and knowledge, a central problem for medieval Muslim thinkers.

The selections include material from Averroes's Decisive Treatise, where he argues that philosophy and revelation do not truly conflict. Other texts show how each thinker drew the line between what reason can prove and what faith must accept. Christian Europe faced the same quarrel a little later, often using Averroes's own arguments. Horten's volume made the Arabic debate readable for German students of philosophy and religion.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud begins Tract Baba Bathra, the Last Gate, with its first part. Baba Bathra is the Talmud's great property tractate. Land, houses, sales, and inheritance all fall under its rule.

Part one opens with partners dividing a shared courtyard and neighbors forced to help build its wall. It moves to rights of light and air, and to claims won by holding land in peace for three years. Then come sales of fields, houses, and ships, and what faults undo a sale. Rodkinson's rendering keeps the dense case law in order. The volume is core reading for the Talmud's law of property.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol6-1913:
Guillaume closed his French edition of Bakunin's works with a sixth volume in 1913. The set had taken years of labor, rescuing letters and drafts scattered among old comrades in several countries. With Bakunin's reputation still fought over, the edition aimed to let the texts speak for themselves.

The final volume gathers late writings and fragments that fit nowhere else, along with the editor's closing materials. Some pieces are rough drafts Bakunin never finished, printed here for the first time. Together, the six volumes hold the life's work of anarchism's founding thinker in the French he used for his widest audience. Scholars still start with Guillaume's edition when they need Bakunin's own words rather than summaries of them.
beard-economic-interpretation-1913:
Charles A. Beard published his bold reading of the United States Constitution in 1913. Beard argues that the men who framed it acted in part from their own wealth and gain. Land, cash, trade goods, and state bonds are his groups for sorting the men at the founding. Those who held such wealth, he claims, gained most from the new frame of rule.

The book stirred more debate than any American history of its age. Fans hailed it as a charter for a new kind of history; foes attacked its proof for decades. Later work softened many claims, yet Beard changed the questions asked. His stress on gain over ideals endures. No student of the founding can skip it.
beaumont-knight-burning-pestle-1613:
Francis Beaumont wrote The Knight of the Burning Pestle as a sharp joke on London theater and its fans. The comedy was first staged around 1607 by a company of boy actors. It was printed in 1613.

As a play about citizens begins, a grocer and his wife climb on stage and demand changes. They force the actors to make their apprentice, Rafe, the hero of a knightly romance. Two plots then collide: the scripted love story and Rafe's wild adventures. The result mocks both chivalric tales and pushy audiences, and its playful energy still feels fresh on stage today.
bedier-tristan-iseult-belloc-1913:
Joseph Bédier rebuilt the scattered medieval fragments of Tristan and Iseult into one smooth romance. His French version drew on many old poets whose works survive only in pieces. Hilaire Belloc translated it into English in 1913, and it became the standard modern telling.

Tristan and Iseult drink a love potion by mistake and are bound for life. Their story moves through secret meetings, exile in the forest, and long partings. At the end, a ship's sails, white or black, carry the news that decides both their fates. Few love stories have been retold so often.
bohr-constitution-atoms-molecules-1913:
Niels Bohr published his trilogy On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules in the Philosophical Magazine in 1913. The three parts form one long argument about the inner build of matter. Bohr pictured electrons moving in fixed orbits around a central nucleus. Only certain orbits, set by quantum rules, were allowed.

That picture explained the bright lines in the light of hydrogen gas. It also gave a first account of why the periodic table falls into its pattern. Chemists and physicists gained a model that tied their fields together. Few papers have reshaped science so fast. The trilogy marks the birth of the modern atom.
bosanquet-value-destiny-individual-1913:
The Value and Destiny of the Individual, published in 1913, prints Bosanquet's Hibbert Lectures, companion to his Gifford course of the year before. Its question is personal: what becomes of the finite self within the Absolute his system describes?

Bosanquet argues that the self's destiny is not extinction but completion: its private aims taken up and transfigured in a larger whole. He faces death, failure, and the apparent waste of lives with idealist composure. The lectures are gentler than the Gifford set, addressed to religious listeners. They close his account of the individual with a doctrine of hope.
bragdon-primer-higher-space-1913:
Claude Bragdon was an architect with a deep love of theosophy and form. His Primer of Higher Space came out in 1913. Cuts and clear plates show the fourth dimension in a way the eye can grasp. Bragdon hoped to lift the mind past flat, dull views of space.

He starts with points, lines, and planes, then steps up to the tesseract. Art, faith, and the soul all take on new shape in his scheme. The book took talk of higher space to artists and occult readers. Its fine plates still catch the eye of new fans today.
carter-the-woman-with-empty-hands-the-ev: The Woman with Empty Hands, the evolution of a suffragette, Carter's 1913 work. The empty hands. This book preserves that book. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cather-o-pioneers-1913:
Willa Cather published O Pioneers! in 1913, a novel about Swedish settlers on the Nebraska plains. Alexandra Bergson takes charge of the family farm when her father dies. Neighbors give up and leave during hard years, but Alexandra holds on. She buys land cheap and studies new methods of farming.

In time the prairie rewards her faith with rich harvests. A late love for her old friend Carl brings both joy and tragedy to her house. Cather writes with calm strength about work, land, and memory. The novel was her first set in the West she knew from youth. It began her fame as a novelist of the plains.
cato-de-agri-cultura-harrison-1913:
Cato the Elder set down the oldest Latin prose that survives in his farm book, De Agri Cultura. Cato on Farming, in Fairfax Harrison's 1913 English rendering, gives the stern Roman's manual whole. Cato wrote in the second century before Christ, as Rome grew rich and hard.

The book mixes plain farm rules with praise of the farming life and scorn for soft city ways. Cato tells how to buy land, plant vines, feed slaves, and time the year's work. His short, blunt sentences set the tone of Latin prose at its birth. The manual opens the whole Latin literary tradition.
cervantes-exemplary-novels-1613:
Miguel de Cervantes published his Exemplary Novels in 1613, a set of twelve short tales in Spanish. Cervantes is best known for Don Quixote, written in the same years. These stories range across Spain and Italy. Lovers, thieves, students, and soldiers drive the plots.

Some tales are comic, while others turn on honor, jealousy, or mistaken identity. The Gypsy Girl and Rinconete and Cortadillo are among the best known. Cervantes claimed he was the first to write such tales in Spanish. Historians credit the book with helping to create the modern short story. The tales remain lively, humane, and quick to read.
charles-apocrypha-pseudepigrapha-1913:
R. H. Charles spent his life on the lost books of the Jews. His Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament came out in 1913 in two stout books. Charles led the work and turned much of it himself. The set is the stock English store of texts from the years between the Testaments.

Book one holds the Apocrypha, texts kept by some churches and dropped by most. Book two holds the rest: Enoch, Jubilees, and the tales of Adam and Eve. Long notes clear the age, tongue, and sense of each text. Few sets have served the field so long or so well.
charles-apocrypha-pseudepigrapha-ot-vol2:
Robert Charles gathered the great Jewish writings left out of the Bible in his landmark edition of 1913. The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, volume two, holds the Pseudepigrapha in English. These are works written in the names of old heroes like Enoch and Ezra.

Jubilees, the books of Enoch, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Baruch, Fourth Ezra, and the Psalms of Solomon all stand here. They tell of angels, last days, and the hopes of Jews under foreign rule. Charles's notes made the hard texts plain to English readers. The volume stayed the scholar's standard for most of a century.
cia-0000007613:
Volume 13, number 2 of Studies in Intelligence appeared in spring 1969, near the end of a hard decade for the CIA. A heading asks, in another language, what the CIA is, a question the journal's readers knew well. The journal remained an internal forum for officers.

Self-definition was no small matter for an agency pressed by war and public doubt. Its pages carried argument about craft, purpose, and standards from people doing the work. Read now, the issue documents how American intelligence described itself to itself in 1969. Declassification moved that private conversation into the public historical record.
cia-0000008013:
National Intelligence Estimate 64-58 took up the Federation of Malaya in January 1958. Malaya had just won independence from Britain after years of fighting a communist uprising, the Malayan Emergency. An NIE carries the agreed judgment of the whole US intelligence community.

The estimate weighs the new state's stability, its economy, and the fading insurgency's threat. Malaya mattered to Washington as proof that a communist revolt could be beaten. Readers can compare its relatively hopeful case with Vietnam's darker path nearby. The file also shows how NIEs packaged shared judgment for senior decision makers in Washington at the time.
cia-0000009713:
A Viet Cong Military Region 3 prison camp holding 200 prisoners is located in a September 1971 report. The heading adds that the prisoners included a group the title cuts off before naming. Two hundred prisoners made this a major site in the southern system.

Large camps mattered because they concentrated men whose fates could be checked together. A location fix for 200 prisoners outweighed dozens of single sightings. Officials would guard such information carefully, since rescue and bombing plans both touched it. The file preserves the fix as reported, a rare large point on the southern prison map.
cia-0000010013:
Eight American helicopters were seen brought down, with four pilots killed, in a January 1973 report from a place the title cuts off. Helicopters flew every mission of the late war: assault, supply, rescue, and evacuation. A single report of eight losses implies a fierce action.

Mass-loss reports tested the accounting at its weakest point, matching airframes to crews across units. Some reported losses proved exaggerated; others matched dark days in squadron records. Analysts checked before any name was attached. This file preserves the claim as sighted, at the very start of the ceasefire year.
cia-0000011513:
When Egypt seized the Suez Canal in 1956, the CIA examined President Nasser and the wider Middle East situation that June and after. Nasser's move against the canal company defied Britain and France, the canal's owners. The paper treats the nationalization and Egypt's wider aims as one connected crisis for the region.

Analysts weighed Nasser's strength at home, his standing among Arabs, and his ties to Moscow. They also judged how Britain, France, and Israel might answer the seizure. Written as the crisis built toward the Suez war that fall, the study shows Washington reading the colonel's great gamble.
cia-0000012313:
To the Director of Central Intelligence went this Helms memo of January 1962, concerning military matters in the Penkovsky channel. The subject line names Military Thought, the Soviet journal the colonel's reporting so often drew upon. Summit memos in the crisis year carried the case to the one desk where all threads met.

The director's need for the colonel's latest had not dimmed with the new year. The file's high-water mark runs through pages like this one. For readers, the memo marks the spy's last full year of service, with his product still briefed at the peak.
cia-0000012413:
Meeting number thirty-two, September 22, 1961, keeps the Paris phase moving at pace. Two days after the phase opened, the debriefings were in full swing. They ran on French ground now, in new rooms with new cover. The Seine's city hosted secrets as readily as London had. Its hotels and meeting rooms served the same quiet purpose for the same extraordinary guest.

The record preserves the session's place in the autumn run. Questions deepened as the colonel's time in the West grew shorter. For readers, the page shows the operation's momentum surviving a change of capital, language, and police.
cia-0000013213:
An Australian and an American prisoner were seen together under Viet Cong escort, and a CIA report from November 1972 records the sighting. Men from both nations fought side by side in Vietnam, and the captured shared the same cells and the same roads north. Sighting reports like this one were gold for the accounting: a place, a date, two men alive on a given day.

The report fixes the pair in the file's record while the war was ending. Such sightings steadied families and checked the enemy's lists. For readers, the page keeps an allied chapter of the captivity story: the foreigners held as one group.
cia-0000013613:
Argentina, in one word, titles a CIA country brief from November 1967. The brief sketches the land's Cold War face in short form. The generals were in power by then, having seized the state the year before. Few in the capital said aloud that worse waited in the wings, but the storm before the storm can be sensed between the brief's compact lines.

Such briefs were the file's quick reference for a standing watch. This one catches Argentina between coups, prosperous and unsettled at once. For readers, it is the country in miniature: rich, proud, and ruled by soldiers.
cia-0000014713: Refuting Communist charges tied to the Rosenberg case is the task of a CIA paper dated January 5, 1953. The paper set out answers to claims spread by the Communist press. The case had become a contest of stories as much as of law. Papers like this armed officials for that public fight in the case's last months.
cia-0000015313: A letter to Thornton Page from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It takes up Leon Davidson's possible role, like its twin to Goudsmit. Sending the same thought to two men on one day marks a small campaign. Page, the astronomer, kept his seat in the saucer circle for years.
cia-0000029013:
Adolfo Calero led the Nicaraguan FDN, and a CIA record from 1984 cites him in the mining of ports. The mining of Nicaragua's harbors became one of the contra war's biggest scandals. The record ties the opposition leader's name to that operation in the agency's own files.

Readers see how the harbor mining story reached the record, with a named leader attached to it. The file is a small piece of a much larger fight over American support for the contras. It helps show why the mining caused such anger in Congress and in the press.
cia-0000036813:
Hanoi broadcast in English to American servicemen in South Vietnam, and a CIA record dated September 1, 1967 kept the item. The broadcast material names John Sydney McCain among its subjects. Radio aimed at enemy troops was a standard weapon of the war.

Broadcasts like this tried to weaken morale by speaking straight to soldiers in the field. Naming a captured pilot made the message personal for men who knew the risks. The file preserves one piece of that radio war, filed by the monitors who listened daily. Broadcasts were beamed at night, when lonely troops were most likely to be listening to the radio.
cia-0000045913:
In November 1956, CIA analysts finished an estimate asking what would follow if the United States joined the Baghdad Pact or stayed out of it. The pact was a defense alliance linking Turkey, Iraq, Britain, Pakistan, and Iran against Soviet pressure. Washington backed the alliance but had never signed as a full member.

The paper weighs both branches of the choice: what joining might gain, what it might cost, and how allies and rivals would react. Papers of this kind show how the agency gamed out big alliance decisions before presidents made them. The question faded within a few years, when Iraq quit the pact after its 1958 revolution.
cia-0000046513: A spokesman deflated the summer's big sensation in 1991: the supposed prisoner pilot in the famous photograph was, he said, a farmer. A CIA item dated September 1, 1991, kept the correction. The claim had raised the hopes of hundreds of families, which made its collapse a hard public moment. Few corrections in the whole affair traveled as fast.
cia-0000049013: A CIA item from 1981 reports the civilian extreme right in El Salvador as disorganized and short on armed activity at that moment. The lull surprised watchers used to steady death-squad violence. Reports of quiet mattered as much as reports of attacks, since each side's strength was guessed from just such signs.
cia-0000049113: President Duarte instructed his minister of justice in 1985 to open an investigation, and a CIA item preserves the instructions. A president ordering a probe was the easy half; courts and police doing the work was the other. The item survives among the Truth Commission records, a marker of intent filed before the outcome.
cia-0000049213: El Salvador's Foreign Ministry worried over the Jesuit case in 1991, and a CIA item preserves the concern, including the foreign minister's own belief about it. Diplomats carried the case's cost abroad: every capital they visited raised the murders, and asked what would be done. The item survives among the Truth Commission records.
cia-0000049413: A statement on El Salvador and certification issues before the Senate committee is preserved as declassified CIA document 0000049413, dated July 1, 1982. The heading is cut short in the catalog but names the setting plainly. Readers find a short record of a formal statement, tied to the certification debate that runs through several Salvadoran files.
cia-0000098713: Police officers spot UFO; rapid reaction force alerted is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098713, dated May 3, 1996. A semicolon joins the sighting to the alert in one breathless title. Readers find a short incident record unlike any neighbor, its subject an unidentified object sighting preserved in the agency's declassified files.
cia-0000109013: Soviet Forced Labor: an Update is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109013, dated November 1, 1985. The title marks a revisiting: an update on Soviet forced labor, not a first report. A system update with a near matching name shares the same date in the files. The brief record is a system update item from the autumn of 1985.
cia-0000112813: Untitled Supplmentary Report is the heading, with supplementary misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000112813, dated January 1, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then gives this short label. A supplementary report adds to a file already open, by its own name. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released in the wartime files as filed there.
cia-0000119213: Notice of Priority Change no. 6 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000119213, dated November 5, 1982. The title marks a numbered notice: the sixth change of a priority, in the heading's terms. What priority changed is not stated in the title itself at all. The brief record is an administrative notice item, filed in the autumn of 1982 as released.
cia-0000119713: A May 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Indonesia. The young republic faced revolts in its regions and disorder in its parliament. Washington counted the islands a Cold War prize, and the paper weighs where the country might turn. The republic was only a few years old, and its hold on the outer islands was still being tested when the forecast was written.
cia-0000124313: Dated July 1951, this CIA document addresses Communist treatment of United Nations prisoners, with the word treatment misspelled in the original heading. The error survived into the released file along with the substance. The paper records that treatment as the agency understood it then. Treatment reports fed the public argument over the war at home, where stories from the camps shaped how Americans judged both the enemy and the armistice talks.
cia-0000132213: From January 1991, situation report 530 covers political developments including a Baghdad radio call, the heading breaking off. Iraqi state radio served as Saddam's mouthpiece to the world during the crisis. The report notes what the broadcast said that day. Baghdad radio was heard worldwide through monitoring services, and a call noted in a sitrep usually meant a message aimed at Iraqis and enemies at once.
cia-0000132413:
A break in relations between the Castro government and the United States is weighed in a CIA report dated October 3, 1959. The report treats the rupture as a real possibility. The open question was when it might come, not whether feelings were souring.

Inside, analysts weigh the signs pointing toward a formal break. Relations did in fact end in January 1961, little more than a year later. For readers, the report is an early marker of how soon the agency saw the end coming. It shows the split being forecast while public ties between the two countries still held.
cia-0000132513:
Fallout for the United States from a failed attack on the Castro regime fills a CIA document dated April 5, 1961. Its headline calls the findings preliminary, and the title breaks off before finishing that word. The failed attack it names already lay in the past when analysts wrote.

The document assesses what the attempt cost and what it changed. Coming twelve days before the Bay of Pigs landing, it reads as a warning from a smaller failure. For readers, it shows the agency studying defeat in Cuba once already. The larger defeat that followed that month would echo many of the same lessons.
cia-0000132613: Haiti seeking closer ties with Cuba fills item 4 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 5, 1960. The pairing was an odd one: a harsh dictatorship courting a young revolution. Duvalier's Haiti was hunting for friends wherever they could be found that year. The short item reports the outreach and what Haiti hoped it might bring.
cia-0000135613: Brigade 2506's declassified Spanish files hold this document, dated 5 March 1961. The exile brigade was then in its last weeks of preparation for the April landing in Cuba. Nothing in the catalog record states what this document covers, who wrote it, or which unit it came from. It stands as a dated primary source in the original Spanish, released by the CIA, and any account of its contents must come from reading it rather than from its file title.
cia-0000135713: This Spanish text, dated 2 February 1961, belongs to the 2506 Brigade document set released by the CIA. The brigade was then in final training for the invasion of Cuba. The catalog title is generic, offering no subject, author, or unit. The document is kept in Spanish as a primary source. Its date places it among the last records of the training period, weeks before the brigade sailed.
cia-0000135813: The declassified CIA document dated 1 February 1954 takes up political action talks and debriefings, with the names in the heading deleted by the censors. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000135913: Filed on 4 May 1954, this CIA meeting record concerns a report of meetings with undisclosed persons, written as the situation began to change. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136113: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 4 April 1954, covers a review of a report that urged playing the waiting game, patience weighed against speed. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136313: Radio material from 1400 to 2300 hours is summarized in this 26 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. Castillo asked that Chajon attack Zacapa at 0800 the next day in a synchronized action, and that planes find and bomb enemy artillery near Cumbre Ingeniero. A delayed message from another operator called the situation very bad, with enemy units reported at Entre Rios, Morales, and Champona. The summary captures the confused final days of the Arbenz government.
cia-0000136613: A Spanish-language paper dated 4 January 1961, filed with the 2506 Brigade documents released by the CIA. It shares its date with companion items in the same stretch of the file. The exile brigade was in winter training for the April landing. The catalog names no subject for this document. Preserved in Spanish, it is part of the dense early-January layer of the brigade's surviving paperwork.
cia-0000136713: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, cataloged under an estimated date of 5 January 1960. That is strikingly early for this file, since the brigade was formed during 1960; the estimated flag in the title is part of the record and worth noting. No subject is named for the document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, dated by estimate to the brigade's first days or before them.
cia-0000137313: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA briefing for the National Security Council, the body that advises the president on security policy. Cuba dominated that council's agenda in 1960 as Castro's government turned toward Moscow and against Washington. A group of near-identical Cuba briefings from 1960 survives in these files, and the catalog does not set this one's contents apart from theirs. It is best read as part of that run: the steady flow of Cuba papers reaching the top of the U.S. government that year.
cia-06146213: CIA IN KOREA 1946 - 1965 VOLUME III, a CIA history. The Korea history. This file preserves that declassified volume. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
cia-06859713: What if Charles Taylor left Liberia's scene? The agency gamed out the strongman's departure. The West African question. It retains its place in time. This file preserves that declassified assessment. Its contents inform the historical record.
cieza-war-of-quito-markham-1913:
The War of Quito, in Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society translation of 1913, is Pedro Cieza de León's account of civil war among Peru's conquerors. After the Inca empire fell, the Pizarro and Almagro factions turned their swords on each other. Cieza, who knew Peru from years of travel in 1532 to 1550, wrote the record of that fratricidal struggle.

His narrative follows plots, marches, and battles around Quito with a chronicler's care for names and dates. Cieza stands out among the conquerors' writers for fairness: he blames greed on every side. The work shows the conquest eating its own children within a few years of triumph. It is documentary history of the first order.
commons-labor-and-administration-1913:
Commons gathered his papers as Labor and Administration in 1913. The pieces came out of his double life as a university scholar and a working reformer in Wisconsin. That state was then famous as a laboratory of democracy, testing new laws on work, safety, and insurance.

The essays treat the day-to-day problems of reform: joblessness, the arrival of immigrants, and the hard task of making labor laws work in practice. Commons writes about administration with respect, arguing that a good law badly run is a bad law. His high theory is tested here in committee rooms and factory inspections. The book shows the institutional school of economics at its most practical, and it helps explain how Wisconsin's experiments spread to the whole country.
commons-races-immigrants-america-1913:
Commons published Races and Immigrants in America in 1913, when immigration to the United States stood near its historic peak. An earlier version had appeared in 1907, and he revised it as the debate over new arrivals grew hotter. Commons studied the newcomers as an economist: who came, what work they found, and what they earned.

The book sorts immigrant groups by the terms his age used and asks how each fared in American industry and city life. Commons writes as a liberal of his time, sympathetic to the newcomers yet sharing some of the era's assumptions about race and fitness. That tension is part of the book's value now. It stands as a pioneering work of immigration history and a record of how a thoughtful reformer wrestled with the questions of his day.
conrad-chance-1913:
Chance, published in 1913, was the novel that finally made Conrad famous and sold in large numbers. His narrator Marlow returns, this time piecing together the fate of Flora de Barral from the talk of others.

Flora's father, a swindler whose crash ruined thousands, leaves her to the mercy of fortune hunters and a sinister captain husband. Marlow follows her through danger toward an unlikely rescue. The telling is layered, ironic, and full of Conrad's doubts about chance, gender, and respectability. Its success freed him from money worries for the first time in his writing life.
constitution-austria-2013: Austria's Constitution, rooted in 1920 and amended, frames its federal republic. It guards rights and neutrality. The Tower library holds the full text. It rebuilt after war. Ashes settled. Rights stood. Neutral held. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-croatia-2013: Croatia's 1990 Constitution, amended through 2013, frames its republic. It joined the EU. The Tower library holds the full text. It left Yugoslavia. War raged. Peace won. Europe welcomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-cyprus-2013: Cyprus' 1960 Constitution, amended through 2013, frames its divided republic. It splits Greek and Turk. The Tower library holds the full text. It bridged a split isle. Communities parted. Law straddled. Peace waited. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-fiji-2013: Fiji's 2013 Constitution, decreed after coups, frames its republic. It seeks equal votes. The Tower library holds the full text. It calmed coup cycles. Soldiers ruled. Decree ordered. Votes returned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-honduras-2013: Honduras' 1982 Constitution, amended through 2013, frames its republic. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It weathered coups. Soldiers came. Courts stood. Votes returned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-iceland-2013: Iceland's 1944 Constitution, amended through 2013, frames its republic. Crowds sought rewrite. The Tower library holds the full text. It left a king. Cod warmed. People voted. Change brewed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-israel-2013: Israel's Basic Laws, amended through 2013, serve as its constitution. No single text exists. The Tower library holds the full collection. It built a state. Wars raged. Laws layered. Democracy held. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-montenegro-2013: Montenegro's 2007 Constitution, amended 2013, frames its republic. It joined NATO. The Tower library holds the full text. It left Serbia. Mountains voted. Alliances shifted. West welcomed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
croce-philosophy-vico-1913:
The Philosophy of Giambattista Vico, published in English in 1913 in R. G. Collingwood's translation, is Croce's study of the Neapolitan thinker who first saw history as man's own creation. The translator was the young Collingwood, later a philosopher himself.

Croce presents Vico's new science: nations passing through ages of gods, heroes, and men, with poetry as the first form of thought. He credits Vico with founding the philosophy of history and of spirit. The study launched serious Vico studies in English almost single-handedly. It is also a meeting of minds: Croce finding his own system anticipated two centuries early.
crowley-book-4-part-2-1913:
Part two of Book Four, printed in 1913, turns from stillness to the tools of rite. Book 4, Part II: Magick gives the first theory of Crowley's ceremonial system in full. Mary D'Este Sturges again worked with him on the text.

The temple, the circle, the triangle, and the wand, cup, sword, and pantacle are each defined and placed. Crowley tells what each tool means and why the plan of the rite takes its shape. The book made his magic a teachable craft with clear rules and reasons. It is the working mate to part one's mystic training.
crowley-book-of-lies-1913:
Ninety-three short chapters make up Crowley's Book of Lies, printed in 1913. Each chapter is a paradox, a jest, a riddle, or a brief shock of prose or verse. The book is also called, in jest, Breaks, and its full title warns the reader not to trust it.

Crowley said each chapter held a truth that flat statement would spoil. Thelemites have read the squibs as doctrine, as humor, and as traps for the too-literal mind. Few of his books have drawn so much commentary line by line. It remains the central Thelemic book of wit and contradiction.
dawson-woodward-piltdown-1913:
Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward presented the Piltdown finds to the Geological Society in 1913. Gravel pits at Piltdown in Sussex had produced skull pieces and a jaw. They named the supposed creature Eoanthropus dawsoni, Dawson's dawn man.

The authors describe a big-brained skull paired with an ape-like jaw. Britain celebrated a first Englishman of great antiquity. Forty years later, tests exposed the bones as a planted forgery. The paper remains history's most famous scientific fraud, read now as a warning about wishful thinking. Schoolbooks repeated the dawn-man story for the next forty years.
deleuze-histoire-critique-magnetisme-181:
J. P. F. Deleuze published his Critical History of Animal Magnetism in 1813. By then the quarrel over Mesmer's fluid had run for thirty years. Deleuze set out to survey every tract written for and against, and to weigh the whole affair with care.

He was a believer, but a judicious one, and his history reads fair to both sides. Mesmerism's rise, its royal trials, and its fall all find their place. Deleuze then traces its quieter afterlife in medical practice. His book remains the pivotal history of the debate. Anyone studying the episode starts with his summing-up of the evidence.
devisser-dragon-in-china-and-japan-1913:
Marinus Willem de Visser was a Dutch sage of the East. His The Dragon in China and Japan came out in 1913. The book is a full study of the dragon in the faith and tales of both lands. De Visser worked from the old texts in their own tongues.

In China the dragon brings rain, rules seas, and marks the throne of kings. In Japan the beast takes new forms from the lore of India and China. Tales of dragon kings, gems, and maids fill the rich text. The book is the great store of dragon lore of the East in English.
doe-osti-3013553-neutrinoless-double-bet: Xe-136 got double-beta-decayed, and this DOE final studies neutrinoless structure. The pages detail the scientific findings. The physicists get their closeout. The decay was double beta. The closeout was physicist. The isotope was Xe-136. The studies were nuclear.
doyle-poison-belt-1913:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Poison Belt in 1913. Professor Challenger calls his old crew to his home with tanks of air in hand. Earth, he says, is about to cross a belt of bad ether in space. The crew of The Lost World meets once more at his side.

One by one, the folk of the world fall in a death like sleep. Cars crash, trains halt, and towns stand still as the hours pass. The crew watch from a sealed room as the hush takes all lands. The tale is a stark end of world piece in the Challenger line.
dunbar-complete-poems-1913:
Paul Laurence Dunbar's complete poems were gathered in 1913, after his early death. Dunbar wrote both in standard English and in Black dialect, as it was then called. The volume includes Lyrics of Lowly Life, his best-known early book. An introduction by W. D. Howells, who championed Dunbar, opens the collection.

The poems cover love, nature, faith, work, and the pain of slavery's memory. Some are light songs, while others carry grief and protest. Dunbar was the first Black American poet to win wide national fame. This full collection lets readers judge his whole range. It remains the standard way to read him.
edgar-great-pyramid-passages-vol2-1913:
John Edgar and his brother Morton measured the Great Pyramid passage by passage. Volume two of Great Pyramid Passages and Chambers appeared in 1913. The first volume, from 1910, began their survey of the monument. The brothers worked in the years when Charles Taze Russell's movement prized such measures.

Their records give lengths, angles, and chambers in dense detail. Photographs and plans support the text of the survey. The set became the measurement canon of the Russell era pyramid studies. Believers read prophecy in its numbers; engineers checked its care. Volume two completes the set as planned. It preserves a strange, devoted piece of fieldwork.
elias-artista-redivivus-oder-das-buch-vo: Elias Artista redivivus, 1913. The revived Elias. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-13: The thirteenth volume ranges over Montaigne's later reflections. He considers vanity, glory, and the shortness of human life. The style is looser now, the wisdom deeper and kinder. An old friend thinking out loud by the fire.
europmc-pmc10021213: Mulchandani and co-authors chart global trends in the use of antibiotics and similar drugs in farm animals from 2020 to 2030. Their study maps how much of these drugs food production uses now and where use is heading. The work speaks to worries that heavy farm use feeds drug resistance that can reach people.
europmc-pmc10129313:
Ruffolo, Chu, Mahajan, and Gray present a deep learning method that predicts antibody structures fast and accurately, in a 2023 study. Antibodies are proteins that bind targets with great precision, and they have become key drugs and lab tools. Their grip comes from six flexible loops whose shapes are hard to predict.

The team trained their model on a huge set of natural antibody sequences and shapes. The method predicts loop shapes quickly for new antibodies. Faster, reliable shapes help scientists design better antibody drugs without slow lab work for every candidate.
europmc-pmc10211313:
Lv and colleagues review obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in a 2023 paper, covering its mechanisms and treatment approaches. In this disorder, the airway narrows or closes during sleep, so breathing stops again and again through the night. It is increasingly common worldwide, above all in middle-aged and older adults, and it strains the heart and brain.

The review explains why airways collapse and what the broken sleep does to the body. It surveys treatments, from air pressure masks to surgery and oral devices. The paper is a full guide to a common, under-treated disorder.
europmc-pmc10356613:
Lake and a huge team built a cell atlas of the human kidney in 2023. The KPMP Consortium was among the groups behind the work. The team tested over 400,000 cells and cell cores from 45 healthy donors and 48 patients. Tests read gene activity in single cells and mapped cells in place inside tissue.

The atlas names 51 main cell types, some rare and some never seen before. It also names 28 cell states seen across kidney parts. Those states cover growth, good repair, poor repair, change, and decline after injury. Lake tied some repair signs to a later drop in kidney function. Maps of about 1.2 million tissue zones linked the states to immune activity nearby.
europmc-pmc10481913:
Dijkstra led a five-year check of the RAPIDO trial in 2023, with Collaborative Investigators across many centres. The trial tested two care paths for rectal cancer before surgery. One path used short radiation, then chemo, then surgery. The standard path used long radiation with chemo, then surgery. In all, 920 patients joined the trial.

At a median of 5.6 years, local failure split the paths. Dijkstra reports failure in 12% of the short-path group and 8% of the standard group. Return of cancer near the first site hit 10% versus 6%. Survival after such failure was much the same in both arms. The short path still cut spread to distant sites, so the team urges finer tuning of it.
europmc-pmc10730913:
Janesick and co-authors joined three gene mapping tools in 2023, with the 10x Development Teams, to read a tumour in fine detail. Each tool alone gives one view: single-cell genes, spatial genes, or targeted reads in place. The team ran all three on large human breast cancer sections kept in wax. The joint view aimed to catch how regions of a tumour differ.

Merged data split tumour zones by their gene marks. Janesick found signs tied to the step toward invasive cancer, the point where it breaks its bounds. Rare cells sat at the muscle-like border that pens the tumour in. Those border cells may hold the key to spread. Each tool alone gave part of the tale; the merge gave the depth.
europmc-pmc10963913:
Riesco and Trujillo update the rules for naming microbes from their genome data in this 2024 paper. Prokaryotes are single-celled life forms without a nucleus, such as bacteria. Naming them once rested on looks and traits, which gave a poor view of their true variety. DNA reading changed that, and genome-based naming now defines species and higher ranks too.

The paper revises the minimal standards set in 2018 for using genome data in this naming work. It adapts measures such as average amino acid identity, which compares proteins between two genomes, and the share of proteins two genomes hold in common. Data and code behind the checks are posted openly online. The authors say fresh standards are vital as sequencing tools and databases keep growing. Outdated rules, they warn, would let naming drift out of step with the data.
europmc-pmc12159213:
Xu, Pang, and Fan reviewed mitochondria in stress, swelling, and aging in 2025. Mitochondria are the energy centers inside cells. They carry their own small set of DNA. When they fail, cells face deep trouble.

Failure sparks excess reactive oxygen, a form of chemical stress. It also triggers swelling responses and cell death signals. Similar changes build up as tissues age. Xu casts mitochondria as hubs linking stress, inflammation, and aging. Fixing their function could open new treatment paths. The review spans mechanisms to early therapy ideas. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1297513:
Patwardhan, Warude, Pushpangadan, and Bhatt compared two ancient medical systems in 2005. Ayurveda is Indian medicine, and TCM is Chinese medicine. Both remain living traditions with global interest rising. Herbal drug monitoring and regulation efforts are underway.

China has promoted its therapies with stronger research backing. Ayurveda still needs a wider scientific evidence base, they argue. Shared principles and differences are laid out side by side. Success factors for global markets get direct discussion. Patwardhan urges evidence building without losing traditional foundations. Side effects and drug cost drive much of the new interest. Both schools of care are still in wide use in Asia and in the West. Old texts sit at the root of both of them.
europmc-pmc1679813:
Fungi get their own family tree built from whole genomes. Fitzpatrick and co-authors constructed it in 2006 from 42 complete fungal genomes, covering 345,829 genes. Older trees rested on one or a few genes.

Two methods agreed closely: a supertree merging 4,805 single-gene trees, and a joined alignment of 153 universal genes. One merging method suffered long-branch attraction, a known artifact; the other stayed immune. Within the largest fungal phylum, the tree resolved two great sub-groups and placed the Leotiomycetes as closest kin to the Sordariomycetes. Fitzpatrick offers the tree as scaffolding for comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc1796613:
Lartillot, Brinkmann and Philippe showed in 2007 how a better evolution model can fix a known tree-building error. The error is long-branch attraction, where fast-evolving species get wrongly grouped together. In animal family trees, fast-changing nematodes and flatworms had been placed either at the base of other bilaterians or inside the protostomes, depending on the outgroup used.

The team compared a standard model, called WAG, which treats all sites in a protein alike, with a mixture model called CAT. CAT lets each site favor its own set of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. With CAT, the false grouping largely vanished. Cross-checks showed CAT also fit the data better and matched the true level of repeated change. Site differences, they argue, must be modeled for reliable trees.
europmc-pmc1867813:
Rosenberg and colleagues reviewed malignant hyperthermia in 2007, a dangerous inherited reaction to common anesthetics. In susceptible people, gases such as halothane and sevoflurane, or the relaxant succinylcholine, trigger runaway muscle metabolism. Reactions strike between one in 5,000 and one in 100,000 anesthesias, while the underlying gene faults may affect one in 3,000 people.

The classic signs are steep fever, racing heart and breathing, excess carbon dioxide, acid buildup, rigid muscles, and muscle breakdown. Untreated, the syndrome is often fatal. The root fault is uncontrolled calcium release inside muscle cells, which burns through energy stores and ruptures the cell membrane. A rise in exhaled carbon dioxide is the earliest clinical clue. Inheritance in humans follows a dominant pattern, so one faulty copy suffices.
europmc-pmc1885213:
Ayoub, Hayashi and co-authors read in 2007 the first complete genes for spider dragline silk. Dragline silk beats nearly all natural and manmade materials for combined strength and toughness. Making it artificially is a major goal, yet earlier designs used only short, partial gene copies.

The team sequenced the full genes for the two proteins, MaSp1 and MaSp2, that form the black widow's dragline. Each gene carries one enormous coding stretch over 9,000 letters long, translated into a highly repetitive protein. Comparing the repeats showed that selection plus recombination within and between genes shapes these modular proteins. The flanking non-coding regions were strikingly conserved between the two genes and held candidate control elements. The full blueprint now exists for anyone engineering true spider silk.
europmc-pmc1978513:
Parekkadan and colleagues tested a new approach in 2007 for fulminant hepatic failure, a sudden and deadly loss of liver function. They used molecules released by mesenchymal stem cells, which are bone marrow cells that calm immune activity. Instead of transplanting cells, they gave only the liquid the cells had grown in. Rats with liver failure received that liquid, or blood filtered through a device holding the cells.

Both forms gave a clear survival benefit in the rats. Benefit depended on cell number, and too many cells removed the gain. Treated livers showed far less immune cell invasion and cell death. Tracking studies showed immune cells were diverted away from the liver. The active part bound to heparin, pointing to chemokines, signals that guide immune cells.
europmc-pmc2043013:
Cragg and co-workers traced in 2007 how the lung cancer drug gefitinib kills tumour cells. Gefitinib blocks EGFR, a growth signal receptor that is mutated in some non-small cell lung cancers. How blocking it causes tumours to shrink was unclear. The team used biochemical and genetic studies in human lung cancer cell lines, including gene silencing to test each step.

Gefitinib triggered the intrinsic death pathway, centred on mitochondria, the cell's energy centres. It activated BAX and released cytochrome c, starting the caspase enzyme cascade. The drug rapidly raised BIM, a pro-death protein, through gene activity and protein stabilising. Blocking the MEK-ERK signal path prevented that rise. Silencing BIM stopped the killing, and a BH3-mimicking drug, ABT-737, made gefitinib kill more strongly.
