europmc-pmc2202913:
Coll, Farooqi and O'Rahilly reviewed in 2007 how hormones control food intake. Body weight stays remarkably steady over years despite daily swings in eating and activity. That stability implies precise matching of intake to energy use. Circulating peptides and steroids act on the hypothalamus, brain stem and autonomic nerves to adjust appetite. The review synthesises recent evidence on those signals.

The hormones come from three main sites: fat cells, the gut and the pancreas. Early rat experiments showed the hypothalamus is essential, since damage there caused overeating or refusal to eat. Joined-animal experiments proved a blood-borne satiety factor exists and needs an intact hypothalamus. The molecules behind those classic observations took over forty years to identify. Leptin, the fat-cell hormone, leads the modern account.
europmc-pmc2214813:
Hromádka, Deweese and Zador recorded brain activity in awake rats in 2008 to learn how the auditory cortex represents sounds. Earlier work used anaesthetised animals, where responses looked mainly brief. The team used cell-attached recording, a method that samples neurons regardless of their activity. Rats heard tones, frequency sweeps, noise bursts and natural sounds while recordings were taken from primary auditory cortex.

The population response proved sparse, meaning only a few neurons fire strongly at any moment. Stimuli typically drove high firing rates, over 20 spikes per second, in under five percent of neurons. Some neurons stayed almost silent, below 0.01 spikes per second. Others exceeded 50 spikes per second. Overall firing followed a lognormal distribution. The results support a model where most neurons rest while small, shifting subsets carry the representation.
europmc-pmc2234413:
Hallez and colleagues reviewed methods in 2007 for solving the EEG forward problem in source analysis. Electroencephalography records brain waves at the scalp, and researchers want to locate their sources. The forward problem calculates electrode voltages from a known brain source. Solving it is required before the inverse problem, finding sources from measurements, can be attempted. The review is aimed at newcomers to the field.

Brain signals arise from post-synaptic currents in pyramidal neurons, modelled by Poisson's equation. Simple three-shell spherical head models allow exact solutions. Realistic head shapes from 3D medical images need numerical methods: boundary element, finite element and finite difference approaches are compared. The last two handle direction-dependent tissue conductivity easily. Reciprocity tricks and iterative solvers speed the large calculations involved.
europmc-pmc2323613:
Alonso-Magdalena and colleagues studied in 2008 how the hormone estrogen affects insulin-making cells in the pancreas. These beta cells make and release insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. Two estrogen receptors, named ER alpha and ER beta, sit in these cells, but their roles were unclear.

The team showed both receptors are present in beta cells. Long exposure to natural estrogen raised insulin content, insulin gene activity, and insulin release, without adding new cells. The plastic chemical bisphenol-A, a widespread pollutant that mimics estrogen, did the same at low doses. Tests in mice lacking each receptor pointed to ER alpha as the one responsible. Its effect ran through a signal pathway called ERK1/2.
europmc-pmc2394813:
Long, Vagin, Young, and Murshudov presented an automated crystallography pipeline in 2008. Crystallographers work out protein shapes from X-ray patterns, and one standard trick is molecular replacement: using a known similar structure as a starting model. The archive of known structures then held over 40,000 entries and grew by thousands a year.

Their pipeline, BALBES, searches that archive through a rebuilt database organised by protein domains and by how pieces assemble into multi-part units. Given only the X-ray data and the protein's letter sequence, it picks candidate models and solves the replacement problem with no human steering. Older domain libraries, built for general biology, had proved awkward for this job, so the team redesigned the hierarchy for it. They offered BALBES as a fully automatic route from raw data to a starting structure.
europmc-pmc2410013:
Satagopan and colleagues explained a trap in survival statistics in 2004. The trap is competing risks: a patient may meet a different event first, which removes any chance of the event being studied. Treating that patient as merely censored, the standard Kaplan-Meier habit, distorts the answer.

Their paper shows how to estimate cumulative incidence, the chance of the event by a given time, while handling rival events properly. They work through two published data sets, computing incidence both ways. The Kaplan-Meier figures overshot the true incidence, because they pretend rival-event patients could still have the studied event later. The corrected method counts them as permanently out of the running. The authors addressed the note to clinical researchers, stressing that the choice of method changes reported risks in real studies.
europmc-pmc2584113:
Hulsen, de Vlieg, and Alkema built a web application called BioVenn in 2008 for drawing area-proportional Venn diagrams from biological lists. Genomics projects produce many lists of gene or protein identifiers, and researchers want to see overlaps at a glance. In a proper Venn diagram the circle and overlap sizes match the list sizes, but no existing tool tied that to biological databases.

A user pastes two or three lists and presses submit. The result is a diagram whose areas are proportional to the overlaps. Colours and text size adjust through the page, labels drag into place, and the picture exports as SVG or PNG image files. BioVenn also lists the identifiers in each subset. It links recognised ones to their source databases. It converts between Affymetrix, EntrezGene, and Ensembl identifiers.
europmc-pmc2702413:
Peng and colleagues published a United States study in 2009 on which parts of fine particle pollution send people to hospital. Fine particles are a mix of chemicals from traffic, diesel, wood smoke, and other sources. The question was whether some parts of that mix are more harmful than others.

They used daily hospital and air data from 2000 to 2006 for 119 urban areas and 12 million older adults on Medicare, which is public health cover for older people. Elemental carbon, a soot-like part, was linked to same-day heart admissions. Organic carbon matter was linked to same-day lung admissions, while other parts showed no clear link.
europmc-pmc2772813:
Comas, Homolka, Niemann, and Gagneux tested in 2009 how well standard genotyping methods reconstruct the family tree of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a pathogen with very little DNA diversity. Such monomorphic bacteria are usually typed by mobile or repeated elements: spoligotyping and MIRU-VNTR typing in this case. Using full sequences of eighty-nine genes from a global strain collection as the gold standard, they compared the trees each method produced.

Sequence-based trees were highly consistent and strongly supported, with almost no conflicting signal. Trees from spoligotyping and fifteen-locus MIRU-VNTR clashed with them, distorted by convergent evolution, where unrelated strains gain look-alike patterns. The twenty-four-locus version did better but still missed some lineages, and its power varied by lineage. They advise defining lineages by robust sequence markers and tailoring repeat-based typing to each lineage.
europmc-pmc2777313:
Capra and co-authors introduced in 2009 ConCavity, an algorithm that predicts where small molecules bind on a protein by combining evolutionary conservation with three-dimensional structure. Knowing a protein's functional sites is a key step toward knowing what it does. Earlier methods used sequence or structure alone. Their direct comparison showed the two approaches carry largely complementary information.

ConCavity merges conservation scores with a search for pockets on the protein surface. In large tests on diverse single- and multi-chain structures, it beat existing methods at finding both whole binding pockets and the individual residues that line them. It also reached top performance on catalytic sites and drug binding pockets. Blending the two evidence types, they conclude, improves on either alone and sharpens the link between conservation and function.
europmc-pmc2781113:
Schnoes, Brown, Dodevski, and Babbitt measured in 2009 how often public protein databases mislabel what an enzyme does. Most sequences in these databases were never tested in a lab; computers assign their functions by similarity, and errors can spread. The team audited four major databases using thirty-seven enzyme families with strong experimental records, grouped into six superfamilies.

The hand-curated Swiss-Prot database showed almost no errors. The other databases, including GenBank NR and TrEMBL, averaged error rates from five to sixty-three percent across the superfamilies. In ten families, over eighty percent of entries in some database were wrong. Errors grew in one database between 1993 and 2005, and most came from overpredicting, assigning a specific job the protein does not have. The authors suggest fixes for the systematic causes they found.
europmc-pmc2807913:
Nishimura and colleagues hunted in 2010 for plant proteins that work with ABI1, a brake on signaling by the drought hormone abscisic acid, called ABA. ABA helps plants survive dry spells and keeps seeds dormant. Because backup copies hide many signals from gene studies, the team fished out ABI1's partners directly from Arabidopsis plants.

Nine of the fourteen members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family, the plant's ABA sensors, bound ABI1 most strongly in living tissue. The grip between one sensor, PYR1, and ABI1 tightened within five minutes of ABA treatment. Plants missing four sensor genes barely closed their leaf pores in response to ABA, hard proof the sensors matter for water saving.
europmc-pmc2826413:
Krebiehl and colleagues showed in 2010 that losing a protein called DJ-1, a rare cause of inherited Parkinson disease, gums up both the cell's power units and its recycling system. DJ-1 was known to guard cells against oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen. The team used cells from knockout mice and from human carriers of a faulty DJ-1 version.

Without DJ-1, mitochondria breathed poorly, leaked more reactive oxygen, and changed shape in set ways. Recycling through lysosomes, the cell's digestion sacs, ran slowly at baseline, so defective mitochondria piled up instead of being cleared. A signaling protein called ERK2 was also underactive. The work ties DJ-1 directly to keeping mitochondria sound through steady housekeeping.
europmc-pmc2831913:
Clougherty reviewed the evidence in 2010 on whether air pollution hits male and female lungs differently, and whether the split is social or biological. Studies repeatedly find effects differing by sex, but the pattern is patchy and the reasons tangled: men and women differ in jobs, chores, and hormones, all at once.

Across adult studies, stronger effects more often appeared in women, especially in older groups and in studies using home-based exposure measures. Among children, boys looked more affected early in life and girls later in childhood. The author offers a framework borrowed from gender analysis, which separates social roles from body traits, to help future studies pull the two apart.
europmc-pmc2852313:
Emsley, Lohkamp, Scott, and Cowtan presented Coot in 2010, the graphics program crystallographers use to build and check molecular models by hand. Automated builders can draft a protein chain into an electron-density map, but scientists must inspect, fix, and validate the result interactively, especially at low resolution where errors creep in.

Coot displays atomic models, contoured density maps, and helper objects in a rotatable three-dimensional view built for ease of learning. Its tools cover model building, real-space refinement, and validation checks, with scripting access to nearly everything underneath. The paper surveys the program's features and design choices, including its library foundations, and traces how development has shifted emphasis toward validation as automatic building has improved.
europmc-pmc2855713:
Wang, Henning, and Heber showed in 2010 that two of the most popular lab tests for cell growth quietly misread green tea's star compound. Laboratories reported wildly varying potency for EGCG against cancer cells, and the team suspected the measurement method itself. They compared five assays on prostate and breast cancer cells treated with the compound.

Tests counting DNA or energy molecules agreed closely with direct counting. The dye tests MTT and MTS, which read mitochondrial activity, overestimated surviving cells and made EGCG look about half as potent as it truly was. A different plant compound, apigenin, showed no such distortion. The authors warn that assay choice must match a compound's chemistry when judging botanical extracts.
europmc-pmc2891813:
Oliveira-Ferreira and colleagues overviewed in 2010 the state of malaria in Brazil, a country that cut the disease hugely yet cannot finish it. Annual cases fell from around six million in the early 1940s to about three hundred six thousand registered in 2009. The main mosquito carrier lives across most of the country, but transmission now clings almost entirely to the Amazon Basin.

Disorderly settlement of the Amazon from the 1960s onward pushed cases back up and keeps them there. The milder parasite Plasmodium vivax causes over four fifths of cases and most of the economic burden, while the dangerous falciparum causes most of the rest. Worryingly, vivax has begun producing unusual severe complications in recent years, challenging its benign reputation.
europmc-pmc2930213:
Summers and colleagues reviewed neutrophil kinetics, the birth, movement, and removal of the most common white blood cells, in a 2010 article. Neutrophils kill germs but live only hours in the blood, so the body must replace them at a huge daily rate.

The review covers release from bone marrow, guided in part by signals acting through the CXCR4 receptor, and the split between freely flowing cells and a slower marginated pool. It also covers how aged cells are cleared and how stress or inflammation disturbs the balance. Too much neutrophil activity can injure healthy tissue.
europmc-pmc2936113:
Aggleton and co-authors reviewed the linked pathways between the hippocampus and the front part of the thalamus in 2010. These brain areas connect through several routes, and together they seem central to remembering past events.

Evidence from brain studies, patient work, and electrical tests shows parallel direct and indirect streams, the indirect ones passing through the mammillary bodies. The streams often push activity in opposite directions while staying partly separate. Damage at one site can disturb distant partners across the network. The system matters most for vivid recollection rather than simple feelings of familiarity.
europmc-pmc2936313:
Cole reviewed the biology of human chorionic gonadotropin, better known as hCG, in a 2010 article. The name covers four separate molecules, each made by different cells and each doing distinct work.

Standard hCG from placental tissue supports progesterone output, blood vessel growth in the womb, and quieting of the mother's immune response near the placenta. A sugar-heavy form drives growth and invasion of placental cells during implantation. A free fragment appears in many cancers outside the placenta, while a pituitary form comes from hormone cells in the brain. Each variant gets its own account.
europmc-pmc3000813:
Fiehn and co-authors profiled blood chemicals in obese African-American women with and without type 2 diabetes in a 2010 study. Insulin resistance disturbs the handling of many fuels at once, and mapping that disturbance may expose early markers.

Measuring several hundred fasting metabolites, they extracted components tracking closely with a long-term blood sugar score. Diabetes samples ran high in certain amino acids and their by-products, a hydroxy acid, long-chain fats, and sugar derivatives. Two amino acids climbed steadily with worse sugar control and matched a marker of fuel burning. The pattern hints the cell's central furnace runs inefficiently.
europmc-pmc3017113:
Gao led a large team sequencing two Metarhizium fungi used as living insecticides in a 2011 comparative genome study. One species attacks many insects while its cousin targets only grasshoppers and locusts, a contrast written somewhere in their genes.

The two genomes proved highly aligned in structure, with signs the genus descends from plant-associated fungi. Both devote an unusually large share of genes to secreted proteins, many with no known match. The broad attacker carries expanded families for cutting insect armour, detoxifying, and making toxins, matching its wider menu, while the specialist shows a genome defence trick the generalist lacks.
europmc-pmc3053313:
Izawa and Shadmehr asked in 2011 whether the brain learns movements from two kinds of error at once. One kind is sensory errors, where a movement feels different than predicted. The other is reward errors, where an outcome is worse than hoped. Volunteers adapted their reaching while the quality of visual feedback was varied. The team watched how learning spread to nearby movements and whether predictions themselves changed.

With crisp feedback, learning ran almost entirely on sensory errors. That learning rewrote the brain's predictions and spread broadly to neighboring movements. As feedback grew fuzzy, reward errors took a larger share. Reward driven learning changed the movement just as much, but left predictions untouched and spread only narrowly. The two signatures were so distinct that a person's learning style could be read from them. The work suggests rehabilitation and training should match feedback quality to the learning route they want.
europmc-pmc3156713:
Juliette Stehlé and colleagues recorded every close contact in a French primary school in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. How children mix drives how respiratory infections spread, yet hard numbers were scarce. Pupils and teachers wore radio badges for two days, logging tens of thousands of face-to-face encounters among more than two hundred people.

Each child averaged several hundred contacts a day with dozens of others, totalling nearly three hours of close time, though most single contacts were brief. Contact concentrated inside each class, with children spending about three times longer with classmates than with other classes. The resulting contact matrix, split by class and age, gives disease modellers a realistic alternative to assuming everyone mixes evenly, and helps rank measures such as class closure.
europmc-pmc3228813:
A. P. Jason de Koning and colleagues argued that far more of the human genome is repetitive than textbooks say, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. The standard way to find transposable elements, matching DNA against known element sequences, had credited repeats with about half the genome. Their alternative method hunts for clusters of abundant short fragments related to one another.

The new approach predicted hundreds of millions of additional repetitive bases, pushing the estimate to roughly two-thirds of the genome. Detailed checks on two common element families showed the standard tool misses even moderately long fragments, while the new method stays sensitive down to small pieces. They also identified large amounts of previously unannotated element sequence. The message is that genome annotation needs combined, probability-aware methods.
europmc-pmc3270013:
Ravi Patel and Mukesh Jain introduced the NGS QC Toolkit, software for cleaning next-generation sequencing data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Modern sequencers pour out enormous datasets, and bad reads can poison every downstream result, so quality control is essential. Fast, efficient tools were needed to handle the volume.

The toolkit is written in Perl as a free, standalone, open-source application. It checks quality and filters for high-grade data. It serves the two dominant platforms of the day, Roche 454 and Illumina machines. Extra utilities convert between sequence formats, trim reads, and compute statistics. Users can set their own thresholds at each step rather than accepting defaults. The authors expect the toolkit to improve the reliability of analyses built on sequencing data across many laboratories.
europmc-pmc3356313:
Agustí and the ECLIPSE investigators asked whether lasting inflammation throughout the body marks out a distinct group of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The large ECLIPSE cohort followed patients for three years with repeated blood measurements, letting the team separate persistent inflammation from temporary spikes.

Of 1,755 patients, about thirty percent showed no systemic inflammation while sixteen percent stayed inflamed, based on a panel of six blood biomarkers. Despite similar lung damage, the persistently inflamed group died at far higher rates and suffered more exacerbations. The authors identify this as a distinct COPD phenotype that might benefit from targeted anti-inflammatory treatment.
europmc-pmc3418213:
Steinsbekk and co-authors pooled trials in 2012 on group-based self-management education for type 2 diabetes, compared with routine care. Group courses are popular because they cost less and let patients learn from each other. The review gathered twenty-one randomized trials with several thousand participants followed for at least six months.

Blood sugar control improved in the group courses at six months, a year, and two years, and fasting glucose fell too. Knowledge of diabetes and self-management skills rose clearly, and patients felt more empowered early on. Satisfaction and body weight improved at one year, while death rates, blood pressure, and blood fats did not differ. Quality of life results were too mixed to judge. Group teaching, they conclude, earns its place.
europmc-pmc3473013:
Kim and co-authors tested how a high-fat diet stirs inflammation through gut bacteria, in a 2012 PLoS ONE mouse study. Obesity travels with low-grade inflammation, but where that inflammation starts was unknown. Mice ate a high-fat or low-fat diet for eight weeks, and the team tracked gut microbes, gut leakiness, and inflammatory signals in body and colon.

The high-fat diet shifted gut microbes, raised a bacterial toxin called endotoxin in blood and stool, and loosened the gut wall's seals. Mice bred without the toxin sensor TLR4 still gained weight on the diet, but gained far less fat and showed no rise in inflammatory signals. Kim's group concludes the diet drives inflammation by raising endotoxin that acts through that sensor.

file-no-113: File No. 113, Émile Gaboriau's detective novel. The numbered file. This book preserves that mystery. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
frobenius-the-voice-of-africa-1913:
Leo Frobenius led an expedition across the Western Sudan in 1910 to 1912 and told it in The Voice of Africa, published in 1913. The German ethnologist sought the roots of African civilization among Yoruba, Nupe, and Jukun peoples. Sacred art, bronzes, and temples amazed him, and he carried word of them to Europe.

Frobenius argued that Africa held high cultures of great age, a claim Europe resisted hearing. His finds and photographs changed how the West saw African art forever. The book stands as both travel record and manifesto, the voice of a continent speaking through its shrines.
frost-boys-will-1913:
Robert Frost published A Boy's Will in 1913, his first book of poems. Frost was an American farmer and teacher who had moved to England. The poems speak in a young man's voice about nature, love, and finding his own path. Into My Own and Storm Fear are among the best-known pieces.

Many poems pair a plain scene with a quiet doubt or hope. Frost uses traditional forms but a fresh, spoken tone. The book won notice in England and helped launch his career back home. Readers can hear his later themes starting here: work, weather, isolation, and choice. It is a modest and lovely debut.
frus-1861-d113:
Mr. Jones wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 July 1861. The dispatch is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Jones wrote on the eve of Bull Run, the war's first great battle. His July report is the second of his two papers in this file. Read with his April note, it brackets the season in which the short war became a long one. His two reports, spring and summer, frame the war's first season from one post. One post, two seasons: the frame shows how much the war had changed by July.
frus-1861-d13:
Norman Judd, the American minister to Prussia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 July 1861. The dispatch is document 13 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd was a friend of Lincoln's from Illinois politics, sent to Berlin that spring. Prussia was rising as the strong power of north Germany, and its stance mattered. Judd's reports told Washington how the Berlin court read the American war in its first summer. Berlin watched the war through the lens of its own struggle with Austria and France. Berlin's cool tone suited the Union, which asked no more than strict fairness.
frus-1861-d213:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Marsh on 21 June 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 213 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d113:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 31 July 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 113 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d13:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 February 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 13 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d213:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 5 April 1862, in a note printed as Document 213 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, received it at the legation.

Early April 1862 brought the great battle of Shiloh in Tennessee and the start of the campaign against Richmond. Each swing of the war changed the odds that Europe might step in, so envoys traded paper at a fast rate. A note from this week sits in the file as part of that quick, watchful exchange. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d313:
On 20 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton another dispatch, printed as Document 313 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark the post-battle rush.

Seward wrote on the eve of Lincoln's emancipation announcement, which he had helped shape and knew was coming. The proclamation would give the war a cause that European publics could cheer. His letters to Paris in these days prepared his envoy for the new ground, on which defending the Union also meant defending freedom. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d413:
From Madrid on 9 November 1861, Carl Schurz sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 413 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message.

Schurz wrote in the weeks when Britain, France, and Spain had just agreed to act together in Mexico, a move that worried Washington deeply. As minister in Madrid he could watch Spanish motives at close range. His reports home fed the Union's effort to keep the European powers separate and neutral. The dispatch is part of the first season of that long campaign, before Schurz left Spain for army service.
frus-1862-d513:
Two days after Pike's latest report was dated, on 8 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 513 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The crossed dates are the Atlantic mail at work: each man wrote from news the other had not seen. Seward's August orders to The Hague kept up the standing themes of Dutch neutrality and colonial ports. They also kept up the Union's refusal to treat the rebellion as a nation. Pike's replies, arriving a month later, show how those themes landed. The pair of files, order and report interleaved, is the true shape of the record the volume preserves. It is a slow conversation. Two governments carried it on in good faith across an ocean.
frus-1862-d613:
The Danish file opens on 22 January 1862 with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister at Copenhagen. It is Document 613 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Denmark was a small maritime kingdom. Its ports and its Sound dues touched Baltic trade. Wood, a New York lawyer, held the post through the war. Seward's opening order set out the Union's case for the Copenhagen court. The Baltic was far from the fighting, but its states' goodwill counted in the general European balance the Department tracked. The letter begins a quiet, regular file in the volume's northern tier.
frus-1862-d713:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington, a lawyer who had long handled his land's affairs in the United States. The letter is document 713 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Foreign envoys in Washington wrote to Seward on the business between their lands and the United States. For Costa Rica, trade and the transit routes of Central America were never far from the talks. Molina's letter is part of that formal exchange, in which small republics dealt with a great power then fighting for its life. The file that follows shows the talk run both ways.
frus-1863p1-d113:
On 11 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the first of three letters to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 113 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three letters in a day, a week after a batch of twelve, show a desk that never let the London file cool. Seward split his points across the sheets so Adams could use each on its own. This one opens the day's set. It is part of the spring press on Britain, kept up sheet by sheet from Washington.
frus-1863p1-d13:
On 13 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 13 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on the day of the battle of Fredericksburg, though its news had not yet reached London.

Letters crossed the Atlantic in about ten days by steamer, so each side wrote in the dark about the other's last moves. Seward's mail set the claims Adams was to press on Britain. They were fair dealing, a tight rein on warships built for the South, and no aid to the rebellion. This letter is one link in that chain of orders.
frus-1863p1-d213:
The mail from London dated 11 June 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 213 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d313:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 313 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Stuart served at the British legation in Washington and handled business with the State Department when the minister himself was away or occupied. His notes form part of the same Anglo-American exchange. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d413: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 March 1863. It is document 413 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d513:
A dispatch dated 14 May 1863 went from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d613:
Document 613, dated 14 August 1863, records a letter from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d113: On November 10, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, and his message is Document 113 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two leaders wrote almost daily that week, even with a meeting a fortnight ahead, because the plans for two conferences still had loose ends. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series' pre-departure papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d13: Roosevelt replied to Churchill on June 28, 1943, and the message stands as Document 13 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The same day produced a Churchill note in return, a sign of how fast the exchange moved that week. The record lists the parties and the date only. In the State Department's published series, the letter belongs to the build-up toward the Quebec talks of August and the summits that closed the year.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d213:
The Joint Staff Planners sent report J.C.S. 600 to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on 11 November 1943. Its subject is airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area, tying the question to the decisions taken at the Quebec conference that August.

The planners say B-29s could be ready early in 1944, and that attacks on Japan could start sooner if fields were built in time. They call for at least four fields near Calcutta and five near Chengtu in China, built with British and Chinese help. Their recommendation is that all nine be authorized and finished, as far as possible, by May 1944.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d313:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 410 at Cairo on 25 November 1943, an examination of how weather limits any postponement of Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion of France. It was ammunition in the Anglo-American argument over the invasion's date.

The assault needs a quiet spell of four days with winds of force three or less. Counting ten years of weather, such spells came eighteen times in April and twenty-one in May. They came nineteen times in June, and still seventeen in September. On the assault alone, the operation could slip to September. The build-up after landing needs about three months of workable weather. Tides confine each attempt to two short windows a month, and missing the full-moon window, needed for the air lift, costs twenty-four days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d413:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent Ambassador Harriman a confidential telegram, numbers 1342 to 1344, from Washington at midnight on 4 December 1943. It reports the uproar in the American press over Moscow's early announcement of the Tehran Conference.

Morning papers in the United States headlined London stories about a Moscow radio broadcast. The broadcast, an official Soviet news agency one for provincial papers, had announced the Tehran meeting. It spoke of talks on the war against Germany and on political questions. Decisions, it said, would be made public later. No word of the conference's end had reached America, and Washington had nothing to announce. Hull says the publication has created a furor. Elmer Davis of the Office of War Information asks the department to learn one thing: whether the broadcast broke any release date the conferees had agreed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d513:
Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador in Ankara, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 9, 1943. Days earlier, Roosevelt and Churchill had met Turkey's President İnönü at Cairo and failed to bring Turkey straight into the war. The State Department printed Steinhardt's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's post gave him the Turkish view of that refusal: what Ankara feared, what it wanted, and what it might still do. Reports from the man on the spot guided Washington's next steps with a neutral country the Allies badly wanted. For readers, the message continues the Turkish story beyond the conference room doors.
frus-1944-quebec-d113:
An editors' note in the Quebec Conference volume points readers to records from August 1944 about aid to the Polish underground army. That force had risen against the Germans in Warsaw as the Soviet army neared the city. The note lists the published sources where the full documentation on the episode can be found.

The note also records an unresolved detail. President Raczkiewicz of Poland had written to Roosevelt on August 12, and a reply was drafted on August 31. No copy of that reply was ever found in American files. It was sent by pouch to London on September 8. The note shows the volume's editors flagging a gap in the record rather than hiding it.
frus-1944-quebec-d13:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff in Washington prepared this memorandum on July 14, 1944. The British Joint Staff Mission in Washington kept London's military views in front of the American chiefs between conferences. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff missions did the alliance's daily military diplomacy: papers exchanged, positions tested, and disputes cooled before they reached the leaders. A July memorandum from the British mission belongs to the preparation of the autumn's great questions, which the Quebec Conference would settle in September. For readers, it shows the professional layer where allied strategy was drafted before it was decided.
frus-1944-quebec-d213:
Hull forwarded two enclosures to Roosevelt on September 11, 1944. One was Ambassador Winant's telegram on the European Advisory Commission. The other was the draft protocol on occupation zones in Germany and the administration of Greater Berlin. Winant reported from London that Ambassador Gousev, chairing the commission, was calling a meeting for Monday afternoon.

Gousev was ready to recommend acceptance of the zones protocol with one gap: the American and British zones left blank, for the two governments to decide themselves. The commission's coming work included control machinery, basic proclamations, and the Austria protocol, where Winant had won agreement for tripartite control with only a small American contingent. Bulgarian armistice terms were in hand, and Hungary's were being formulated.
frus-1945-50-intel-d113:
Hoyt Vandenberg, the new director of central intelligence, wrote to Hoover on 3 July 1946. Vandenberg had taken over the CIG in June, full of plans to make it a real agency. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Vandenberg's arrival changed the group's pace: he wanted the SSU's operations, a bigger budget, and a clear field abroad. His first letters to Hoover opened the sharpest phase of the border war with the FBI. Readers should watch the difference in tone from Souers's careful papers. Where Souers conciliated, Vandenberg pressed. The volume's second half runs on the friction his pressing created, with departments, with the bureau, and with the White House itself.
frus-1945-50-intel-d13:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent a joint memorandum to Secretary of War Henry Stimson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal on 19 September 1945. It carried the settled view of the nation's top military body. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the Joint Chiefs spoke together, the armed services presented one front to the civilians above them. Their memorandum on the eve of the OSS order shows the military claiming its share in whatever intelligence system came next. Readers should weigh the channel: the chiefs wrote to both service secretaries at once, binding Army and Navy to a common line. Much of the volume's later bargaining grows from positions fixed in papers like this.
frus-1945-50-intel-d213:
A memorandum dated 9 May 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 213 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d313:
A letter from Secretary of Defense Johnson reached Secretary of State Acheson on 7 October 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 313 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

Between offices that did not answer to each other, a letter was the polite but firm way to press a point. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d413:
John Steelman, acting chairman of the National Security Resources Board, wrote to Sidney Souers of the National Security Council on 2 February 1950. The memo is document 413 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Resources Board planned how the nation's farms, plants, and workers would serve in a war. Its place in an intelligence volume shows how wide the word security had grown by 1950. Steelman's memo links war planning at home with the secret work of watching threats abroad. The Board's link to the Council gave its chairman a direct line into war planning at the top.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d113:
Ambassador Winant looked back nearly three years in this personal letter to the President of 28 January 1945. Writing from London, he recalls a Foreign Office meeting where Eden, Maisky, and he first weighed how the three great powers should treat Europe. The letter is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Maisky, the Soviet ambassador, had set out two roads. One divided Europe into eastern and western fields of chief concern. The other had the three nations work as one to destroy fascist rule and rebuild a Europe at peace. His government, he said, chose the second road. Winant traces the Moscow Conference and the European Advisory Commission to those early talks, and his own seat on the commission to Tehran.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d13: Roosevelt answered Churchill on 22 October 1944, the same day the prime minister's message reached him. Filed as document 13 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, the quick reply shows how fast the two men worked by cable. Their exchanges that fall aligned British and American positions well before the Yalta Conference opened.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d213:
Foreign Minister Bidault gave Hopkins and Caffery France's German terms over lunch in Paris, and Caffery reported them on 30 January 1945. His cable to the Acting Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The talk ran forty-five minutes before the meal.

Bidault set out the stand he and de Gaulle had often given before. All war industry, and near-war industry too, must be wiped out in Germany. A world body should govern the Rhine region, its south held by France alone and its north under mixed control. Germany must be cut down so she can never wage war again. But, Bidault added, he would not like a red flag over Germany to be followed by a black one, the pirate's flag. He also spoke with sympathy of the Security Council voting plan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d313:
America's Joint Chiefs of Staff met at Floriana, Malta, on the morning of February 1, 1945, and these minutes cover the session. General Kuter opened with a fix to an earlier record: his remarks on British help in the long-range bombing of Japan had been left out. A letter from Sir Charles Portal, Britain's air chief, had since reached General Arnold with Kuter's comments.

Kuter asked that his message be attached to the earlier minutes so the file would be complete, and the chiefs agreed. The detail is small, but it shows how carefully the chiefs guarded the record. Even a missing paragraph could matter when allies compared notes.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d413:
Three staff men did the paperwork for the founding conference in this draft report of February 9, 1945. The subcommittee — Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss — had been charged a day earlier with two tasks. They were to advise on consulting France and China about the conference decisions. They were also to draft the invitation text.

On consultation, they advised that the United States speak for the three powers to both governments. On the invitation, they attached a draft for the ministers' approval. The report is short and unsigned in feel. Yet it settled the mechanics by which fifty nations would be summoned to San Francisco.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d113:
Churchill cancelled the King's Berlin visit in telegram number 99 to President Truman, sent July 1, 1945. The short message is document 113 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman had earlier agreed to Churchill's plan for King George VI to spend a day in Berlin during the conference, lunching and dining with the leaders.

The King has now decided, Churchill writes, that he must visit Ulster during the conference period instead, so Truman's kind telegram on the subject no longer applies. Churchill adds that Truman will no doubt have received the King's invitation to visit Britain. The dropped visit removed a bright social occasion from the Potsdam schedule, though the King's invitation to Truman still stood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d13:
De Gaulle wants a seat, and Grew's memorandum to the President of May 16, 1945, prepares Truman for the ask. Stettinius had telegraphed that French Foreign Minister Bidault, arriving in Washington the next day, expected to plead strongly for de Gaulle's inclusion. The proposed meeting of Churchill, Stalin, and Truman was the occasion in view. A copy of the Secretary's telegram is enclosed.

Grew suggested how Truman might open the subject when Bidault called. He could refer to a question asked at the press conference the day before. It concerned whether a meeting of the Big Five would take place at San Francisco. He could then cite his reply, as it was interpreted. The memo scripts a delicate refusal in advance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d213:
Ambassador Harriman reported a hitch in the Soong talks in an extract dated July 12, 1945. The extract is document 213 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. China's foreign minister, T. V. Soong, was in Moscow trying to settle with Stalin the terms tied to Soviet entry into the war against Japan.

Soong suggested to Stalin that he return to Chungking to consult the Generalissimo on the points still at issue. Stalin answered that it was better to reach agreement before he met Truman at Berlin. He wished to settle with the President the date of his entry into the war. The fragment shows the Soviet timetable for joining the Pacific war being tied directly to the Potsdam meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d313:
A farewell call in Budapest gave Schoenfeld one of his darkest reports, sent on July 13, 1945. Valentiny, Hungary's resigning Minister of Justice, came to take his leave. He repeated a warning he had made before: the government did not control its own political police.

The police, Valentiny said, served the Communist Party, and that made them the most dangerous force in Hungarian politics. His successor would fare no better, and repression of non-Communist parties would grow. He hoped America would use its influence for free politics, yet he believed Moscow meant to Sovietize Hungary in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d413:
Philip Mosely laid the French zone dispute before Assistant Secretary Dunn in a memorandum written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. The European Advisory Commission had completed the draft agreement on the French zone in Germany. Its submission to the four governments, though, was held up by one point: how France's area of occupation in Berlin would be defined.

The American proposal of June 30 simply sent the whole question to the Control Council. It prejudged nothing about whether the French area came from two zones or three. The Soviet proposal of July 11 claimed the Soviet area's greater destruction meant the French area should come from the American and British areas, leaving Moscow's share unchanged.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d513:
Germany's eastern frontier is introduced in a briefing book statement dated July 4, 1945. The inter-divisional committees on Germany and on Russia and Poland, it reports, have recommended a settlement. Germany should be required to cede Upper Silesia, East Prussia, and the portion of Pomerania east of the Kreuz-Dramburg line.

The remainder of German territory east of the Oder, and the territory between the Oder and the Neisse, should remain in German possession. For the summary recommendations that follow, the frontier is divided into six segments, each discussed on its own page. Two underlying studies, the statement notes, tried to analyze the whole problem and frame as reasonable a settlement as its complexity allowed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d613:
Eugene Dooman, a Japan specialist at the State Department, wrote a top secret memo dated July 15, 1945. It is document 613 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is the occupation and military government of a defeated Japan.

Dooman says the State, War, and Navy departments have agreed a draft stance, now with the Joint Chiefs. Japan's occupation, he argues, should be unified, not split into zones. The United States should also hold the controlling voice on policy there. Allied troops would serve under one commander, an American, with an advisory council of their senior officers. Dooman allows one possible exception to unified rule. Southern Sakhalin and the Kurile Islands, promised to Moscow at Yalta, could be run apart without harm to Japan proper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1013:
Soviet delegates renewed their claim on the German fleets in this proposal of July 30, 1945. A third of the German surface navy would pass to the Soviet Union. Ships still building or in repair at the surrender are included in that share.

Most of the submarine fleet would be sunk. Boats of the greatest technical interest would be kept and split among the three powers. A third of naval stores, matched by ship class, is also claimed. So is a third of the merchant marine. Transfers would run from August 1 to November 1, 1945, under a Maritime Technical Commission.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1113:
John McCloy, Assistant Secretary of War, sent this message to the War Department on 19 July 1945. McCloy was one of the War Department's top civilian leaders. He had a strong hand in shaping American plans for postwar Germany, and he was with the team at Potsdam.

His message carried the view from the summit back to the Pentagon's leadership in Washington. The War Department ran the army that held Germany, so its chiefs needed word from the talks. A cable of this kind shows the direct line between the men who would rule Germany and the envoys fixing the terms. It is the military half of the peace talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1213:
Patrick Hurley, the American ambassador in China, wrote to the Secretary of State and to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 19 July 1945. Hurley dealt with the China file: a Nationalist government at war, a communist rival in the north, and American hopes for a joined front.

Sending one dispatch to both the secretary and the Moscow envoy tied the China and Soviet files together. Soviet moves in Asia bore hard on China's future, as all three men knew. This cable shows that link being worked in practice. It is Washington's China hand writing to its Russia hand, mid-summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1313:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 30 July 1945. The letter came in the summit's final days. By then Truman had been fully briefed on the atomic test, and the terms to Japan had gone out with the weapon held behind them.

A war secretary's letter at that hour carried the counsel of the man who had overseen the bomb from its birth. Stimson's advice joined the military and moral weight of the choices ahead. This message is part of the last counsel the president received at Potsdam. It shows the cabinet's elder hand still on the brief at the close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1413:
Secretary Byrnes answered Ambassador Caffery in Paris on 15 August 1945. The reply came nine days after Caffery's great cluster of cables to the secretary. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Replies from the secretary close the loop that cables open. After reading Caffery's six messages of 6 August, readers reach Byrnes's answer with a sense of what Washington decided to give, refuse, or postpone. The date matters too: 15 August was the day the war against Japan ended. So the reply belongs to the first day of the postwar world. The French file, like everything else, turned a page that day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-113:
The United States delegation produced this memorandum at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. It is one of several staff memos dated that day in the second Potsdam volume. Such papers moved facts and views around a large team at speed. Some briefed the Secretary of State. Others armed officers heading into committee rooms.

A memo's plain style is the point. Writers skipped ceremony and stated what the reader needed. For later readers, the memo fixes a moment's knowledge inside the delegation. It helps explain why the American side acted as it did in the sessions that followed. The record gains texture from papers never meant to be public.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-13:
A rapporteur's report sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 18, 1945, at Potsdam. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The report lists what the ministers agreed to put before the heads of government that afternoon.

Three subjects were recommended for the afternoon session. First came procedure and machinery for peace negotiations and territorial settlements. Second came the authority of the Control Council for Germany in political questions. Third came Poland, above all the winding up of the London Polish government and the carrying out of the Yalta agreement. On the first subject, the U.S. draft for a Council of Foreign Ministers was approved in principle. A redraft of its third paragraph was also approved. The Soviet team reserved the right to propose a change in the first paragraph.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d713:
Document 713 preserves a text the heads of government approved at Potsdam on July 20, 1945. Approval by Truman, Churchill, and Stalin marked the top level of the conference. Few papers reached that stamp in the first week. The text stands in the second Potsdam volume among the early agreed acts.

An approved text is a fixed point in a moving negotiation. Readers can build around it: what came before, what it settled, what it left. The document shows the leaders acting as a body, not just debating. Such texts became the bricks of the final protocol. Each one narrowed the field of dispute a little more.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d813:
The American team on the Allied Control Commission for Bulgaria wrote to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on July 24, 1945. Document 813 is a military report from Sofia's commission. It carried the team's account to Washington's top soldiers. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A commission's report to the chiefs shows the military line of the occupation story. The team reported its treatment and its findings in formal terms. Readers can set this beside the diplomats' Bulgaria letters. The two channels did not always sing in tune. Their difference teaches how a government sees one place through several eyes at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d913:
The American reparations team in Moscow answered Edwin Pauley's urgent request in this telegram of July 23, 1945. Pauley had asked for 1938 output figures for the Russian zone of Germany. The reply separates factory and mining output from farm output, and gives each as a share of the old Reich.

Industry and mining in the Russian zone produced about 12 billion Reichsmarks, near 31 percent of the Reich total. Farm output came to roughly 6.5 billion, about 48 percent. Land east of the Oder-Neisse gave about 7 percent of industrial and mining output in 1939. The figures leave out the Russian sector of Berlin.
gao-gaoreports-b-297313: PHT Corporation took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297413: Puglia Engineering tripled its January 2006 protest — three case numbers, one shipyard fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one careful answer. Three dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297800-13: INDUS Technology took its June 2007 contract dispute to GAO — thirteenth round in a long docket — and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Long-running bid sagas still get a careful, final answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-311313: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Consolidated Engineering Services, Inc. Decided June 10, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-213: Overlapping food safety watchers needed trimming in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies should cut the overlap and leverage their work. The review calls for the scissors. The inspectors deserved the focus. The overlap had to shrink. The inspectors deserved the focus.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-313: The SEC's late catch on fund abuses got a GAO autopsy in 2005, and the report says lessons could be learned from the missed violations. The review asks why the cops were late. The investors deserved earlier alarms. The lessons had to be learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-413: Unemployment reemployment services needed better data in 2005, and GAO's report says improved figures were required to assess the help. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the jobless deserved proven services. The data had to be better. The jobless deserved proven services.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-613: Clean Air Act actions were mostly done but late in 2005, and GAO's report says EPA completed most required steps, though many ran behind. The findings balance credit and tardiness. The report warns that the air deserved timely rules. The lateness had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-813: Workplace immigration raids were falling flat in 2005, and GAO's report says the weak tools failed the job. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the illegal hiring deserved stopping. The illegal hiring deserved stopping. The tools had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1013: Katrina aid was a fraudster's feast in 2006, and GAO's report says unprecedented challenges exposed the household aid program to abuse. The findings document the looting. The report warns that the storm's victims should not compete with thieves. The aid had to be guarded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-13: The Pentagon's resource decisions needed better risk analysis in 2005, and GAO's report says additional actions were needed to enhance the approach. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the defense dollars deserved careful choices. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-313: Yucca Mountain's quality assurance needed attention in 2006, and GAO's report says management focus was required at the planned waste repository. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the atomic tomb needed building right. The attention had to be paid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-413: Treasury's governmentwide financial system needed discipline in 2006, and GAO's report says the lack of a disciplined process threatened implementation. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the nation's books needed a solid system. The process had to be disciplined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-613: Courthouse rents were climbing in 2006, and GAO's report says increases from new space and energy and security costs needed better tracking. The findings demand the accounting. The report warns that the marble palaces' bills deserved daylight. The tracking had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-713: Backup-site and telework planning needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says selected agencies could improve their continuity preparations. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the alternate offices should be ready. The planning had to improve. The alternate offices should be ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-813: Medicare's anti-fraud funding needed reallocating in 2006, and GAO's report says the agency's approach for allocating integrity funds should be revised. The findings target the formula. The report warns that the fraud-fighting dollars should chase the fraud. The funds had to be aimed right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-113: Biodefense planning needed clearer orders in 2007, and GAO's report says updated intelligence, clear guidance, and steady priorities were required. The findings demand the direction. The report warns that the germ-war shield needed a real strategy. The priorities had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-213: Social Security's rescue math needed sunlight in 2007, and GAO's report says the public deserved clearer numbers on general-revenue financing. The findings demand real transparency from the trustees. The report's creed is simple: the retirement promise should be priced in the open, not in the dark.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-513: The island trust funds were running dry in 2007 — GAO's report warns the Micronesian and Marshallese nest eggs might not last. The findings do the long math on the compacts' money. The report's question hangs over the Pacific: what happens when the trust runs out?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-713: Biofuels were booming without a map in 2007 — GAO's report says the Energy Department lacked a strategy to match rising production with pipes and pumps. The findings expose the infrastructure gap. The report's warning: fuel nobody can move is fuel nobody can burn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-913: Homeland Security's money hygiene was poor in 2007, GAO found — the young department lagged at sizing up wrong payments and clawing them back. The report grades DHS against the clean-books law Congress wrote for every agency. The verdict: a security giant still learning to count its own change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-113: GAO's 2007 report grades the guard plans written for banks, power grids, and other must-run sectors — and finds the cyber parts wildly uneven. Some plans faced the hacker threat head-on; others barely waved at it. The report shows a nation defending its lifelines with a patchwork shield, strong in spots and tissue-thin in others.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-13: GAO's 2007 report looks at the Navy's mine hunters — ships, choppers, and sub drones that sweep sea mines. The gear held real promise, GAO found, but only if the Navy licked its build and fielding troubles. The report covers a quiet, vital mission: keeping the sea lanes open against one of war's cheapest killers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-313: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on disconnected Youth: Federal Action Could Address Some of the Challenges Faced by Local Programs That Reconnect Youth to Education and Employment. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-913: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on gulf Opportunity Zone: States Are Allocating Federal Tax Incentives to Finance Low-Income Housing and a Wide Range of Private Facilities. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
glasgow-virginia-1913:
Ellen Glasgow published Virginia in 1913, opening the great sequence of novels in which she retold her native state's history through fiction. Glasgow, born in Richmond, set out to show what the Southern ideal of womanhood cost the women who lived it. Her heroine shares the state's name.

Virginia Pendleton is raised to be a perfect Southern lady: selfless, gentle, and wholly devoted to husband and children. She sacrifices her mind, her beauty, and finally her health to that ideal. Her husband thrives, grows away from her, and finds her faded devotion a burden. Glasgow's quiet irony builds a devastating case. The novel began her lifelong argument with the sentimental South.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-09-1913:
Volume 9 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1913, titled The Scapegoat. James George Frazer studied the custom of loading a community's sins or evils onto one being and driving it out. Scapegoats could be human, animal, or even objects cast away.

Cases range from ancient Greece and Rome to villages in Asia and Africa in Frazer's own time. He described yearly expulsions of disease and sin, and human scapegoats put to death in some lands. The rite, he argued, let a whole people feel cleansed at one stroke. The volume gathers some of the strangest evidence in the set, and the word scapegoat in daily speech descends from this theme.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-10-1913:
Volume 10 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1913, as Balder the Beautiful, Part 1. James George Frazer took his title from Balder, the Norse god whose death all nature mourned. The volume turns to fire festivals, the great theme of the work's close.

Frazer described bonfires at midsummer, Easter, and other seasons across Europe, lit on hills and in village streets. He asked why people leaped through flames, rolled burning wheels, and carried torches around fields. His answer tied the fires to sun magic and the guarding of crops. Part 1 builds the evidence country by country, in the dense, patient style that marks the whole twelve-volume work.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-11-1913:
Volume 11 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1913, completing Balder the Beautiful. James George Frazer closed his argument with fire festivals beyond Europe. He also treated the external soul, the idea that a person's life can rest outside the body.

Tales and rites show souls hidden in trees, beasts, and locks of hair, safe until the hiding place is harmed. Frazer then returned to Nemi, where his whole inquiry began. There the priest was slain by his successor. The circle closes after thousands of pages of matched customs. Whatever readers think of his theory, the gathered lore changed how the world studies myth.
gorky-my-childhood-1913:
My Childhood, the first volume of Maxim Gorky's autobiography, appeared in Russian in 1913 and in English in 1915. Orphaned young, Alexey is taken to his grandparents' house in Nizhny Novgorod. His grandfather rules the dye-works family with beatings, while his grandmother answers hardship with prayer, tales, and warmth.

Uncles fight over the business, fires flare, and the boy learns work and cruelty early. Gorky recalls it all in scenes of startling clarity and color. The book turned his hard youth into a landmark of Russian memoir. It also explains the writer: pity for the beaten, love of story, and a will to learn. Two later volumes continue the life.
hale-history-common-law-1713:
Matthew Hale, a chief justice of England, wrote his History of the Common Law in the late 1600s, and it appeared in 1713, after his death. Hale was famed for his fairness on the bench. His book is the first great historical account of the common law.

Hale traces English law from Saxon and Norman roots through the growth of the courts. He weighs common law against statute and explains how custom gains force. The calm, orderly mind that lawyers admired in Hale runs through the prose. Later giants like Blackstone built on his frame. The book still opens many courses on English legal history.
hallaj-kitab-al-tawasin-massignon-1913:
Mansur al-Hallaj, the wool carder of Baghdad, was crucified in 922 for saying Ana al-Haqq, I am the Truth. His Kitab al-Tawasin is his strangest and densest book, a set of short chapters named for the Arabic letters Ta and Sin. Louis Massignon, who gave his life to Hallaj, edited the Arabic text at Paris in 1913, with French introduction, commentary, and notes. No English version in the public domain exists.

The chapters circle the fall of Iblis, the light of Muhammad before time, and the soul's union with God, in prose like struck sparks. Massignon's notes open the riddles line by line. The edition founded the modern study of Hallaj.
harrison-ancient-art-ritual-1913:
Jane Ellen Harrison published Ancient Art and Ritual in 1913, a short book with large influence. Harrison argues that art is born from ritual. Dance, drama, and image begin as acts done together for urgent needs: rain, food, fertility, and the return of spring. Only later do they become art for contemplation.

She draws on Greek festivals, primitive rites, and modern folk customs. The book is a manifesto of the Cambridge ritualist school. Anthropology and classics both felt its force. Harrison writes with verve and learning in short compass. Readers new to her work should start here. It remade how many thought about the roots of theatre and art.
heath-aristarchus-samos-1913:
Thomas L. Heath published Aristarchus of Samos, the Ancient Copernicus, in 1913. Aristarchus had proposed a sun-centered system in the third century BCE. Heath traces Greek astronomy through this bold pioneer's surviving evidence.

Eighteen centuries before Copernicus, Aristarchus set the earth in motion. His only surviving work measures the sizes and distances of sun and moon. Heath gives its first English translation inside his study. The geometry is ingenious even where the measurements fall short. Other astronomers rejected the moving earth, and Ptolemy's system won instead. Heath's book restored Aristarchus to his proper place in astronomy's history. The sun-centered idea's true birthday sits here. He got the big point right, and the world took note at last.
henderson-fitness-environment-1913:
Lawrence Henderson was a Harvard chemist who studied the chemistry of blood and the balance of acids in the body. His 1913 book The Fitness of the Environment turns a familiar claim around. Life fits its setting, he argues, because the setting itself is strangely fit for life.

Henderson shows how water, air, and carbon suit living tissue in many fine, linked ways. Change those traits a little, and no chemistry of life as we know it could run. His book gave an old teleological idea, that nature shows purpose, a fresh scientific hearing. His argument still turns up wherever fine balance in nature is debated.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume thirteen: Frederick's writings, the Anti-Machiavel, and the king as author. Carlyle explores the mind behind the sword with deep sympathy. The philosopher in uniform, revealed through his own words. Frederick's flute and pen were as famous as his sword.
husserl-ideen-i-1913:
Husserl published Ideas, the first book of his program for pure phenomenology, in German in 1913. The full title promises an introduction to a science of consciousness and a philosophy built on it. Husserl had already shaken philosophy with his Logical Investigations; the Ideas announced the mature system behind them.

The book's famous method is the epoché, the bracketing of belief in the outer world so that experience itself can be studied cleanly. Husserl describes how consciousness aims at objects and builds a world of meaning from that aiming. The slogan of the school became a return to the things themselves. Few books shaped twentieth-century philosophy more deeply. Continental thought, from existentialism onward, still works in the space the Ideas opened.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-13:
Disease strikes Huronia hard in Volume 13, from 1898, covering 1637 and 1638. Thwaites prints the reports as sickness sweeps town after Huron town. The dying turn in fear and anger toward the black robes.

Many Hurons blame the baptism water for bringing death with it. Priests face threats, closed doors, and grief in every village. Still they baptize the dying and nurse the sick each day. The fathers tell the horror plainly, in their own firsthand words. Tragedy, faith, and blame collide on nearly every page here. Nothing in the telling is softened or held back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyons-israel-10:
Israel Lyons, a Hebrew teacher at Cambridge, is profiled briefly in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Poland, he emigrated to England and settled in Cambridge. There he worked as a silversmith while building a name as a Hebrew scholar. That reputation won him the post of teacher of the Hebrew tongue at the university. He died in 1770.

The article centers on his two books. The Scholar's Instructor was a Hebrew grammar shaped by his long experience of teaching the language. A second edition appeared in 1757, and a fourth as late as 1823. His Observations and Enquiries, on parts of Scripture history, was printed by the Cambridge Press in 1768. The entry records a Jewish craftsman who became a university teacher in an age when few Jews held such posts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makkot-blows-pu:
Makkot, meaning blows or punishments, names a tractate described in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It stands fifth in the Mishnah's order Nezikin, on damages. A Tosefta and both Talmuds accompany it. It was once joined to Sanhedrin, to which its contents stay close. Its three chapters hold thirty-four mishnayot in all.

The article summarizes the tractate's three subjects. First come conspiring witnesses, who by law suffer the penalty they plotted for another. Where the same penalty cannot be returned, flogging replaces it. The second subject is the killer sent to a city of refuge. The third is flogging itself, when it is earned and how it is given. Worked examples fill the summary, such as witnesses who fake a loan's term and must pay the difference. The entry gives readers the plan of a short, sharp tractate on court punishments.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mari-ben-dimi-1:
Mari ben Dimi, second gaon of Pumbedita, is profiled in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. When Jewish scholars were driven from the Babylonian academies, Mari went with others to Firuz-Shabur. There they founded a new academy that became linked with his name. After Gaon Hanan of Iskiya died in 609, Mari was elected his successor.
