The article admits how little else survives of him. Only two of his legal decisions have been preserved. One, quoted by Judah Gaon, concerns two unknown plants named in the Talmud. The other concerns the marriage of a mamzer, a person of tainted birth under Jewish law. Both come down inside later collections of geonic rulings. The entry rests on Gratz, Weiss, and Sherira Gaon's famous letter. It preserves a name from the academies' hardest years, when Babylonian learning had to rebuild itself in exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayer-constant-:
Constant Mayer was a French painter who made his career on both sides of the Atlantic. Cyrus Adler and Florence N. Levy profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Besançon on October 4, 1832, and trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Léon Cogniet. In 1857 he crossed to America and settled in New York. He later returned to Paris, where he was living when the entry was written.

Mayer painted genre scenes and portraits, and the entry lists his best-known canvases in order. They run from “Consolation” in 1864 to “First Grief” in 1885. Along the way stand “Maud Müller,” the “Episode in the Campaign of 1863,” and “Song of the Shirt.” His portraits included Generals Grant and Sherman. The National Academy of Design in New York made him an associate, and France gave him the Legion of Honor in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-memor-book-germ:
Memor-Book, in German Memorbuch, was a hand-written register of persecutions, martyrs, and the community's dead. Joseph Jacobs and Siegmund Salfeld describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such books listed places of suffering and the names of the martyrs. Their lists of the dead leaned toward scholars, leaders, and benefactors. Their reading, the "memmern," was heard in synagogue on two Sabbaths, the one before the Ninth of Ab and the one before Pentecost. It inspired the living.

The article insists on the custom's Jewish origin. Christians had their diptychs and books of life. But the oldest surviving memor-book is Nuremberg's, begun in 1296. It is so full it must have had models before it. It grows from Israel's own practice of praying for the dead. The Church itself took that practice from Judaism, the writers argue. Set prayer forms frame the names in each book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-j:
Meshullam ben Jacob of Lunel was a French Talmudist who died in 1170. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was head of a school that produced several famous men. Abraham ben Isaac, the ab bet din of Narbonne, was his intimate friend, addressed responsa to him, and spoke of him in high terms. Meshullam's decisions are quoted in the "Sefer ha-Terumot."

His second distinction is philosophical. It was Meshullam who encouraged Judah ibn Tibbon to translate Bahya's "Al-Hidayah." In Hebrew it became the "Hobot ha-Lebabot," the Duties of the Hearts. Meshullam wrote on moral philosophy himself. He advised and assisted other writers, and kept a large library. Ibn Tibbon never tires of praising his zeal. The zeal was for investigating every branch of knowledge. So the notice doubles as a portrait. It portrays Provençal learning's great enabler.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midwife-10813:
Midwives in biblical and rabbinic times are the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906. Its authors were Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Solomon Schechter. The Bible mentions midwives rarely. Rachel and Tamar were helped by midwives, both in hard births. In Egypt only two are named, Shiphrah and Puah, in the book of Exodus.

Most Hebrew women, the article says, delivered with help from friends or relatives. Exodus claims they often gave birth before the midwife even arrived. The writers then quarrel over words. One Exodus term, built on the word for two stones, is read by Rashi and the Targums as the delivery-stool. Other commentators read it as the womb. Legal and Talmudic material fills the rest of the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mo-ed-katan-sma:
Mo'ed Ḳaṭan, the smaller festival, is the Mishnah treatise on the in-between days of Passover and Sukkot. Solomon Schechter and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach summarize it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Those middle days are half-holy. Work is restricted but not banned. The treatise, eleventh in the order Mo'ed, runs three chapters and twenty-four paragraphs.

Its first chapter asks what may still be done. Fields may be watered, and broken irrigation ditches repaired. By extension, canals, water-works, and public streets may be kept in order. Labor for the public welfare is allowed. Older manuscripts call the treatise Mashkin, they water, after its opening word. The article walks through the chapters of permitted work, mourning rules, and festival exceptions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moresheth-gath-:
Moresheth-Gath, possession of Gath, is a town of Judah's lowland named in Micah's opening oracle and apparently the prophet's own home, as Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Micah strings it with Lachish, Achzib, and Mareshah in a chain of doomed towns. Jerome placed it just east of Eleutheropolis, still a village with a church over Micah's tomb.

Modern travelers Robinson and Thomson put it near or even at Mareshah, though Micah's text keeps the two apart. The Jewish commentators split: Ibn Ezra and Ḳimḥi read a place-name, while the Targum and Rashi dissolve it into a phrase — those who caused you to inherit Gath, meaning David's house. Wellhausen cuts the knot by addressing Gath itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-herz-b:
Naphtali Herz ben Jacob Elhanan was a German cabalist born at Frankfort in the later sixteenth century. Kaufmann Kohler and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He moved to Palestine and became a disciple of Isaac Luria. His one great book grew directly out of that discipleship.

His Emek ha-Melek is an introduction to the Cabala and a commentary on parts of the Zohar and on Luria's writings. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1648. A second part, Gan ha-Melek, comments on passages of the Zohar and is still in manuscript. The short entry ties Frankfort to Luria's Palestine by one man's life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neyar-sefer-ha-:
Sefer ha-Neyar is an anonymous handbook of Jewish law. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Louis Ginzberg for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was compiled soon after 1319, in the 1300s. Its maker was probably a Provençal scholar. Most of it extracts French authorities' works.

A book by Baruch of Niort served as its basis. Baruch had studied under Isaac of Corbeil. Halakot Gedolot and Maimonides were also consulted for it. Legal rulings and Tosefta pieces fill its pages, especially Simon's. Tales of real historical interest appear among the laws. Almost no medieval scholar knew the book at all. Colon and Azulai are the rare exceptions named. Copies rest with De Rossi and in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novomoskovsk-11:
Novomoskovsk is a city in Russia's Yekaterinoslav government. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It counts 12,862 people, including 1,147 Jews. Over 900 Jews work as artisans or day-laborers. Few factory hands in the city are Jewish.

Schools there teach Jewish children in small numbers. Eight ḥadarim hold seventy pupils between them. The year 1883 brought an anti-Jewish riot. A rumor blamed Jews for a church burglary. On Sept. 4 a mob wrecked the Jewish houses. Only three houses and the synagogue escaped ruin. The rioters finished their work unhindered at first. Cossack troops arrived only afterward and arrested them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onkeneira-isaac:
Isaac ben Samuel Onkeneira was a Turkish scholar and poet. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He thrived at Constantinople in the mid fifteen hundreds. He was a friend of Don Joseph Nasi. Nasi was made Duke of Naxos by the sultan.

Onkeneira is thought to have copied a famed debate text. It told of a clash between Nasi and a Christian scholar. He gave it the title Ben Porat Yosef in 1577. The work both guards Judaism and answers its rival faith. He wrote a book on the laws of slaughter too. That work notes the Re'umah of Rabbi Nahshon. His Ayummah ka-Nidgalot holds tales and word games. It tells of a clash of the letters at the birth of the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolenghi-abra:
Abraham Azariah Ottolenghi was an Italian rabbi from Acqui. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Acqui in the year 1776. He died there in the year 1851. His brother was Israel Emanuel Ottolenghi of that town.

In 1796 the French army came into the town of Acqui. Abraham spoke on the tree of liberty set up then. In 1799 the mob rose against the Jews of Acqui. The Ottolenghi brothers were hunted by the foe party. They fled to the Alps and hid from the mob. Their father was seized and borne off to Genoa. When calm came back, Abraham went home to Acqui. He took up the rabbi's work there with no fee. He kept that work up till close to his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parish-alvars-e:
Elias Parish-Alvars was an English harpist and song writer. Joseph Jacobs and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Teignmouth, in England, in 1810. He died at Vienna on January 25, 1849. Dizi, Labarre, and Bochsa were his teachers in art.

In 1831 Elias toured Germany and played in great towns. He played at Bremen and at Hamburg with great success. In 1834 he made a tour of all Italy in music. Two years on, he went to Vienna and stayed to 1838. From 1838 to 1842 he roamed the East for songs. He brought back a store of tunes from those lands. He then gave shows in Leipzig, Berlin, and Prague. In 1847 he settled at Vienna for the rest of life. The emperor made him his own chamber harpist there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peor-12013:
Peor is a mountain named in the story of Balaam. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Balak, king of Moab, brought Balaam up its slopes. From there Balaam was to curse Israel below. The entry is short because the clues are few.

The peak stood in the plains of Zophim. It looked out over the waste called Jeshimon. Jerome placed it across from Jericho, near Danaba. No one has fixed the site with full certainty. Recent study points to a hill called El-Mushakkar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-philip:
Philip Phillips was an American lawyer and congressman from the South. He was born in Charleston in 1807 and died in Washington in 1884. Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied law after a military schooling.

Phillips practiced first in South Carolina, then in Mobile. Alabama sent him to its legislature several times. He sat in Congress from 1853 to 1855. The Civil War drove him to New Orleans for safety. After the war he returned to practice in Washington. His legal digests served courts in two states.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-possart-felix-1:
Felix Possart was a German painter of scenes and landscapes, born in Berlin in 1837. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He first meant to follow the law. For some years he held a post as a local judge. In time his love of painting grew too strong to resist.

Possart gave his whole time to art at last. He studied hard under Eschke and under Gude. He painted scenes of southern Spain most of all. He went to Spain again and again from 1882 on. He traveled in the Black Forest as well. The Bavarian highlands gave him subjects too. His work shows a judge turned painter by choice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psantir-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Zelig Psantir was a Rumanian writer on Jewish history. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Botoshani in 1820. He died at Bucharest in 1901. From childhood he gave himself to music. He led a band of traveling Gypsy players when young.

Once his band played at a feast in a monastery. Guests fell to arguing the Jewish question there. Some held that all Rumanian Jews were foreign-born men. Psantir was asked how long his own house had lived in Rumania. That talk turned him toward the past of his people. He spent his later years on the tale of Rumania's Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinowitsch-ke:
Lydia Rabinowitsch-Kempner was a doctor and student of germs. Isidore Singer and Regina Neisser wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born at Kovno in Russia in 1871. She was schooled at the girls' school of her town. Latin and Greek she learned in private lessons at home. Science drew her to the schools of Switzerland.

She studied nature at Zurich and then at Bern. She took her medical degree in that Swiss training. At Berlin, Professor Koch let her work in his institute. That was the famed house for the study of infections. In 1895 she went to Philadelphia in America. A post in her field awaited her there, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rebuke-and-repr:
Rebuke and reproof had set forms in rabbinical life. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A mild rebuke for bad manners was called hakpadah. A severe rebuke for contempt was called nezifah.

The article notes that both forms address unwitting faults. They differ from the ban, a stronger punishment. Nezifah carried only a mild form of shunning. Stories then show rabbis rebuking in practice. Raba corrected a guest who sat without wiping his feet. He did so by posing a legal question, not by scolding. Other tales show teachers guarding their honor. The entry shows correction kept within clear limits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revelation-1271:
Revelation is a term used in two senses in Jewish theology. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In one sense it means a showing of God's presence. Rabbinical language calls that Gilluy Shekinah.

The article gives the second sense as God's will made known. That will comes through words, signs, statutes, or laws. Old Bible terms for the first sense mean sight or vision. Genesis shows God speaking with Adam, Cain, and Noah. He appears to Abraham in several scenes. He comes in dreams to Abimelech, Laban, and Jacob. Moses first met him at the burning bush. Isaiah and other prophets received visions too. The entry sorts kinds of divine showing across Scripture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salaman-charles:
Charles Kensington Salaman was an English pianist, composer, and controversialist born in London in 1814. Joseph Jacobs and Francis L. Cohen wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His talent showed early, and he joined the Royal Academy at ten.

At fourteen Salaman played his own compositions in public in London. In 1830 he composed the ode for Stratford's Shakespeare Jubilee Festival. His setting of Shelley's I Arise from Dreams of Thee stayed well known for decades. He set poems from many languages, including Hebrew verse and the liturgy. In Rome he conducted a Beethoven symphony's first performance there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jona: Samuel ben Jonah was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is perhaps identical with Samuel ben Inijah, or Inia, of other passages. Samuel ben Jonah once gave an opinion on Samuel ben Nahman's system for reckoning the new moon. Under the Inia name he passes on traditions of Aha about Daniel, called Hamudot three times over.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sason-abraham-1:
Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Abraham Sason. He was an Italian cabalist. Sason flourished at Venice at the start of the seventeenth century. The entry is brief, and it rests on the old Hebrew catalogs. It lists three works that came from his pen.

His Ḳol Mebasser, printed at Venice in 1605, comments on the Book of Daniel. With it appeared Ḳol Sason, a work on the coming of the Messiah. His Appiryon Shelomoh followed at Venice in 1609. That book holds essays on the Cabala and on mysticism. Together the three works show a Venetian scholar steeped in hidden lore. He read Daniel's visions through the lens of the expected redemption.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seminaire-israe:
France's Jewish seminary grew out of a yeshivah founded at Metz in 1704. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the school. Abraham Schwab and his wife Agathe endowed it for five rabbis as teachers. A deed of 1705, still kept in its archives, set out the gift.

The entry follows the school as the Metz consistory reshaped it in 1820. Pupils then numbered only eight, and some paid no fees. They also had to study French and arithmetic each day. Later government action changed the school again. Readers see how France trained its rabbis in a changing state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shear-jashub-13: Shear-Jashub was a son of the prophet Isaiah, given a name that was itself a prophecy. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. The name points to God's promise to restore the remnant of His people. Isaiah says the remnant of Jacob shall return to the mighty God. Isaiah took the boy along when he went to warn King Ahaz. He urged Ahaz to trust in God against Damascus and Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shroud-13613:
Shroud is the robe in which Jews array the dead for burial. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the garment. It is made of white linen cloth called sadin. Large stitches join its pieces, with thread ends left unknotted.

The garment need last only until the body decays. In practice several garments replace one single shroud. A man's set includes cap, breeches, shirt, and over-garment. A girdle completes the outfit for burial dress. A woman's set swaps breeches and girdle for an apron. Her cap is flat rather than miter-shaped. A leading man's prayer shawl is added, fringes cut. Before the Temple fell, Jews were buried in everyday clothes, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smyrna-13813:
Smyrna was a seaport of Asia Minor in the Turkish vilayet of Aidin. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Galante wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews lived there as early as the second century. No more is heard of them until 1605, though. Spanish refugees settled there slowly after the expulsion from Spain.

Joseph Escapa founded the congregation in 1631 as first chief rabbi. Smyrna became the center for all Asia Minor communities. Disaster struck the city again and again over the years. In 1772 every synagogue in Smyrna burned down. A fire in 1841 destroyed nearly all the synagogues again. Earthquakes, cholera, and plague also ravaged the Jewish quarter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-son-of-man-1391:
Son of man renders the Hebrew ben adam in the Bible. Emil G Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The phrase names mankind in general as a whole. It sets human life apart from non-human life. It also stresses the wide scope of humanity beyond nations.

In Balaam's blessing, God is not a son of man. That contrast marks God's truth against human change. In the Psalms the phrase stresses human weakness and brevity. God looks down on the children of men from heaven. The faithful fail among them, one psalm laments in sorrow. Most often the phrase simply means mankind or the human race.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinfeld-emanu:
Emanuel Steinfeld was an Australian statesman born at Neisse, Silesia, in 1827. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinfeld died at Melbourne on May 6, 1893. After years in London he settled at Ballarat in Australia. There he founded the firm of Steinfeld and Levison in 1866.

Steinfeld became the first mayor of Ballarat East and held that office for three years. He helped found the Ballarat orphan asylum and its water scheme. In 1887 he became president of the Victoria Chamber of Manufactures. He pushed for free trade between the Australian colonies. In 1892 he won election to the legislative council of Victoria. The entry traces a migrant who rose to public office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sun-blessing-of:
The Blessing of the Sun marks the sun starting a new cycle. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Jews recite the formula on the first Wednesday of Nisan. The event returns only once every twenty-eight years. The last cycle began on April 7, 1897.

The count rests on Samuel's calendar of 365 and a quarter days. Seven planets rule the hours in a fixed order. Saturn leads, then Jupiter, Mars, and the sun follow. Short cycles of four years shift the start day forward. Seven short cycles make one long cycle of twenty-eight years. Then Saturn returns to the first hour of Wednesday eve. The ceremony recalls the sun's birth at creation. The entry lays out the math behind a rare rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temurah-midrash:
Midrash Temurot is a short ethical work in three chapters. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The work argues that contrast and change keep the world in balance. Wealth and poverty, beauty and ugliness, all serve the whole.

Its third chapter reads a psalm through the famous list in Ecclesiastes. That list names a time for every thing under heaven. The first chapters speak in the names of R. Ishmael and R. Akiba. Scholars doubt that early dating, the article notes. Style and sources point to the late twelfth century instead. The work first appeared in print in 1786.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titus-arch-of-1:
The Arch of Titus at Rome honored the emperor's victory over the Jews. Morris Jastrow, Jr., and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The arch stands on the Via Sacra near the Forum. One face looks toward the Colosseum. Pope Pius VII had its worn sides restored.

Three reliefs line the arch's passage. One shows Titus crowned by Victory in a four-horse car. Rome herself leads the horses beside him. Another shows soldiers carrying spoils from the Jerusalem Temple. Viewers can see the seven-branched candlestick and golden table. A third relief shows Titus riding an eagle to heaven. Roman Jews long avoided passing beneath the arch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-seligmann:
Seligmann Meyer Trier was a Danish physician who pioneered stethoscope use in Denmark. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born poor at Copenhagen in 1800, he was meant for trade. A family doctor noticed his brightness and sent him to university. He graduated in medicine in 1823.

He became physician to Copenhagen's Jewish poor in 1825. Laënnec's stethoscope discoveries drew his close study soon after. His 1830 manual on chest examination long stood alone in Danish. He also co-edited a work on Asiatic cholera. His board of health seat in 1836 drew comment over his religion. He led the Royal Frederik's Hospital for eighteen years. The king named him Etatsraad in 1857.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-usishkin-michae:
Michael Usishkin was a leader of the Russian Zionists, born in 1863. Herman Rosenthal and S. Hurwitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Dubrovna and moved to Moscow in 1871. Heder study of Bible and Talmud came first. He graduated as an engineer in 1889. Since 1891 he has lived at Yekaterinoslav.

He helped found the Bilu student group at school. That group formed the first Jewish colony in Palestine. He also organized Chovevei Zion societies in Moscow. In 1890 he co-founded the Odessa colonists' aid association. Herzl won him as an ardent collaborator from 1896. He attended nearly every Zionist congress thereafter. In 1903 he went to Palestine to buy colony land. He fiercely opposed the Uganda project.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vita-della-volt:
Solomon Hayyim Vita della Volta was an Italian doctor and Hebraist. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on September 24, 1772. He died on March 29, 1853. He lived and worked at Mantua.

Della Volta owned a large Hebrew library. It held 131 manuscripts among its books. After his death the library passed to Marco Mortara. Della Volta wrote for the periodical Kerem Hemed. A letter to him from I. S. Reggio was later printed. The brief entry preserves the record of a learned collector. His library kept Mantua on the map of Hebrew learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-week-hebr-shabu:
The week is a span of seven days. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew name shabua states that count plainly. Older traces suggest a rival system of ten day parts. The month once split into three such decades. Bible verses hint at that older reckoning.

The seven day week likely ties to the moon. Four weeks roughly fill one lunar month. Hebrews and Babylonians both used the pattern. It may have arisen from watching the moon's four phases. The first week of a month began with the month itself. Pentecost required its weeks to be complete. The entry weighs these roots with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-15013:
Worms is a town in Hesse with one of the oldest Jewish groups in Germany. Gotthard Deutsch, Abraham Lewinsky, Joseph Jacobs, and Schulim Ochser wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A tale says its Jews came from the tribe of Benjamin. Proof starts much later, near the year 1000.

In 1034 the town group first stands clear in the records. In 1074 the emperor freed its Jews from road tolls. They had stayed loyal to him in hard times. Jews there lived in their own quarter by then. In 1090 the emperor gave the group free trade rights. A Jew-bishop spoke for the group at court. The entry then tracks the town through long years of growth and pain. It is one of the deep town tales of German Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedner-joseph-1:
Joseph Zedner (1804-1871) was a German book man and keeper of books. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Gross-Glogau, he taught at a Jewish school first. That school was at Strelitz in the Mecklenburg lands.

In 1832 he went to Berlin as a home tutor there. His host was the book seller A. Asher of that town. He then tried the book trade on his own in vain. In 1845 he took a post at the British Museum. He kept the Hebrew books of that great house in London. He held that post till ill health made him quit in 1869. He made the list of a great book hoard bought then. His own list of the Hebrew books there came in 1867.
journal-of-discourses-vol-13:
Volume Thirteen, from 1871, wrestles with dissent inside the kingdom's gates. The Godbeite schism splits off Saints who question Young's tight rule. Silver strikes outside Utah pull other minds toward quick wealth.

Young's sermons thunder against apostasy in some of his fiercest terms. Economic independence gets pressed as a shield for the faith itself. Trials now rise from within as much as from outside foes. The prophet meets each threat head-on from the Tabernacle stand. Readers see a theocracy defending its borders of belief and home trade. The fight for Utah's soul turns inward in this tense volume.
julian-works-wright-vol1-1913:
Julian ruled the Roman Empire for less than two years, from 361 to 363, and spent them trying to bring back the old gods. He also wrote speeches, satires, and letters in Greek. Wilmer Cave Wright translated his works for the Loeb series, and the first volume appeared in 1913, with the Greek text facing the English.

Orations one through five fill this volume. They praise the emperor Constantius and the empress Eusebia, and they hymn the Sun and the Mother of the Gods. Readers see the last pagan emperor argue for his faith in formal court style. The volume gives his public voice before the sharper attacks of the later books.
julian-works-wright-vol2-1913:
The second Loeb volume of Julian's works, in Wilmer Cave Wright's translation, appeared in 1913 beside the first. Julian, the emperor who tried to restore pagan worship, wrote in Greek across many forms. This volume gathers his later orations, fragments of lost pieces, and a set of his letters.

Two famous works stand out. The Caesars is a satire in which dead emperors are judged by the gods. The Misopogon is a mock attack on himself and on the city of Antioch. The letters show the emperor at work, ruling, coaxing, and scolding. Together they give the sharpest picture of Julian's wit, temper, and aims.
kafka-das-urteil-1913:
Das Urteil, The Judgment, was written in a single night in September 1912, and Kafka called it his breakthrough. Published in 1913, it tells of Georg Bendemann, a young merchant. He is writing to a friend in Russia about his engagement.

Georg takes the letter to his aged father, and the visit turns. The old man rises, denounces the friend as his own ally, and sentences his son to death by drowning. Georg obeys at once, running to the river. The story's dream logic and sudden verdict announce the whole later Kafka in one burst of writing.
kropotkin-fields-factories-workshops-191:
Kropotkin argued for joining farm and factory in Fields, Factories and Workshops, in its 1913 form. Small workshops, gardens, and local industry fill his picture of a free economy. He holds that decentralization beats the giant factory and the distant market. Regions could feed and supply themselves with far less waste.

Science and invention, he shows, make small scale production stronger than critics think. Workers who mix brain work and hand work stay fuller human beings. The book grows from his studies of farming and industry in several lands. It remains a founding text for decentralist thought. Its examples come from real places and trades. The tone is practical, not dreamy.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-1-1813:
Plutarch, the Greek writer of the first century, composed paired lives of famous Greeks and Romans. John and William Langhorne turned his Lives into English in the 1700s, and this first volume of the 1813 edition opens the set. It begins with a life of Plutarch himself.

The lives here cover Theseus and Romulus, the founders of Athens and Rome, then the lawgivers Lycurgus, Numa, and Solon. Later chapters give Publicola, Themistocles, and Camillus. Plutarch judged character more than battles, and his paired lives shaped how later ages pictured the ancient world. For centuries they served as a main source for plays, essays, and school lessons.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-2-1813:
Plutarch wrote the Lives of famed Greeks and Romans in pairs. John and William Langhorne gave the work English dress in 1813. Their set runs to six books in all. Book Two takes the run of lives on from the first book's close.

Each pair sets a Greek by a Roman of like bent: a law man, a lord of war. Plutarch cares less for dates than for the soul of each man. Small acts, he holds, bare a man's make more than great wars. The Langhorne dress was the stock English Plutarch of its age.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-3-1813:
Book Three of the Langhorne Plutarch's Lives came out in 1813. John and William Langhorne made the dress for a set of six books. Plutarch was a Greek scribe of the Roman age. His Lives pair a Greek with a Roman in each tale.

Great captains, law makers, and kings pass in pairs through the book. Plutarch draws morals from each life for the use of his own day. He is frank on flaws as well as on high deeds of his men. The set was a chief school book of the age that made it.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-4-1813:
Book Four of Plutarch's Lives in the Langhorne dress came out in 1813. The full set runs to six books. John and William Langhorne were kin who shared the work of the dress. Plutarch's pairs of Greek and Roman lives march on here at mid run.

War and state craft form the meat of most lives in the book. Plutarch sets the two men of each pair side by side at the close. His aim is to teach by lives, not to write a dry roll of the past. The dress reads smooth and grave, fit for the theme.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-5-1813:
Book Five of the Langhorne Plutarch's Lives came out in 1813. The set of six books nears its end with this part. John and William Langhorne gave the Greek sage his English voice for the age. Plutarch wrote the Lives in the first years of the Roman Empire's height.

Kings, orators, and men of war fill the pairs of this book. Each life ends with a weigh up of the two men in one view. Plutarch's love of small tales that bare the soul marks each life. The set held its place in homes and schools for a long span.
langhorne-plutarch-lives-vol-6-1813:
Book Six ends the Langhorne dress of Plutarch's Lives. The full set came out in 1813 in six books. John and William Langhorne shared the long work of the dress. Plutarch paired the great men of Greece and Rome for all time in these tales.

The last lives close the run of pairs that starts with Theseus and Romulus. Plutarch's art is in the small act that shows the man, not the great deed. His morals still speak to men who hold power or seek it. The Langhorne set was the English Plutarch for scores of years.
lawrence-sons-and-lovers-1913:
D. H. Lawrence published Sons and Lovers in 1913, his autobiographical triumph of a miner's son in Nottinghamshire. The novel tells of Paul Morel's suffocating bond with his mother and his struggle toward love in life. Lawrence drew the Morels from his own parents, their marriage, and his Eastwood childhood in the coal country.

Gertrude Morel, wed to a drinking miner, pours her thwarted ambition into her sons William and Paul. William dies, and Paul, a painter, becomes his mother's companion, confessor, and emotional prisoner at home in Bestwood. Miriam's soulful love and Clara's married passion both fail against the mother's prior, total claim on his heart. Paul helps his dying mother with an overdose, then turns, alone, toward the town's lights and life. The book founded the modern novel of family psychology in English, raw and unreconciled.
letters-of-travel-1892-1913:
Rudyard Kipling's Letters of Travel gather pieces written between 1892 and 1913. Some first ran in The Times, others in the Morning Post. A third group, Egypt of the Magicians, ran in Nash's Magazine.

Contents begin with From Tideway to Tideway, written in 1892. Letters to the Family, from 1907, report a Canadian journey. Kipling crosses continents and watches an empire's far edges. Earthquakes, ships, and winter notebooks fill the varied pieces. The book shows his reporting eye at work across twenty years. Kipling's American and Canadian pieces stirred debate at home. He writes as an insider who had become an outsider.
levi-history-of-magic-waite-1913:
Eliphas Levi was the pen name of a French occult scribe of the 1800s. A. E. Waite gave his History of Magic English dress in 1913. The book sweeps the whole tale of magic from old times to Levi's day. It is the tale that framed the new occult age.

Mystery cults of Greece and Egypt open the long march. Templars, alchemists, and Rosicrucians take their turns in the line. Levi holds that one hid lore runs through all the ages. His grand sweep gave the occult world a past it could claim as its own.
lindsay-general-william-booth-1913:
Vachel Lindsay published General William Booth Enters into Heaven in 1913, a book of poems meant to be chanted aloud. The title poem honors William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army. Lindsay imagines Booth leading a parade of the saved into heaven. Drums, banjos, and brass bands set the beat.

Lindsay gave stage directions for voice, song, and movement with the poems. He toured widely, performing his work like a revival preacher. Other poems praise heroes, towns, and American scenes in bold rhythm. Critics call his style sung or chanted poetry. The book made him one of the most popular American poets of his day.
london-john-barleycorn-1913:
Jack London published John Barleycorn in 1913, naming it for the old folk name for alcohol. The book is a memoir of his whole life told through drinking: oyster pirate saloons, Yukon camps, and literary success. London insisted it was not a temperance tract but the truth as he lived it.

He tracks how drink threaded through his work, friendships, and adventures, brought on by what he called the White Logic of despair. The memoir covers his support for women's suffrage and his own vote for prohibition, which puzzled his friends. It closes with fame, money, and illness closing in. John Barleycorn is the first major American memoir of alcoholism, still startling in its honesty.
marx-poverty-philosophy-quelch-1913:
Karl Marx attacked Proudhon's Philosophy of Poverty with The Poverty of Philosophy in 1847. Harry Quelch's English translation appeared in Chicago in 1913, from Charles H. Kerr. Proudhon, a French socialist, had offered his own system of economic ideas. Marx answered with a fierce, point by point demolition.

Against Proudhon's moral hopes, Marx sets history and class struggle as the real movers. He sketches historical materialism, his view that production shapes social life. The polemic became a founding text of Marxist political economy. Its sharpness still startles readers used to drier theory. Young Marx writes here with a whip in hand. The book marks his break with utopian socialism.
maunder-planets-inhabited-1913:
E. Walter Maunder was a star man at Greenwich who knew Mars well. His book Are the Planets Inhabited? came out in 1913. He wrote it to test the claims of Percival Lowell. Lowell held that wise beings built canals on Mars.

Maunder shows how the eye can join dots and blobs into false straight lines. He weighs heat, air, and water on Mars and finds them thin and harsh. His calm case broke the back of the canal tale. The book marks the turn when most star men gave up a peopled Mars.
meghaduta-wilson-1813:
Horace Hayman Wilson translated Kalidasa's Meghaduta into English verse in 1813, at the College of Fort William in Calcutta. His Cloud Messenger was the first English rendering of the poem. An exiled yaksha, a minor spirit of the god of wealth, pines for his wife in the far north of India.

When the monsoon cloud rises, he begs it to carry his message across India to her. The cloud's route becomes a tour of rivers, cities, and temples in Kalidasa's glowing verse. Wilson, a surgeon turned Sanskrit scholar, opened much of Sanskrit poetry to English readers. His version, with notes, stayed standard for a century. The poem itself remains Kalidasa's lyric masterpiece.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-13: Etext 3563, released in December 2002, is volume thirteen. Its author is Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary in his rising years. Gutenberg's head note marks the file with the year 1815. That head note, plus the license that trails it, is the whole sample. Not a single paragraph of the memoir is included in the held portion. Reporting must therefore rest on the series, author, and file facts, and go no further.
mitchell-business-cycles-1913:
Wesley Clair Mitchell published Business Cycles in 1913, the fruit of years spent gathering facts about booms and slumps. Mitchell, a Columbia economist, distrusted theories built without evidence. He set out to describe the business cycle exactly as it happens before daring to explain it.

The book follows prices, wages, interest, and profits through prosperity, crisis, depression, and revival, using long runs of statistics. Mitchell shows the cycle as a process in which each phase breeds the next. The facts-first program made the treatise the founding work of the empirical study of cycles. It also launched the research institute Mitchell later led, where measuring the economy became an organized national task.
montgomery-aramaic-incantation-texts-nip:
James A. Montgomery published his edition of Aramaic incantation texts from Nippur in 1913. Excavators had found clay bowls inked with spells under house floors there. Families buried the bowls to trap demons beneath their homes.

Montgomery's volume was the first scholarly publication of these Jewish Babylonian bowls. He transliterated, translated, and explained the spiraling Aramaic inscriptions. The spells name angels and demons and quote scripture for protection. Everyday magic of late antiquity comes alive in these household objects. The edition founded a whole field of bowl studies. Archaeology and linguistics meet on every page of Montgomery's work.
munro-prehistoric-britain-1913: Robert Munro wrote this short survey of the deep past of Britain for the Home University Library in 1913. The set was made to put sound learning in the hands of plain readers. Munro was a Scots doctor who had dug much of his own proof in the field. In a small compass he sets out the stone age case for the isles, from flint tools to cave finds. It is the clear word on the deep past as its age knew it.
nasa-tm-19680027791-experimental-perform:
Samuel M. Futral Jr. and Donald E. Boleski of Lewis Research Center tested a small axial-flow turbine across Reynolds numbers in this 1968 report. The five-inch, single-stage turbine was designed for a Brayton cycle power application. Argon served as the working fluid during the tests.

Inlet pressures varied widely, giving Reynolds numbers from high to quite low. Efficiency and equivalent mass flow both fell as Reynolds number dropped. Torque fell notably across the test range as well. Exit diffuser effectiveness stayed high throughout the tests. Performance losses were greater than those of a radial-inflow turbine designed for the same job. The data warn designers that small turbines suffer at low Reynolds numbers.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, gathers Chrysostom's homilies on eight of Paul's letters: Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. The volume came out in 1886 under Philip Schaff. It is the Chrysostom volume of short courses.

His commentary on Galatians runs whole, one of the few complete ancient ones we have. The prison letters get warm, pastoral treatment, full of praise for Paul's chains. The talks to Timothy and Titus turn to the duties of clergy and household. Taken together, the volume is a school of Pauline preaching. It also shows how the early church read nearly the whole of Paul in public worship.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-13:
Volume thirteen of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, holds more of Gregory the Great, then turns east: Ephraim Syrus and Aphrahat, the Persian sage. Schaff and Wace edited the series. The Syriac fathers here wrote in the language of Jesus's own country.

Gregory's later letters and his book of dialogues, full of Italian saints and wonders, open the volume. Ephraim, the fourth-century deacon of Edessa, then sings the faith in hymns of unmatched imagery; the English here is prose, but the music shows through. Aphrahat's demonstrations, written under Persian rule, are the earliest Syriac theology we have. The volume is the series' window on the eastern church.
nukariya-religion-of-the-samurai-1913:
Kaiten Nukariya, a Japanese Zen scholar of the Soto school, wrote for Western readers in 1913. The Religion of the Samurai sets out Zen thought and training as it grew in China and Japan. No earlier English book by a Japanese Zen teacher had reached so far.

Nukariya tells the rise of Zen, its view of mind and world, and the hard drill of sitting and koan work. He shows how the warrior class of Japan took Zen as its inner rule of life. His tone is calm, clear, and free of mystic fog. The book first opened Zen to the English-speaking world.
odd-charges-odd-craft-part-13:
William Wymark Jacobs wrote the comic sea tale Odd Charges. It is part thirteen of his book Odd Craft. The scene opens in the Cauliflower inn tap room. A stranger eats and drinks in quiet comfort. An old man nearby longs for beer and tobacco.

The old man wishes a conjurer could fill his mug. The stranger then raps his pipe on the table. Beer and tobacco appear as if by magic. Talk turns to a conjurer who once performed in Claybury. Jacobs builds humor from talk, timing, and surprise. The tale shows his gift for inn talk and quiet trickery.
openalex-w146743813:
Betty Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in August 2012. The team studied a particle called J/psi in lead collisions. Collisions ran at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN. They compared lead results with proton collision results.

The team found fewer J/psi particles than scaling predicted. That shortfall is called suppression in the report. The shortfall showed no strong link to collision centrality. Results differed from those at lower collision energies. Models with charm quarks in hot, free matter fit. Such matter is called quark-gluon plasma by physicists. The work probes matter formed just after the Big Bang.
openalex-w1648382113:
Viviana Fanti and the NA48 Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physics Letters B in October 1999. The team worked at CERN and partner institutes across Europe. Their subject is direct CP violation in kaon decays. A neutral kaon can decay into two pions.

CP violation means matter and antimatter behave slightly differently. Direct forms of it are rare and hard to measure. The paper presents a new measurement of that effect. The hosted sample preserves the long author and institute lists. It gives no abstract text stating the numeric result. Readers can confirm the team, venue, and topic from the sample.
openalex-w2023422813:
Marcelo Samsa, Juan Mondotte, Nestor Iglesias and colleagues studied how dengue virus builds new copies of itself. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2009. Dengue causes high rates of illness worldwide. Vaccines and antivirals were urgently needed. How the virus packs its genome was poorly known.

The team watched the virus capsid protein inside infected cells. The protein gathered on fat droplets inside the cell. Small changes to the protein broke that targeting. Those changes also blocked new virus particle formation. Changing droplet amounts in cells changed virus growth. The authors propose the droplets hold the capsid early on. They may then serve as a platform for packing the genome.
openalex-w2054504313:
Stefan Monecke, Geoffrey Coombs, Anna Shore and colleagues compiled a field guide to resistant staph bacteria. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. MRSA bacteria resist common antibiotics. They have become a global health challenge. New strains now appear outside hospitals too. Some strains produce a toxin that raises concern.

The team typed over three thousand bacterial isolates. Samples came from clinics and animal sources worldwide. A DNA microarray identified each strain's type. The guide sorts strains into pandemic, epidemic and sporadic groups. It describes where each major clone occurs. Tracking clones helps hospitals spot outbreaks early. It also guides infection control across countries.
openalex-w2062462813:
Miriam Scheel, Mario Rohrer, Christian Huggel and colleagues tested satellite rainfall estimates in the Central Andes. Their paper appeared in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences in 2011. Mountain regions often lack good rain gauges. Climate projects still need solid rainfall records. Satellite products could fill the gaps.

The team compared a satellite rainfall product with gauges. Study areas covered Cuzco in Peru and La Paz in Bolivia. Daily satellite amounts showed large biases. The product caught strong rain events well. It still underestimated how heavy they were. Near La Paz it raised many false alarms. Averaging over longer periods improved agreement strongly. The results guide careful use of satellite rain data.
openalex-w2138831913:
Catrine Tudor-Locke, Cora Craig, Wendy Brown, and colleagues published this review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2011. They ask a simple public question: how many steps per day are enough for adults? Step counters make the question practical, but published step targets varied widely.

Healthy adults typically take between four thousand and eighteen thousand steps a day. The authors judge ten thousand steps a reasonable target for this group. Programs that add walking usually raise counts by about two thousand to twenty-five hundred steps. Studies also tie walking pace to effort: about one hundred steps per minute marks the floor of moderate intensity walking.
openalex-w2154052713:
Humberto Lara, Elsa Garza-Treviño, Liliana Ixtepan-Turrent, and Dinesh Singh published this review in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2011. They survey silver nanoparticles as broad killers of bacteria and viruses. Silver has served medicine since ancient times, and shrinking it to nanoscale size has opened new uses in wound care and infection control.

The review explains how the particles attack microbes, with HIV as the best-studied virus case. The particles bind the outer coat of enveloped viruses and block them from entering cells. Work on HIV showed blocked transmission in human cervix tissue culture. The authors argue such nanosystems could strengthen infection prevention and antiviral therapy, while much about virus interactions remains unexplored.
openalex-w2164613013:
Catrine Tudor-Locke, Cora Craig, Yukitoshi Aoyagi, and colleagues published this review in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity in 2011. They translate activity guidelines into daily step counts for older adults and special populations. These groups, including people with disabilities or chronic illness, gain from moving more, but adult step targets may not fit them.

Healthy older adults average roughly two thousand to nine thousand steps a day. Special populations average somewhat lower, from about twelve hundred up. Walking programs added modest gains in older adults and larger gains in special groups. No firm pace threshold exists for older adults yet. The authors offer guiding values built from adult pace data, taken above daily living activity.
openalex-w2780728213:
The International Helminth Genomes Consortium reported this study in Nature Genetics in 2018, with Avril Coghlan and James Anthony Cotton among its authors. It compares genomes of the major parasitic worms: roundworms and flatworms. These parasites infect over a quarter of humanity for years on end. They also stunt crops and livestock, and slow growth in poor regions.

The team analyzed eighty-one worm genomes, from parasites and free-living kinds alike. They found gene families born and expanded at key points in worm evolution. Some help parasites dodge host immunity, move through tissues, or feed. Core metabolism differed widely between lineages, including in families long targeted by drugs. A computer screen then ranked fresh drug targets and candidate compounds. The resource gives worm researchers a shared basis for fighting these neglected parasites.
openalex-w3084362113:
Valentina Zavala, Paige Bracci, John Carethers, and colleagues wrote this review in the British Journal of Cancer in 2020. It summarizes cancer health disparities among racial and ethnic minorities in the United States. Gaps in cancer rates and outcomes by race are well established.

Those gaps grow from an interplay of structural, economic, social-environmental, behavioral, and biological factors. Yet most large studies of cancer causes have drawn mainly on people of European origin. Data and tissue samples from diverse groups remain scarce, which deepens the knowledge gap and risks widening the disparities themselves. The review covers the most common cancers, plus stomach, liver, pancreas, and blood cancers, to show how complex the pattern is.
openalex-w4385691013:
Unai Pascual, Patricia Balvanera, Christopher Anderson, and colleagues argue that nature's many values must guide sustainability choices, in Nature in 2023. Twenty-five years after landmark work on valuing ecosystem services, the biodiversity crisis deepens. Decisions still rest on a narrow slice of what nature means to people. Property rights and current norms decide whose values count, and many are simply ignored.

The authors organise values in layers, from worldviews down to measurable indicators. People value nature as a means to human ends, for its own sake, and through relationships of care and reciprocity. Broad values like justice and stewardship often support sustainability. Bringing these diverse values into policy, they argue, is essential if decisions are to protect both nature and human wellbeing.
openalex-w4406161213:
Catherine Overed-Sayer, Eresha Fernando, Randall Jiménez, and colleagues present the first full global assessment of freshwater animals. Their paper appeared in Nature in 2025. Rivers and lakes hold rich wildlife and support billions of people's livelihoods. Yet conservation policy has relied on data from land animals.

The team assessed extinction risk for freshwater fishes and invertebrates using the IUCN Red List. Their headline result is stark: one quarter of freshwater fauna faces extinction. Land species turn out to be poor stand-ins for freshwater ones. The findings give governments, for the first time, direct evidence for protecting freshwater life rather than guessing from other habitats.
openalex-w7205009213: What happens to mining engineers after graduation? This study tracks 548 graduates of the Federal University of Ouro Preto from 2013 to 2023, drawing on surveys of 125 alumni plus faculty records. The picture is tough: new graduates face outsized demands for prior experience, software skills, and English, and nearly half of jobs come through personal contacts. A data-rich reality check on the path from engineering degree to mining job.
openalex-w7205013813: Septic shock is the deadliest face of sepsis, and survival depends on speed. This literature review surveys current strategies for the early management of septic shock: recognizing it fast and acting immediately. The authors synthesize what intensive care research says about the measures that save lives in the first critical hours. A clinical review where the takeaway is blunt, in septic shock, delay kills.
openalex-w7207867013: Can practicing on actors make medical students more caring doctors? Researchers at a medical school in western Parana, Brazil, measured students' empathy before and after simulated patient consultations, practice visits with trained stand-ins. Using a before-and-after design, the study tests whether rehearsal builds the human side of medicine. The result speaks to a simple idea: empathy can be taught, and practice is how.
openalex-w7208815613: Lays Batista Fitaroni leads a team of authors in a study of the internship market in Mato Grosso, Brazil, published in 2026 in the journal Research, Society and Development. The sample available for this entry gives the title, authors, and journal only, without an abstract. The work's stated scope is the conditions of internship openings in the state, how attractive they are to candidates, and how organizations compete for interns.
openalex-w7208828113:
Samira Sbardelatti Regis Pereira and Jaqueline Ronconi Borba track leprosy in Rolim de Moura, a town in the interior of Rondonia state in Brazil's Legal Amazon. Leprosy, caused by a slow-growing bacterium, attacks mainly the skin and peripheral nerves, and Brazil remains among the three countries with the most new cases worldwide. The authors reviewed official notifications recorded in the national reporting system over six recent years, from 2020 to 2025.

Across those years the town notified just under two hundred cases, a steady presence rather than a fading one. The study ties that persistence directly to the region's health conditions: distance, poverty, and hard access to services keep the chain of transmission alive. For local health teams, the message is that leprosy in the Amazon interior is a standing public health problem shaped by social conditions, not a leftover of the past.
openalex-w7212017413:
Maria Fernanda Goncalves Pereira, Emilly Paschoal de Oliveira, and Valeria de Lima Kaminski review how one group of immune cells helps colorectal cancer grow. The cells are called myeloid-derived suppressor cells. They calm the immune attack that should fight the tumor. The team read studies from 2020 to 2025 in two databases. Their aim was to map the tricks these cells use.

The cells starve immune cells of nutrients they need. They release harsh molecules that blunt lymphocytes, the white cells that kill tumors. They also pour out signals that damp the whole response. Gut microbes, above all one common species, feed their growth and keep the tumor zone inflamed. The authors see the cells as a prime drug target. But the cells vary a lot, and labs still lack one standard way to spot them.
openalex-w7213272813: Weber de Santana Teles leads a large team on the path from strain to fire in the brain. Their study traces how hardships of social life — want, strain, and loss — can stir the body's guard, and how that stir can reach the brain itself. The lens joins three fields: the study of the nerves, of the guard, and of the mind's health.
openalex-w7213777613:
Catarina Fontana Gomes leads a scoping review, written in English, on changeable risk factors for cognitive decline. Their 2026 review follows PRISMA scoping guidance and searches four databases between March and April 2026. Ten studies from the last five years were selected, with emphasis on Brazil.

Decline proved many-sided, spanning clinical, behaviour, psychosocial, and social factors. Low schooling, high blood pressure, and diabetes stood among the main factors. Physical inactivity, depressive symptoms, and social isolation also appeared. Poor social conditions raised exposure to those risks and weakened protection. Since many factors can be changed, the authors frame prevention as a social task, not only a medical one.
openalex-w7213951513:
Veronica Souza de Oliveira and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva analyse digital technology in early childhood schooling. Their 2026 library study uses thematic analysis of academic work and official documents. A historical-cultural view treats technology as a cultural tool whose value depends on teaching intent.

Digital tools can widen children's languages, support creativity, and enrich interaction and learning, they find. Such gains hold when technology is tied to play and face-to-face experience. Teacher training gaps remain a central challenge, alongside excessive screen use. Integration therefore demands critical, ethical, and carefully mediated practice, the authors conclude. The child's full development, not the device, must direct classroom choices.
openalex-w7214361913:
Wandrya Karolina de Oliveira Macedo, Davi Abiner Soares Amaral, and Delner do Carmo Azevedo wrote a 2026 Brazilian legal article on children exposed on social media. Parents who post their children's lives online, sometimes for money, raise hard questions about privacy and image rights. The authors ask where civil liability falls: on parents, on legal guardians, or on the digital platforms that host the posts.

Reading constitutional protections, child law, data protection law, and internet rules, they find parent liability lacks clear, settled standards in court decisions. Platform rules, long tied to court orders for removing content, are judged too slow for cases involving children. A new 2025 digital child statute now makes careful moderation a legal duty for platforms, though courts still must settle how it applies.
openalex-w7215129713:
Dennis Soares Leite led a 2026 study of what quilombola women in Itacuruçá, Abaetetuba, Brazil, know about cervical cancer and its prevention. Quilombola communities, founded by descendants of escaped enslaved people, face weak public policy and poor access to health care, including preventive exams. One hundred women filled in a semi-structured questionnaire in a study carried out in 2017 and reported here.

The women knew least about syphilis, condom use, and the right age for the exam, gaps the team checked directly. The women described public health policy for their population as precarious despite government efforts. Few studies exist on this theme, the authors note. Their conclusion is a call for more health education research with traditional peoples, so information reaches these women well and health risks shrink.
openalex-w7220980513:
Francisco Rafael Bispo dos Santos and five co-authors reviewed studies on physical training for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with aging. Their 2026 integrative review searched health databases for work published between 2019 and 2025 on older adults, exercise, and daily functioning.

From an initial pool of well over a hundred studies, four met all their criteria. Those studies found that resistance training and its variants raised muscle mass and strength, cut body fat, and improved functional capacity. The gains point toward fewer falls, more independence, and better quality of life. The review supports regular strength work as a practical defense against frailty in old age.
original-short-stories-volume-13: Guy de Maupassant's short stories, volume thirteen: the last volume. The master's final tales, poignant and true. The complete Maupassant. The thirteenth and last volume, the master's final tales, complete at last, the last volume.
ouspensky-symbolism-of-the-tarot-1913:
P. D. Ouspensky wrote The Symbolism of the Tarot in 1913. Ouspensky was a Russian thinker drawn to hid lore and higher space. The book reads the tarot pack as a scheme of signs. Its heart is the set of two and twenty great cards, the Major Arcana.

Card by card, he draws out the sense of the Fool, the Magus, and the World. Each card, he holds, holds a key truth on man and the cosmos. The tone is that of thought, not of fate tells for pay. The book is a chief text of the tarot as a path of the mind.
pirke-avot-gorfinkle-1913:
Joseph I. Gorfinkle translated Pirke Avot into English in 1913, with an introduction and notes. Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, is a tractate of the Mishnah, gathered between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. It holds no law; instead, the rabbis of the early centuries hand down maxims on study, humility, and conduct.

Sayings ascribed to Hillel, Shammai, and their successors fill its six short chapters. If I am not for myself, who will be for me, is among its most quoted lines. Gorfinkle, a Cincinnati rabbi, made the little book handy for English readers and students. The Gutenberg text is ebook 8548. Jews still study Pirke Avot on spring Sabbaths.

plos-pone-0000013:
Pia Leppänen, Ivana Kholová, Anssi Mähönen, and co-authors switched on a growth gene in mice and watched what happened over time. The gene makes hVEGF-A165, a signal that tells the body to grow new blood vessels. In their transgenic mice, a Cre switch let them activate the gene in chosen tissue, then track short and long-term effects.

Vessel growth is a double-edged tool: it can heal starved tissue, but it can also feed tumors or leak and swell. Seeing both the early response and the lasting state of the tissue shows where the risks settle. The study informs gene therapy plans that hope to use this same signal in patients.
plos-pone-0000113:
Avihay Apatoff, Eddo Kim, and Yossef Kliger published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It tackles a practical problem in bioinformatics. The question is how to judge whether computer tools that detect homology, shared ancestry between proteins, do a good job.

Most checks of these tools lean on sequence alignment, which can bias the score. The authors work toward a scoring approach that does not depend on alignment, so different detection methods can be compared on fair terms. A cleaner yardstick helps researchers pick tools they can trust when hunting for distant protein relatives.
plos-pone-0000213:
Joana M. Ramis, Clara Collart, and James C. Smith published this developmental biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the frog Xenopus, signals called Xnrs and activin guide early development. The authors show the two signals regulate distinct sets of genes, and that activin in particular controls cell division during development.

An embryo must grow and pattern itself at the same time, and these signals help divide that labor. Separating which genes each signal controls clarifies how a ball of cells becomes an organized body. The frog work informs developmental biology broadly, since the same signal families pattern human embryos.
plos-pone-0000313:
Benoit Foligne, Georgia Zoumpopoulou, Joelle Dewulf, and colleagues published this probiotics study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Probiotics are live microbes eaten for health benefits, and how they work has been unclear. The authors report a key role for dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts, in how probiotics produce their effects.

Dendritic cells sample the gut and teach the rest of the immune system what to tolerate. If probiotics act through them, that explains benefits that reach beyond the gut itself. The paper gives the probiotic field a concrete mechanism to test, in place of vague claims about good bacteria.
plos-pone-0000413:
Sara Calhim, Simone Immler, and Tim R. Birkhead connected sperm shape to mating competition in birds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. After mating, sperm from rival males can compete inside the female, a pressure called postcopulatory sexual selection. The team asked whether species facing stronger competition have more uniform sperm.

Their title states the pattern they found: strong postcopulatory selection goes with reduced variation in sperm morphology. Uniform sperm suggests selection is fine-tuning the design tightly where competition is fierce. Bird sperm vary hugely across species, so this link helps explain what drives that variety, a long-standing puzzle in evolutionary biology.
plos-pone-0000513:
Marcelo M.S. Lima and colleagues examined a small brain region's command over sleep in rats, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The region is the substantia nigra pars compacta, better known for its role in movement and its loss in Parkinson's disease. The team studied its role in regulating sleep patterns.

Parkinson's patients famously suffer disturbed sleep, and the link is usually blamed on other brain systems. If this movement center also regulates sleep, the two symptom families share one source. Rat studies let researchers manipulate the region directly and watch sleep architecture change, something impossible to do as cleanly in patients.
plos-pone-0000613:
Themba Mzilahowa, Philip J. McCall and Ian M. Hastings examined the genetics of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes the most dangerous form of malaria. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tackles a live dispute about how the parasite's populations are structured. The title gives their answer plainly: the organism is essentially sexual in its reproduction.

How fast malaria can adapt matters for every drug and vaccine aimed at it. If parasite genes mix freely through sexual reproduction, new traits can spread in ways that control programs must plan for. The authors set out their evidence for that mixing. Malaria workers and population geneticists alike will find the argument worth weighing.
plos-pone-0000713:
Patrick Hossler, Bhanu Chandra Mulukutla and Wei-Shou Hu analyzed how mammalian cells process sugar chains on proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. N-glycosylation, the attachment of those chains, is key to the quality of many therapeutic glycoprotein drugs. A relatively small set of enzymes gives rise to a large number of N-glycans through a network of reactions and intermediates.

A systems analysis treats that network whole, rather than enzyme by enzyme. For drug makers, the exact sugar pattern on a protein can decide whether a medicine works and how long it lasts. Modeling the network points to which steps to tune in the cells that manufacture biologics.
plos-pone-0000813:
Kenji Matsuura, Takashi Tamura, Norimasa Kobayashi and colleagues unmasked the chemical signal termites use to recognize their eggs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Social insects rely heavily on pheromone communication to maintain their social life. Egg protection is among the most fundamental social behaviors in social insects. A fungus that mimics termite eggs, nicknamed the termite-ball, had recently been discovered, opening the study of egg recognition.

Their title names the pheromone: lysozyme, a protein better known for killing bacteria. Workers apparently read lysozyme on eggs as a do-not-eat, protect-this signal. A defensive enzyme doubling as a social label is an elegant economy, and a caution for pest control by mimicry.
plos-pone-0000913:
Diana Abdueva, Michele Wing, Betty Schaub and colleagues put two Affymetrix gene chips head to head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene chips let labs read the activity of thousands of genes at once. The newer exon arrays promised whole genome readings at the level of single exons, the segments that get stitched into messages.

That design dropped some older features and used a new way to prepare samples. The team ran an experimental comparison against the widely used U133Plus2 array. Head to head tests like this help labs decide whether a new platform earns its claims. They also protect later studies from building on a weaker tool.
plos-pone-0001013:
Tim Schulz, Markus Glaubitz, Doreen Kuhlow and colleagues warned that a common mouse engineering tool can switch off without warning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Cre and loxP system lets researchers delete a gene in one tissue only, a standard route to knockout mice. Studies often check a tail sample to confirm the system is present.

The team report losing Cre expression in a transgenic line, which makes tail checks unreliable. A mouse can carry the gene yet not express it where it counts. Their report is a practical warning: verify the tool itself, not just its paperwork. Many published results rest on this system.
plos-pone-0001113:
Alisha Holloway and David Begun found fast adaptation concentrated in parts of proteins whose jobs are unknown, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Adaptive protein evolution is pervasive in Drosophila fruit flies. Genomic studies had usually analyzed each protein as one unit, averaging change across its whole length.

The authors argue the targets of adaptation may sit in particular parts: domains, or regions tied to folding. In Drosophila simulans they report rampant adaptive evolution in regions of unknown function. Unknown does not mean unimportant; it may mean the most interesting biology is unmapped. Their result redirects attention to the blank stretches of familiar proteins.
plos-pone-0001213:
A protein called HCF-1 helps control cell division and partners with enzymes that add or remove chemical marks on histones. Soyoung Lee and colleagues studied one histone mark under HCF-1's influence, phosphorylation of histone H3 at serine 10, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They worked in both the worm C. elegans and mammalian cells.

The authors report that HCF-1 proteins regulate the status of this mark, which is tied to chromosome behavior during division. HCF-1 was first found through herpes simplex virus, where it helps switch the virus on. Its epigenetic role in normal cells is the subject here.
plos-pone-0001313:
Nitrosylcobalamin is a drug built on vitamin B12 that delivers nitric oxide preferentially to tumor cells, which display extra B12 receptors. Joseph Bauer and colleagues tested it alongside standard chemotherapy agents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The compound induces apoptosis through one pathway and inhibits survival signaling in cancer cells.

The authors report that nitrosylcobalamin potentiates the anti-neoplastic effects of chemotherapeutic agents via suppression of survival signaling. Two attacks are better than one if they do not simply add toxicity. Their study explores whether the B12-based pro-drug makes established drugs work harder against tumors.
plos-pone-0001413:
Maria Allhorn and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how a strep germ blunts human antibodies. The germ makes an enzyme that cuts the sugar chain on human IgG, a key class of antibody. Cut antibodies bind less well to receptors on white blood cells. That weakens the push to eat and kill germs.

The authors show how this sugar cut changes the bond between antibodies and their receptors. The change is enough to damp the immune attack. Learning this trick helps explain how strep germs slip past defense. It may also guide drugs that block the enzyme and restore antibody power.
plos-pone-0001513:
Anastasia Gardiner and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a scent gene locus in fruit flies. Gene families most often grow by copying a gene, then giving the copy a new job. A less used route is to splice one gene in new ways. The team traced that route at a scent gene called Gr39a across fly species.

They chart gains, losses, and splits of the gene's parts over time. The locus grew more complex without simple copying. Such cases broaden the tale of how scent sense evolves. Scent genes shape mating and food choice, so their change can split species apart.
plos-pone-0001613:
Marta Vicente-Crespo and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a fly protein tied to myotonic dystrophy. Proteins of this family run a switch in which gene parts are used as flies grow. That switch fails in the human ill, in part because the proteins are trapped by toxic RNA. The team studied the fly form of the protein.

They show the fly protein steers the splicing of a muscle protein and also shapes cell death. Those twin roles mirror the human protein's reach. A fly model with shared roles lets labs screen drugs fast. Hits there can then be sifted for the human disease.
plos-pone-0001713:
Pernilla Lång, Vanessa van Harmelen, Mikael Rydén, and their co-authors studied an enzyme linked to obesity in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Obesity draws macrophages, immune cells, into fat tissue, which may link fat inflammation to insulin resistance. The enzyme is TRAP, short for tartrate resistant acid phosphatase, made by macrophages and related cells.

The team reports that the monomeric, single-unit form of TRAP induces an obesity that stays insulin sensitive. That is an unusual pairing, since obesity usually brings insulin resistance with it. The full text gives the mouse or cell experiments and the metabolic measures. A form of obesity without insulin resistance is a valuable clue to which parts of fat tissue actually cause diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0001813:
Jonna Soerensen, Cemile Jakupoglu, Heike Beck, and their co-authors studied antioxidant enzymes in brain development in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The thioredoxin system is an essential regulator of cellular redox balance, the equilibrium between oxidants and antioxidants. Oxidative stress has been linked to neurodegenerative disease.

The team studied thioredoxin reductases in the brain using mice whose nervous systems lack the cytosolic form of the enzyme. The full text gives the brain development outcomes and the cell data. If the developing brain cannot manage without this redox control, the system becomes a factor in both birth defects and later degeneration.
plos-pone-0001913:
Steven Woolley, David Posada, and Keith Crandall pitted family-tree methods against each other in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When genes swap parts between lineages, a simple branching tree fails, and a network fits the past better. Many network methods exist, from statistical parsimony to median-joining, yet which one works best was unclear.

The team ran computer simulations with known histories, then scored how well each method rebuilt them. A fair race on fake data with known truth shows which tools to trust on real data. That matters for tracing viruses and other fast-changing germs, where swapped genes are common and the wrong tree misleads.
plos-pone-0002013:
Bram van Raam and co-authors asked what powers the voltage across a key membrane in neutrophils, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Neutrophils, the most common white blood cells, burn sugar for energy rather than using their mitochondria, the cell power units. Yet their mitochondria still hold a membrane potential, a voltage usually made by the respiratory chain.

The team traced the source of that voltage and compared it with other blood cells. As the title states, complex III of the chain maintains it, without the supercomplex grouping seen elsewhere. Odd wiring here reflects the neutrophil's odd, short-lived way of life.
plos-pone-0002113:
Yawei Cheng and co-authors compared men's and women's brain rhythms while watching others, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Females are usually thought to be superior in interpersonal sensitivity, the knack of reading other people. The human mirror-neuron system, which fires both when we act and when we watch others act, is considered the basic mechanism for social cognition.

Whether that system differs by gender was not known. The team measured the mu rhythm, a brain wave tied to the mirror system, in men and women. As the title frames it, they report gender differences in that rhythm. Brain data add weight to a debate long held in psychology.
plos-pone-0002213:
Wolfgang Wagner, Patrick Horn, Mirco Castoldi, and co-authors followed stem cells as they aged in the dish, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mesenchymal stem cells, which can form bone, fat, and cartilage, are a hopeful tool for cell therapy. Clinics must grow them in culture first, yet what long growth does to the cells was not precisely defined.

The team tracked the cells through long-term culture. They found that replicative senescence follows a continuous and organized course. That term means the aging of cells as they divide. Changes arrive in a set order rather than at random. Knowing that timetable helps labs judge when cultured cells are still fit for treatment.
plos-pone-0002313:
Fernando de M. Dossin, Alexandre Dufour, Elodie Dusch, and co-authors built an automated way to watch chromosome ends in a parasite's nucleus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In parasites such as Leishmania major, virulence genes often sit near telomeres, the ends of chromosomes. Telomeres cluster together in the nucleus, and their layout may help control those genes.

The team analyzed microscope images of telomeric clusters automatically, tracking how their organization changes through the parasite's life cycle. An automated count replaces slow manual scoring and makes comparisons fair. Changes in nuclear layout across life stages may track the parasite's shifts between insect and human hosts.
plos-pone-0002413:
Albanese and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Alberto Albanese, Daniele Arosio, Mariaelena Terreni, among others. Its subject is hIV-1 Pre-Integration Complexes Selectively Target Decondensed Chromatin in the Nuclear Periphery. Integration of the double-stranded DNA copy of the HIV-1 genome into host chromosomal DNA is a requirement for efficient viral replication.
