The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002513:
Zwick and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Michael E. Zwick, Maureen P. Kiley, Andrew C. Stewart, among others. Its subject is genotyping of Bacillus cereus Strains by Microarray-Based Resequencing. The ability to distinguish microbial pathogens from closely related but nonpathogenic strains is key to understanding the population biology of these organisms.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002613:
Second, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Gérard Second, Germinal Rouhan, among others. Its subject is human-Mediated Emergence as a Weed and Invasive Radiation in the Wild. The rest of the title points to the CD Genome Allotetraploid Rice Species ( Oryza , Poaceae) in the Neotropics. The rice genus Oryza serves as a model in plant genomic studies.

One open dispute is whether its spread came from natural dispersal across oceans or from recent human action. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002713:
In 2008, Wai-Tsing Chan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was murine leukemia virus spreading in mice impaired in the biogenesis of secretory lysosomes and ca 2+ -Regulated exocytosis. The catalog record names Wai-Tsing Chan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Retroviruses have been observed to bud intracellularly into multivesicular bodies (MVB), in addition to the plasma membrane. A further point appears in the abstract. Release from MVB is thought to occur by Ca 2+ -regulated fusion with the plasma membrane. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002813:
In 2008, Kerstin Diekmann and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was an optimized chloroplast DNA extraction protocol for grasses (Poaceae) proves suitable for whole plastid genome sequencing and SNP detection. Authorship is credited in the record to Kerstin Diekmann and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Obtaining chloroplast genome sequences is important to increase the knowledge about the fundamental biology of plastids. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002913:
Otilia Vieira, Diego Hartmann, Carla Cardoso and colleagues ran a systematic lab study of surfactants in 2008. Cheap, easy protection against both pregnancy and sexually spread disease is urgently needed. Surfactants, soap-like compounds, had drawn interest as possible microbicides and contraceptives for that dual role.

The PLOS ONE work tests surfactants in vitro, meaning in lab dishes rather than in people. It weighs their power to kill microbes and sperm against the standards such products must meet. Public health readers get a sober lab check on a much-hyped idea, before any claims about real-world use.
plos-pone-0003013:
Mika Kivimäki, Debbie Lawlor, George Davey Smith and co-authors asked in 2008 whether high C-reactive protein raises atherosclerosis. CRP marks body-wide inflammation and is linked to coronary events and early artery disease measures. Proof of a causal role would need links that survive adjustment for confounders.

Data came from the Whitehall II study of British civil servants. The paper weighs CRP concentration against atherosclerosis, the artery thickening behind heart attacks and strokes. Published in PLOS ONE, the question in the title is the point: association alone does not prove CRP drives disease. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003113:
Elisabetta Vannoni and Alan McElligott recorded fallow deer groans in 2008 to test honest advertisement. Models predict sexually selected calls should signal male quality. In most vertebrates, high quality males are larger, hold higher status, and gain higher reproductive success, so calls tied to size would be honest signals.

Low frequency groans indicate larger and more dominant males, the title reports, matching the prediction. Previous research had emphasized related links, and this study tests the call itself. Published in PLOS ONE, deer groans join a broad pattern of size written into sound. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003213:
Nataly Kacherovsky, Christine Tachibana, Emily Amos and colleagues study regulation of a yeast activator protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Post-translational modification regulates promoter binding by Adr1, a zinc-finger transcriptional activator of glucose-regulated genes. Support for this model includes activation of an Adr1-dependent gene without new Adr1 protein synthesis, and a requirement for a kinase.

The authors test whether promoter binding by Adr1 may be regulated by phosphorylation in its DNA-binding region. Readers follow a precise molecular switch in a well-studied yeast system. Details like this show how cells turn genes on fast without building new proteins.
plos-pone-0003313:
Gilles Spoden, Kirsten Freitag, Matthias Husmann and colleagues trace how papillomavirus enters cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Infectious entry of human papillomaviruses into host cells is an important step in the viral life cycle. For cell binding, these viruses use proteoglycans as initial attachment sites. Subsequent transfer to a secondary receptor molecule seems to be involved in virus uptake.

The title reports clathrin- and caveolin-independent entry of human papillomavirus type 16, involving tetraspanin-enriched microdomains. Readers learn that this cancer-linked virus uses an unusual entry route. Entry routes matter because blocking them is one way to stop infection early.
plos-pone-0003413:
Daniel P. Bray and colleagues described immune tissues of the common shrew in this 2008 study. Wild animals must fight the parasites they meet in nature. Studying that fight shows how immunity works outside clean labs. The European common shrew had little published detail on its immune organs.

The team examined the shrew's blood-linked and lymph tissues in detail. They recorded what those tissues contain and how they are built. Immune defense may cost resources that other body tasks need. Their survey sets a base for later work on wild small mammals.
plos-pone-0003513:
Matthieu Dacher and Brian H. Smith studied scent learning in honey bees for this 2008 paper. Worker bees are a valued model for learning and brain plasticity. A bee extends its proboscis, its mouthpart, when sugar follows a scent. Pairing scent before reward teaches a lasting link.

Pairing scent after reward creates a backward, inhibitory link instead. That link interfered with other scent learning in their tests. The clash reveals how the bee brain untangles rival scent associations. Small brains still sort new lessons against old ones. Bees learn scents fast, which is why they serve as a model for memory.
plos-pone-0003613:
Marc Liesa and co-authors studied mitochondrial shape control in this 2008 paper. Mitochondria constantly fuse together and split apart. That balance sets their size and health in the cell. Whether gene regulators in the nucleus can shift the balance was unknown.

A nuclear coactivator, PGC-1β, increased mitochondrial fusion in their work. Mice lacking a related factor had shown reduced mitochondrial size. Selective control of gene expression can thus steer organelle shape. The link ties nuclear programs to the cell's power plants. Fusion faults show up in diabetes and muscle wasting, among other diseases.
plos-pone-0003713:
Dominic Schmidt, Rory Stark, Michael D. Wilson, and colleagues published this genomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. ChIP-seq maps where proteins bind DNA across a whole genome. The method is powerful, but access to sequencing machines was still limited in 2008. Bad input libraries waste scarce machine time.

The authors present a protocol for validating deep-sequencing libraries at genome scale before a full run. Checking libraries first lets labs certify their material and avoid failed runs. The work supports a fast-growing method that soon became standard in gene research.
plos-pone-0003813:
Albert O. Edwards, Brooke L. Fridley, Katherine M. James, and colleagues published this genetics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Genome-wide association studies scan hundreds of thousands of variants for links to disease. They produce many promising hits with low p-values, and each hit must be confirmed in fresh samples.

Using the Age-Related Eye Disease Study, the authors evaluated how clustering and genotype distribution affect replication. Their checks help separate true associations from artifacts of genotyping. The work tightens the rules for claiming a gene-disease link in the genome-wide era.
plos-pone-0003913:
Omer Dushek, Sabina Mueller, Sebastien Soubies, and co-authors measured how T cell receptors move in 2008. When a T cell meets its target, receptors gather at a contact zone called the synapse. That gathering is a key step in switching the cell on. How freely receptors drift before gathering was the open question.

Their PLOS ONE article used a light-based method to track receptor movement. They tested how calcium inside the cell changes that movement. They also tested the actin skeleton, the cell's inner frame. The results help explain how receptors get into place fast enough to act.
plos-pone-0004013:
Wei Wei, Tingting Qing, Xin Ye, and co-authors grew germ cell precursors from stem cells in 2008. Primordial germ cells are the first step in making eggs and sperm. Studying them inside embryos is hard and invasive. A dish-based route would open the process to direct study.

Their PLOS ONE article reports specification of those cells from embryonic stem cells. Getting the first germ line step in vitro is a key milestone. It lets researchers probe signals that assign germ cell fate. The method may later support fertility research and conservation breeding. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004113:
Jielin Xu, Eunnyung Bae, Qinghong Zhang, and co-authors studied how cells lay down fibronectin in 2009. Fibronectin forms a scaffold that cells assemble on their surfaces. Cells lacking fibronectin can still assemble soluble fibronectin given the right base. They do so on intact fibronectin, but not on its cell-binding piece alone.

Their PLOS ONE article shows adherence modules control display of assembly sites. Contact with specific fibronectin regions switches those sites on. The work maps how a surface tells cells to build matrix. That process underlies wound healing and tissue formation. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004213:
Theresa Kelly and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neural stem cells can be isolated from different regions of the central nervous system. Whether stem cells from different regions keep their regional identity, or lose it during expansion in culture, was controversial.

The team compared cultured spinal cord neural stem cells with brain-derived ones, checking lineage and regional identity. Their comparison tests whether a stem cell remembers where it came from after weeks in a dish. The answer matters for choosing cells for repair therapies, where identity guides what a graft can become.
plos-pone-0004313:
Nael Lapidus and colleagues published this nutrition study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 2006, a Médecins Sans Frontières nutritional program ran in the Maradi region of Niger. It included 68,001 children aged six to fifty-nine months with moderate or severe malnutrition. Admission used standard weight and arm measures for children under five. The program was among the largest of its kind.

Using that program's records, the team estimated the mortality risk among the admitted children. Knowing which malnourished children die despite feeding helps programs triage scarce care. The study turns a humanitarian operation's records into guidance for the next emergency.
plos-pone-0004413:
A parasitic worm disease still relies on a single drug. Conor Caffrey, Andreas Rohwer, Frank Oellien, and co-authors hunt for new targets in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. Schistosomiasis is a prevalent, chronic helminth disease in tropical regions, treated mainly with praziquantel.

Reliance on one drug is risky if clinically relevant resistance emerges and spreads. The authors use a comparative chemogenomics strategy to predict potential drug targets in Schistosoma mansoni. Comparing drug data across species can reveal the worm's weak points. New targets could back up the sole drug. Chemogenomics borrows drug data from other species to rank the worm's targets fast.
plos-pone-0004513:
A gene called Rx is needed inside the very cells that build the eye, show Olga Medina-Martinez, Felipe Amaya-Manzanares, Chaomei Liu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rx is a homeobox gene, a master control gene, required for eye formation in backboned animals. Mice lacking it develop no eyes and no posterior pituitary, a small brain gland.

To test whether Rx is needed cell by cell, the team built embryos that mix normal cells with cells lacking Rx. Such mixed animals are called chimeras. The results show a cell-autonomous requirement: cells without Rx cannot take part in building the retina or the gland, even beside healthy neighbors. That precision matters for understanding birth defects of the eye.
plos-pone-0004613:
A scaffold protein in a tiny worm tunes both synapses and behavior based on past experience, report Lesley Emtage, Howard Chang, Rebecca Tiver, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is MAGI-1. It is well established that the strength of synaptic connections can be rapidly modified by neural activity. How environment and prior experience modulate that plasticity is only beginning to be understood.

Working in the worm C. elegans, the team shows MAGI-1 modulates the synaptic localization of AMPA receptors, key receivers of the brain's main excitatory signal. It also shapes behavioral plasticity in response to prior experience. A worm with a few hundred neurons lets researchers follow one protein from molecule to behavior, a chain rarely visible in larger brains.
plos-pone-0004713:
Emmanuel Coron and colleagues charted early harm to gut lining and nerves after Shigella infection in human colon, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Shigella is a gut invading bacterium that causes sharp inflammation and bloody diarrhea. Much was known about late damage, but early steps in human tissue were less clear.

The team looked at how soon the lining and the gut nerve network are hurt. They focused on the local setting where immune cells and nerves meet the invader. Early maps can point to new ways to block damage. They may also explain pain and gut upset in this infection.
plos-pone-0004813:
Leo Kenefic and colleagues argued for pre Columbian origins for North American anthrax, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Disease introduction into the New World during colonial expansion is well documented and had major impacts on indigenous populations. However, few diseases have been associated with early human migrations into North America during the late Pleistocene epoch. When Asia and North America were connected by land.

Genetic evidence places anthrax lineages before European contact. That rewrites part of disease history in the Americas. Ancient migrations may have carried spores southward. Findings inform biodefense and evolutionary studies alike. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004913:
Brandi Rollins led a team that read mitochondrial DNA in people with major mental illness for PLOS ONE in 2009. Mitochondria make most of the energy that brain cells run on. Faults in them have been found in people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression. That raised a clear question: do some people carry DNA variants in their mitochondria that raise the risk of these illnesses?

The team read mitochondrial genomes from patients and compared the variants they found. They looked for variants that show up more in one illness, or that are shared across all three. Shared finds would point to a shared energy flaw. Clear results, in either sense, help guide the search for causes.
plos-pone-0005013:
In southern Africa, the clade C form of HIV dominates. Most patients there have chronic, untreated infection. Danni Ramduth and colleagues mapped their T cell targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on CD4 helper T cells. Earlier work had linked strong CD8 responses against the viral Gag protein to lower viral loads.

The study identified the immunodominant epitopes these CD4 cells attack. Epitopes are the exact viral pieces the immune system sees. The hit list shows where immune fire concentrates. Vaccine designs for this region can use it. Clade C is the world's most common HIV form. Matching vaccines to it is a global priority.
plos-pone-0005113:
Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease. Different strains of it invade different tissues. Jorge Freitas and colleagues asked what steers that choice. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They infected mice with two monoclonal strains. Earlier work showed parasite and host genetics both matter. This study focused on the host's MHC gene region.

The MHC region influenced the strains' tissue tropism. The same strain went to different tissues in different hosts. Host immune genes help decide where infection takes hold. That links immune genetics to disease pattern. Chagas disease varies greatly between patients. Host genetics may explain part of that variety. The finding could guide risk prediction in endemic regions.
plos-pone-0005213:
Homeobox genes pattern the growing embryo, deciding where body parts form. Most control over them was thought to happen when genes are first read into RNA. Villaescusa and colleagues found a second layer of control in PLOS ONE in 2009 involving the protein Prep1.

Prep1 is known for work inside the nucleus with partner proteins. Outside the nucleus, the team showed, it pairs with a protein called 4EHP and blocks production of the Hoxb4 protein. So an embryo-patterning gene can be held back after its message is made, not just before.
plos-pone-0005313:
Biologists usually study networks inside single pathways, molecule by molecule. Far less is known about how whole biological processes interact with each other. Dotan-Cohen and colleagues built linkage networks between processes themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009.

These biological process linkage networks connect higher-order systems, such as growth, defense, and energy use. Links between processes can explain side effects that single-pathway views miss. Zooming out to process level gives systems biology a wider map of how the cell is organized. When one process fails, its linked partners often fail too, so these maps help explain why one drug can have side effects in parts of the body far from its target.
plos-pone-0005413:
A frog from Borneo, Huia cavitympanum, is the first amphibian known to call only in ultrasound, above twenty kilohertz. Arch and colleagues tested whether those calls truly serve communication in PLOS ONE in 2009, using playback experiments in the frog's habitat.

Playing recorded calls back to the frogs showed responses to the ultrasonic signals. Pure ultrasonic communication is well suited to life beside loud streams, where low calls would drown. The Bornean frog hears a private channel that most predators and researchers miss. Calls too high for our ears fill the night air in the tropics,. This frog is proof that a whole talk can pass in a range that most ears in the wood will never hear at all.
plos-pone-0005513:
David Schleheck and colleagues studied how a common bacterium lives in liquid in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Bacteria often grow stuck together in films on surfaces, then shed single cells that swim away. The germ studied here, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, can cause hard-to-treat infections.

The team found that in liquid, the germ prefers to grow as floating clumps, like films without a surface. When food ran out, the clumps broke up and cells dispersed. Knowing how these clumps form and scatter may help fight infections in lungs and wounds. The clumps may also shield the germ from drugs and immune attack, much as surface films do.
plos-pone-0005613:
Mariana Dias Batista and co-authors studied a herpesvirus in people newly infected with HIV in São Paulo, Brazil, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Human herpesvirus 8 causes Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer seen often in people with HIV. Its behaviour in the first phase of HIV infection was poorly described.

The team measured how common the virus was, what signs came with it, and how often new infections occurred. The study focused on a group that included many men who have sex with men. Early data like this help clinics watch for a cancer that can follow.
plos-pone-0005713:
Rossana Mineri and colleagues asked in 2009 how human cells cope when their mitochondrial DNA is gone. Mitochondria carry a small ring of DNA that codes for a few key parts of the cell's power chain. Most of the chain's parts, though, are coded in the main genome.

Cells stripped of that small genome must rebalance two whole gene systems. The team tracked how the cells react and adjust. Their work shows which backup paths keep the cells alive. That knowledge bears on diseases where mitochondrial DNA is lost or damaged, and on how cells handle stress to their power supply.
plos-pone-0005813:
Charlotta Lindvall and co-authors showed in 2009 that a Wnt co-receptor is required for normal breast development in mice. Wnt signals pass through receptors called Frizzled plus a co-receptor, LRP5 or LRP6. The group had already tied LRP5 to ductal stem cell activity in the mammary gland.

Removing Lrp6 disrupted normal gland development in their mice. That makes the co-receptor more than a backup for its sibling. Faults in this pathway could underlie some breast development problems, and Wnt signaling is also a cancer lever. Mapping which co-receptor does what refines both fields.
plos-pone-0005913:
Feng Xu and co-authors analyzed in 2009 how mutations in protein kinases move together across their catalytic cores. Kinases form the largest family of signaling proteins in complex cells and touch nearly every cell decision. How they choose and phosphorylate their targets is only partly understood.

Correlated mutation analysis finds residue pairs that change in step over evolution, betraying hidden contacts and mechanisms. Applied to serine and threonine kinases, it highlights the moving parts of catalysis. Those couplings can guide drug design, since kinases are top drug targets. The study is a map of constraints inside the family's engine.
plos-pone-0006013:
Telomeres are the caps that guard the ends of chromosomes, and they shorten with age. Jasen Wise, Richard Crout, Daniel McNeil and colleagues took a finer look in 2009 than most studies attempt. Instead of averaging all telomeres in a cell, their PLOS ONE paper measures the telomere on each chromosome arm and compares its length with the arm's size.

The two track each other, the title reports: longer arms carry longer telomeres. A pattern like that hints at rules that set cap length across the whole genome. Arm-by-arm data could refine how telomere length is used as a sign of cell age and health, since a single average may hide wide differences within one cell.
plos-pone-0006113:
One inflammation signal can drive two vessel diseases in two different ways. Sofia Xanthoulea, Melanie Thelen, Chantal Pöttgens and colleagues split those ways in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper removes the p55 TNF receptor, the main signaling receptor for the inflammatory cytokine TNF, in mice prone to artery disease. It then tests atherosclerosis and angiotensin-driven aneurysms side by side.

Without the receptor, atherosclerosis fell, yet aneurysms changed little, the title reports. A split result warns drug makers that blocking a signal may help one vessel disease and leave another untouched. The work helps set honest hopes for anti-TNF treatment in heart and vessel care.
plos-pone-0006213:
Plague still casts a long shadow, spread mainly by flea bites from infected animals. Jing Geng and colleagues studied a regulator called Hfq in the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Hfq helps the cell manage its messages after they are made, acting like a global switch.

The work ties Hfq to the bacterium's ability to cause disease. Losing a single message manager can weaken a germ built for rapid, severe infection. That makes such regulators interesting targets for new anti-plague drugs. The study also adds to the basic picture of how this feared pathogen coordinates its attack.
plos-pone-0006313:
For people with celiac disease, even traces of gluten in food can restart gut inflammation. Jennifer Ehren and colleagues tested a food-grade enzyme preparation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A gluten-free diet works for most patients, but accidental gluten exposure is common and causes relapse.

Enzymes that digest gluten in food could act as a backup safety net. The preparation showed modest gluten detoxification properties, per the title. Modest is not a licence to eat gluten freely, the work implies. But even partial breakdown might blunt accidental exposures that patients cannot avoid.
plos-pone-0006413:
Glutathione protects cells from chemical damage, and a separate pool sits inside the nucleus. Jelena Markovic and colleagues depleted that nuclear pool in 3t3 fibroblasts in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Glutathione is essential in mammalian cells and yeast, and the nuclear pool's role in proliferation and differentiation was still debated.

Depleting nuclear glutathione impaired cell proliferation in the fibroblasts. The nucleus thus guards its own supply for growth. A protected nuclear stock may shield DNA during division. The result settles part of a long debate with direct evidence. The find may guide work on how cells guard their DNA while they grow.
plos-pone-0006513:
Jiajie Zhang and Hongbin Wang explored how external aids interact with memory in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is commonly hypothesized that external representations serve as memory aids. Diagrams, notes, and displays might improve task performance by expanding the limited capacity of working memory. The authors tested how that expansion actually works.

Their exploration asks when an outside aid truly helps and when it merely adds clutter. Working memory limits shape learning, design, and everyday problem solving. Clear rules for using external representations can improve teaching and interface design. The paper connects a lab question to practical choices in education and technology.
plos-pone-0006613:
Wendy Gordon, Didem Vardar-Ulu, Sarah L'Heureux, and colleagues studied a maturation cut in Notch receptors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Notch receptors are normally cleaved during maturation by a furin-like protease at an extracellular site termed S1. That cut creates a heterodimer of non-covalently associated subunits. The team studied effects of S1 cleavage on structure, surface export, and signaling activity of human Notch1 and Notch2.

If the cut is required for the receptor to reach the surface and signal, it becomes a control point. Notch signaling guides development and is hijacked in cancers. Details of its maturation matter for drugs that aim to block it.
plos-pone-0006713:
Chad E. Green and colleagues studied signals between tumor cells and macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Macrophages that gather in tumors shape how cancer progresses. They can alter immune responses, blood vessel growth, and spread. The chemical conversations behind those effects were poorly mapped. The team used colon cancer cells and a macrophage cell line.

They traced chemoattractant signaling running between the two cell types. That signaling regulated cancer cell migration in their experiments. It also affected metastasis and new blood vessel formation. Blocking the conversation could slow several parts of cancer at once. The work identifies signaling links worth testing as drug targets.
plos-pone-0006813:
Ute Distler and colleagues examined a toxin receptor found on some cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pancreatic and colon cancers remain common killers worldwide. Adjuvant chemotherapy has improved only modestly over decades. Bacterial toxins that bind specific cell-surface sugars offer a possible new therapy. The receptor studied is the glycosphingolipid Gb3Cer, also called CD77.

The team determined where this receptor is expressed. Its association with tumors makes it a promising therapeutic target. Shiga toxin binds this very receptor with high specificity. A toxin aimed at a tumor marker could spare healthy tissue. The work maps the target before such therapy can be tested.
plos-pone-0006913:
Ming-Yi Lee and his team grew vessel-making cells from placenta stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cells are human placental multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells, taken from a full-term placenta. How well they build vessels was not known. The cells bear a set of grips, called integrins, on their skin. In a dish, they could be coaxed to change kind.

The new growth of vessels hung on one grip pair, integrin alpha five beta one. Block that pair, and vessel growth fell off. One grip as the gate keeps the rules plain. Placenta cells are rich in supply and raise no hard qualms to take. If they build vessels well, they may serve the craft of healing with new tissue.
plos-pone-0007013:
Sara Karami, Paul Brennan, Philip Rosenberg, and colleagues studied vitamin D genes and kidney cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The kidney converts vitamin D into its active form. Vitamin D works by binding its receptor, VDR, inside cells. Most genetic studies had focused on that receptor gene alone.

The team widened the lens to the whole vitamin D pathway. They analyzed single-letter variants and haplotypes across those genes. Then they tested links with renal cancer risk. A pathway-wide view can catch effects that one-gene studies miss. It may also hint at how vitamin D protects tissue, if it does.
plos-pone-0007113:
Ewa Pilka, Frank Niesen, Wen Hwa Lee, and colleagues examined detox enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Carbonyl reduction is a first step in clearing many foreign chemicals. In mammals it is run mostly by two protein families. These enzymes also handle natural compounds made by the body. Their tastes for different substrates were the question.

The team studied the structure of human monomeric carbonyl reductases. Structure explained why each enzyme prefers certain substrates. That knowledge helps predict how a new drug will be broken down. It also explains some side effects when clearance routes overlap.
plos-pone-0007213:
Alicia Montesinos, Stephen J. Tonsor, Carlos Alonso-Blanco, and colleagues studied a small flowering plant in its native range in 2009. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, a favorite model in genetics. Understanding plant adaptation needs both population counts and genetic data from real habitats.

Native populations differ in climate and other local conditions. The authors compare demographic and genetic patterns among populations from contrasting environments. Their PLOS ONE work links how populations grow and shrink with how their genes vary. Ecologists can use that link to study adaptation outside the lab.
plos-pone-0007313:
Jason E. Cain, Epshita Islam, Fiona Haxho, and colleagues studied kidney development signals in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mutations that truncate the GLI3 protein cause Pallister-Hall syndrome with kidney malformation. That link suggests Hedgehog signaling is required during renal development, when kidneys build their filtering units called nephrons.

Hedgehog signaling changes GLI3 processing between activator and repressor forms. The authors show the GLI3 repressor controls nephron number. It acts through regulation of Wnt11 and Ret in ureteric tip cells. Their work connects a developmental signal to the final filtering capacity of kidneys.
plos-pone-0007413:
Elisabeth Lippert, Thomas Karrasch, Xiaolun Sun, and colleagues studied gut inflammation in germ-free engineered mice in 2009. Limited information was available on molecular mechanisms behind Campylobacter jejuni diarrheal illness. This bacterium is a leading cause of food-borne diarrhea worldwide, yet its disease mechanisms inside the intestine remained incompletely mapped in animal models.

The authors use gnotobiotic mice lacking IL-10 and carrying an NF-kappaB reporter. These mice develop rapid and severe colitis after Campylobacter jejuni infection. Their PLOS ONE model lets researchers watch inflammatory signaling directly. The system supports studies of food-borne infection and inflammatory bowel disease.
plos-pone-0007513:
Yasuaki Takeda and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how zebrafish embryos protect their future reproductive cells. A microRNA called miR-430 silences germline genes in ordinary body cells. Only the primordial germ cells should keep those genes active. Silencing works partly by shortening the message's protective tail, which leads to its destruction. The team studied a protein, DAZL, that works against that silencing.

DAZL relieves the repression by controlling the length of the poly(A) tail on germline messages. A longer tail means the message survives and can be used. In this tug of war, DAZL safeguards the messages that future sperm and eggs depend on. The study shows tail length as a precise dial for gene control in the early embryo. Small changes at a message's end decide which cells keep their reproductive potential.
plos-pone-0007613:
Duncan Astle, Anna Nobre, and Gaia Scerif published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on attention and memory. People can attend to chosen features of what they see, like color over shape. They can also switch that focus from one feature to another. Most research tests attention on present objects. This study asked whether the same attentional set can be applied to features held in memory. Perception and remembrance were compared directly.

The results show attention reaches back into memory, not only forward into the senses. A mental filter prepared for a feature works on remembered items too. That unifies two literatures that often run apart. Everyday life demands it: we search our memories with the same questions we aim at the world. The study gives that everyday skill a controlled test. It clarifies how the mind's spotlight moves through time as well as space.
plos-pone-0007713:
Dietrich Gotzek and Kenneth Ross published a review in PLOS ONE in 2009. It takes stock of a famous model system in fire ants. A single gene, Gp-9, is tied to how fire ant colonies are organized. Some colonies accept one queen, and others accept many.

The authors sum up what Gp-9 research has shown and where it stands. The system has taught biologists a great deal about the evolution of social life in insects. It also bears on wider questions, such as how genes shape group behavior. The review marks both the progress made and the disputes still open.
plos-pone-0007813:
Sushmita Roy and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It improves computer prediction of which proteins interact with each other. Most prediction methods use protein domains as clues. Domains capture the conserved surfaces where proteins bind.

The catch is that many proteins lack domain information. Those proteins are left out of domain-based tools. The authors instead exploit amino acid composition, the recipe of building blocks in each protein. Composition alone carried useful signal about interactions. Their method widens prediction to proteins that domains cannot describe. Better interaction maps support drug and disease research.
plos-pone-0007913:
Kathleen Averette and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces how anthrax lethal toxin kills immune cells. Sensors inside cells, called NOD-like receptors, detect invasion and danger signals. Their activation can trigger fast cell death programs.

The anthrax toxin pries open lysosomes, the cell's waste sacs. Enzymes called cathepsins then spill into the cell body. The authors show this chain depends on one sensor, Nlrp1b. Naming the required sensor explains why some cells and mouse strains resist the toxin. It also maps a step where protection might be possible.
plos-pone-0008013:
Susana Aguilar and colleagues armed stem cells to protect scarred lungs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lung scarring, called pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lung until breathing fails, and no good treatment exists. The team gave bone marrow stem cells a gene for a growth factor that supports lung lining cells.

The gene could be switched on with a drug pulse, keeping control in the doctors' hands. Treated mice withstood a scarring agent that badly harms untreated lungs. Cell therapy that delivers its medicine on site and on command is a step toward real care for this grim disease.
plos-pone-0008113:
Jon Bohlin and Eystein Skjerve tested how steady a bacterium's DNA dialect stays across its genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Each species favors certain short DNA words, a pattern called its genomic signature. Once adjusted for the genome's letter balance, that pattern can name a species from random scraps.

The team checked whether the dialect holds evenly from one end of a genome to the other. Largely, it does, which is what makes scrap-based naming work at all. The check strengthens a tool used to sort microbes in soil, water, and gut samples without growing them.
plos-pone-0008213:
Francisco Tinahones and colleagues studied fat around the adult thymus in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The adult thymus slowly turns into fat tissue with age. That fat was not thought of as a source of growth signals. Recent work by the group showed it makes factors that grow blood vessels. It also prompts endothelial cells to multiply.

The team measured VEGF gene expression in this thymus fat. They compared it with a hypoxia-related factor and with cyclooxygenase-2. Links among these signals could explain how the fat supports vessel growth. The study treats an overlooked tissue as an active player.
plos-pone-0008313:
Pushpa Malla and colleagues reported tuberculosis treatment experience from Nepal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multi-drug resistant tuberculosis cannot be cured with standard first-line drugs. Treatment is long and difficult for patients. The study described outcomes for outpatients on a standardized regimen in Nepal. Care was ambulatory, meaning patients were not kept in hospital.

Data covered patients enrolled in the national program in 2005 and 2006. The program was approved under the Green Light Committee system. Showing outpatient care can work matters for poor, rural patients. The experience offers a model for similar countries.
plos-pone-0008413:
Andrew Rhyne and colleagues warned of a fishery collapse in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Fishery management has historically been inexact and reactionary. Action often comes only after a stock is overfished or collapses. The ornamental invertebrate fishery in Florida collects animals for aquariums. Catches were increasing across a more diverse array of species.

The authors call this fishery ecologically unsound in their title's phrase, crawling to collapse. Collecting many species at rising rates spreads risk widely. Early warning may allow management before ornamental stocks crash. The study urges proactive rules for the aquarium trade.
plos-pone-0008513:
Maria Camats and co-authors study a Ras protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Ras genes are classic cancer genes that also carry normal signals. Three forms exist in mammals: H-ras, K-ras, and N-ras. Their signals shape growth in healthy and tumor cells alike. The team focus on a form called p19 H-Ras. It arises from processing of the H-ras message. They ask what it does to the cell cycle.

P19 H-Ras induces a delay between the G1 and S phases. Cells pause in a reversible quiescence state, alive but not dividing. The finding assigns a braking role to this Ras form. It contrasts with the growth push of its sister forms.
plos-pone-0008613:
Shilin Chen and co-authors validate a DNA barcode for medicinal plants in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. DNA barcoding identifies species from a short standard sequence. The plant working group recommended a two-locus barcode, rbcL plus matK. That combination discriminated many but not all plant species. Medicinal plants need reliable identification, since substitutes can be unsafe. The team test the ITS2 region as a novel barcode for those species.

ITS2 successfully identifies a high share of medicinal plant samples. Its discrimination at species level exceeds the recommended pair in their test. A better barcode helps verify herbal medicines and protect consumers. It also aids conservation of wild medicinal species.
plos-pone-0008713:
Renee Chan, Kit Yuen, Wendy Yu, and colleagues compared two flu viruses in airway cells. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used human bronchial epithelial cells grown in the lab. H5N1 bird flu kills many of the people it infects. The pandemic H1N1 virus spread widely but killed far fewer. Cell maturity might explain part of that gap.

The team grew airway cells in flat and in more mature, layered forms. They then infected each form with both viruses. Growth of the viruses and the cells' alarm responses shifted with maturity. Lab models of flu should match the real airway state closely.
plos-pone-0008813:
Joseph Poduslo, Emily Gilles, Muthu Ramakrishnan, and colleagues found where amyloid-beta grabs onto nerve cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer disease involves amyloid-beta, a sticky protein fragment. Whether plaques outside cells or buildup inside starts the damage is debated. Amyloid made inside cells must first be produced from a larger parent protein. Binding to the cell surface is an early step in that story.

A segment of amyloid, called the HH domain, provided the gripping structure. It mediated binding in rat PC12 cells and mouse brain neurons. Blocking that grip might slow amyloid's entry into cells. The address gives drug designers a precise target.
plos-pone-0008913:
Xuemin Guo, Nancy Lewis Ernst, Jason Carnes, and colleagues showed two small zinc fingers are vital for a parasite's RNA editing. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness in Africa. Most of its mitochondrial gene messages must be edited before use. Editing inserts and deletes letters to make messages readable. A machine called the editosome does that work, and KREPA3 holds it together.

Removing KREPA3's zinc finger motifs broke editing in living parasites. The same loss mattered less in test-tube assays, a telling gap. Complete editing in the real cell needs those fingers. The parasite's unique editing machinery remains a drug target.
plos-pone-0009013:
Sheng-Li Lin and co-authors traced how a hormone receptor variant can flip a cancer drug's effect, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tamoxifen usually blocks estrogen action in hormone-sensitive cancers. A newer receptor variant, ER-alpha36, lacks the usual gene-switching parts. It works instead through fast signals at the cell surface.

In endometrial cancer cells, this variant made tamoxifen act like estrogen instead. It fired two growth pathways, MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt, in response to the drug. A blocker becoming a trigger helps explain tamoxifen resistance. Tumours carrying the variant may need a different treatment plan.
plos-pone-0009113:
Deanna Navaroli and Haley Melikian fitted tiny glowing handles onto the brain's dopamine pump, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dopamine transporter clears dopamine from the gaps between nerve cells. It is the main target of cocaine and of several prescription drugs. Signals inside the cell retune the pump within minutes.

The team inserted tetracysteine motifs into the pump's outer loops. Those motifs light up when a matching dye is added. Researchers can then watch the pump move and respond in living cells. Seeing the pump's response to amphetamine may clarify addiction's mechanics.
plos-pone-0009213:
Kumi Kaneko and co-authors published this insect brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It looks inside the brain of the European honeybee. Bees depend heavily on vision, and a worker's brain changes shape as she gains foraging experience. The authors focused on bee versions of three genes known from other animals.

The genes, named Futsch, Tau, and MESK2 in flies, help build and run nerve cells. Using in situ hybridization, the team mapped where each gene is switched on in the bee brain. The maps show which brain regions use these genes. That helps link bee brain structure to the visual skills that guide social behavior.
plos-pone-0009313:
Leslie Crews and co-authors published this brain disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lewy body diseases, including Parkinson's and dementia with Lewy bodies, share one mark: clumps of alpha-synuclein in the brain. Cells normally clear such waste through autophagy, a self-eating cleanup system. Signs pointed to that cleanup failing in these diseases.

The team compared brain tissue from patients with lab models of alpha-synuclein disease. They found selective changes in the autophagy pathway, not a blanket breakdown. Knowing exactly which cleanup steps falter matters for therapy. It suggests which parts of the system a drug should aim to restore.
plos-pone-0009413:
Elisabeth Kugelberg and co-authors published this meningitis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neisseria meningitidis is a bacterium that can ride harmlessly in the throat or cause deadly disease. A mobile DNA piece called IS1301 sometimes lands in its capsule-making region. In Spanish group C strains, that insertion made the bacteria harder for the immune system to kill.

The team investigated what IS1301 does in the same spot more broadly. They looked at both carriage in healthy people and invasive disease. A small DNA insertion that shifts that balance matters for vaccines and outbreak tracking. It shows how one jump of DNA can change a germ's character.
plos-pone-0009513:
Andrew Hodges and colleagues used computer models to extend a bacterial gene network in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene networks guide how bacteria respond to stress and form surface films. Most networks are known only in part. Gene activity data, though, are now plentiful. The team used a Bayesian network method, which weighs likely links between genes, to infer missing parts.

Starting from a known core network, their method predicted new regulators. Some govern responses to reactive oxygen, and others govern biofilm growth. Each prediction is a claim that lab work can test. The approach turns piles of activity data into wiring diagrams for the cell.
plos-pone-0009613:
Deepak Sharma and Jayanta Bhattacharya studied a human protein that may hinder HIV in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV must ship its RNA out of the cell nucleus to make new virus. It uses its own protein, Rev, to run that export. A human protein called DDX3X is also involved in the process. The team examined how limits built into DDX3X by evolution affect the export step.

Their analysis suggests those built in limits can interfere with Rev's work. In effect, the human protein is a roadblock in the virus's supply line. Understanding the roadblock could inspire drugs that strengthen it. The study reads evolution's fingerprints for clues to antiviral defense.
plos-pone-0009713:
Donor organs are kept cold to slow decay before transplant, but cold storage still harms cells. Ralf Lösel and colleagues tested a protective compound in PLOS ONE in 2010. The compound is N-octanoyl dopamine, a changed form of the signal chemical dopamine.

Unlike regular dopamine, the new compound does not disturb blood flow, so it is called non-hemodynamic. The team checked whether it guards cells during cold organ storage. Better protection could stretch the time an organ stays usable. That would ease one of the tightest bottlenecks in transplant medicine.
plos-pone-0009813:
Brain-computer interfaces let people control devices with brain signals alone. Martijn Schreuder, Benjamin Blankertz, and Michael Tangermann presented a new auditory version in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most earlier systems relied on vision instead of hearing.

The paradigm uses spatial hearing, the sense of where a sound comes from, as its cue. Different sound positions stand for different choices the user can select. A multi-class system offers more than two options at once. It also widens the options for hands-free control. Hearing-based control could help users who cannot rely on their eyes.
plos-pone-0009913:
Anthrax lethal toxin can kill immune cells, yet some cells learn to tolerate it. Nando Dulal Das and colleagues studied that tolerance in a mouse immune cell line. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tolerance here means surviving doses that should kill.

The cells were RAW 264.7, a standard macrophage line. Two players stood out: NF-kappa-B, a master immune switch, and Jmjd3, an enzyme that removes a histone mark called H3K27me3. Removing that mark can free silenced genes to speak. The pairing may explain how the cells endure the toxin.
plos-pone-0010013:
Christian Stegmann, Reinhard Lührmann, and Markus Wahl reported a protein structure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was PPIL1, a small enzyme that sits inside the spliceosome, the machine that cuts introns out of RNA messages. PPIL1 also binds a partner protein called SKIP through a site apart from its active center.

The team solved the crystal structure of PPIL1 bound to the drug cyclosporine A. From that shape, they proposed how a straight stretch of SKIP might bind. Knowing the shape helps explain how the splicing machine holds together and how drugs can grip one of its parts.
plos-pone-0010213:
The authors were Laura Heath, Susan Conway, Laura Jones, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined HIV passing from mother to child in breast milk. Breast milk transmission remains a major route of infection in children. When a baby is infected, usually only one or few viral variants succeed, a narrow event called a genetic bottleneck.

The team asked whether milk itself holds only restricted viral types, explaining that bottleneck. Their answer was no: restriction in milk does not account for it. The filter must act later, during or after the virus crosses into the child.
plos-pone-0010413:
Kalyan Srivastava and colleagues explored how platelets worsen cerebral malaria in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria of the brain remains very hard to treat and often kills children. Platelets, the blood cells that form clots, had been shown by this group to harm the immune response there. One substance they release is platelet factor 4. The team traced what that factor does to monocytes, a type of white blood cell.

Platelet factor 4 changed a control protein, KLF4, inside those cells. That change may steer monocytes toward harmful behavior in the brain. Naming this chain suggests points where a drug could intervene. It also reframes platelets as immune actors, not just clotting agents. Brain malaria may partly be a platelet problem.
plos-pone-0010513:
Sarah Wernimont and colleagues found a calcium-activated enzyme is not needed for a key T cell adhesion job in PLOS ONE in 2010. When T cells activate, they grip other cells using an integrin called LFA-1. Earlier work credited calpain enzymes with switching that grip on. The team tested T cells lacking calpain 4, an essential part of those enzymes. They checked grip and immune synapse formation carefully.

To their field's surprise, the cells worked fine without calpain 4. Negative findings like this redirect a field away from a wrong lead. They also show why genetic knockouts beat drug-based hints, which can mislead. Immune cell adhesion matters in infection, inflammation, and cancer therapy. Knowing which enzymes are dispensable sharpens the true model.
plos-pone-0010613:
Byoung Woo Kim and colleagues measured how people work to keep or avoid sights and sounds, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In their task, key presses lengthened or shortened the time a stimulus stayed on screen. People pressed more for pleasant items and pressed to escape unpleasant ones.

Across many trials, the effort followed steady, repeating patterns. The patterns scaled smoothly as rewards and aversive items changed in value. That orderliness suggests approach and avoidance obey shared rules. Rules like these could help clinics measure motivation in depression and addiction more precisely.
plos-pone-0010713:
Kathleen Gajewski and Robert Schulz studied how fly flight muscles keep their protein mix in balance, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flight muscles are built from two cable proteins, actin and myosin, in strict ratios. In the larva's body wall, a factor called CF2 turns muscle genes on. In flight muscle its job looked different.

In the developing flight muscle, CF2 held one actin gene down instead. Mutants with faulty CF2 made too much of that actin and upset the cable ratio. The same factor thus builds one muscle type and fine-tunes another. Balanced cables are what let wings beat hundreds of times per second.
plos-pone-0010813:
Shenying Fang and colleagues studied cancer risk in people born with a faulty TP53 gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such carriers face very high lifetime cancer risk, yet age of onset varies widely within families. Variants in three partner genes, MDM2, MDM4, and TP53 itself at codon 72, were candidates to explain that spread.

The cohort study followed carriers and compared onset across variant groups. Some variants shifted risk and timing in measurable ways. Earlier small studies had hinted at the same effects; a proper cohort gives them weight. For families living under this gene's shadow, sharper risk estimates mean screening can start at the right age, not a guessed one.
plos-pone-0010913:
Sarah Polack, Christina Eusebio, Wanjiku Mathenge and co-authors published this eye health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cataract is the world's leading cause of blindness, and it falls hardest on poorer countries. Surgery is cheap and effective, yet its effect on a person's daily life had rarely been measured in hours and activities.

The team interviewed older adults with sight-impairing cataract and matched neighbors with normal vision in Kenya, Bangladesh, and the Philippines, then returned about a year after offering surgery. Just over half of the patients accepted the operation, and most participants were re-interviewed. Comparing time-use before and after shows how restored sight changes work, chores, and rest. Polack and colleagues give aid programs concrete evidence that cataract surgery buys back daily life, not just eyesight.
plos-pone-0011013:
Melissa Paoloni, Christina Mazcko, Elizabeth Fox and co-authors published this comparative oncology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rapamycin blocks the mTOR growth pathway, which drives several cancers and their resistance to chemotherapy. Instead of testing doses first in people, the team used pet dogs with naturally occurring bone cancer, a close model of the childhood disease.

Dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma entered dose cohorts of three, receiving an injected formulation while researchers tracked blood levels, safety, and whether the drug hit its target in tissue. Paoloni and colleagues sought a dose that was safe, reached relevant blood concentrations, and measurably suppressed the pathway. Using companion dogs lets pediatric oncologists skip blind dose guessing, and the dogs themselves may benefit from trials their owners choose.
plos-pone-0011113:
Oliveira, Nakayasu, Joffe and colleagues characterized yeast shipments in PLOS ONE in 2010. Yeast cells release tiny bubbles of membrane, called vesicles, into their surroundings. These bubbles carry proteins and other cargo between cells, yet how yeast builds them was unclear.

The team described what the vesicles contain and which cell routes build them. More than one traffic path inside the cell took part in making them. That finding links yeast vesicle making to routes also used in human cells. It informs both basic cell biology and firms that use yeast to make useful products.
plos-pone-0011213:
Beauliere, Toure, Alexandre and colleagues counted illness costs in Cote d'Ivoire for PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV treatment drugs were free for the adults they studied, all on antiretroviral therapy. Yet getting sick still imposed heavy costs on these patients and their households.

The team quantified that burden from clinic visits, travel, lost work and other illness expenses. Free drugs alone do not protect fragile households from falling into poverty. The evidence argues for broader health coverage around HIV care. It gives policy makers hard numbers on the hidden price of illness.
plos-pone-0011313:
Piron, Nicolai, Minoia and colleagues created a resistant tomato in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two potyviruses cause serious losses in tomato crops. The team induced a mutation in a tomato gene that these viruses need to infect the plant, and then challenged the plants with the viruses.

The mutated plants gained immunity to both viruses. Changing a host gene the virus depends on is a durable protection strategy, since the plant is not attacking the virus directly. Breeders can move this trait into commercial varieties. The approach informs plant protection beyond tomatoes, wherever viruses exploit the same host factor.
plos-pone-0011413:
José Burgos and co-authors weighed in 2010 whether a health program for female sex workers on the Mexico-United States border pays for itself. Workers there face high rates of HIV and other sexually spread infections, and a counseling program promoted condom use. Funders needed to know if the infections prevented were worth the program's cost.

Their cost-effectiveness analysis compared program spending with the medical costs and illness averted when condom use rose and infections fell. Hard numbers of this kind are what health officials need when budgets force choices among many worthy programs. The border setting matters, since infections cross borders with people and one country's prevention protects both. The study gives officials an evidence base for funding, or redesigning, outreach where risk and poverty meet.
plos-pone-0011513:
Joshua Mauney and co-authors showed in 2010 how to steer stem cells toward becoming bladder lining. Tissue engineers who want lab-grown urinary tissue first need a reliable recipe for urothelial cells, the lining of the bladder and urinary tract. The team treated mouse embryonic stem cells with all-trans retinoic acid, a vitamin A relative long used to guide cell fate.

The treatment directed the stem cells to a urothelial identity through signaling involving the GATA4 and GATA6 factors. A defined chemical recipe with named internal switches is what turns stem cell promise into usable tissue. Surgeons who rebuild damaged bladders, in children born with defects and adults after cancer surgery, need exactly such lining cells. The study is an early, concrete step toward growing urinary tissue in the dish.
plos-pone-0011613:
Nicole Klein examined fossil bones of extinct sea reptiles in PLOS ONE in 2010. The reptiles, called sauropterygians, thrived in Triassic seas and are known from many fossils in Germany's ancient Muschelkalk deposits. Their family relationships have long been disputed, partly because complete diagnostic skeletons are rare.

Klein sliced long bones thin and read their inner tissue patterns under a microscope. The bone structures grouped the animals differently than expected from outer anatomy alone. Those surprise groupings challenge the accepted family tree and show how much history is stored inside fossil bone, not just on its surface.
plos-pone-0011713:
Jian-Yang Guo and co-authors studied an unhelpful partnership between a pest insect and a plant virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Begomoviruses cause serious plant disease and depend on whiteflies to carry them between plants. The invasive whitefly Bemisia tabaci spreads many of these viruses, and how infection affects the insect's own reproduction was poorly understood.

Whiteflies feeding on virus-infected plants produced more eggs and achieved higher lifetime reproduction than those on healthy plants. The virus thus boosts its own carrier. That mutual boost helps explain the rapid joint spread of this pest and the diseases it carries.
plos-pone-0011813:
Venkata Dasari and co-authors used cord blood stem cells against brain tumour cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. XIAP is among the most important proteins that block programmed cell death, and it is raised in many cancers including human glioblastoma. It promotes invasion, spread, growth and survival of malignant cells.

The team hypothesised that stem cells from umbilical cord blood could counter glioma by driving this blocker down. Their experiments show cord blood stem cells induce glioma cell death while downregulating XIAP. The one-two effect reveals a possible natural weapon against a deadly brain cancer.
plos-pone-0011913:
Mathieu Gautier, Toby Hocking, and Jean-Louis Foulley proposed in 2010 a statistical test for finding DNA under natural selection. Cheap genotyping had begun producing huge SNP data sets for whole populations. Genome scans hunt for markers that stand out from the rest, a footprint left when selection favors one variant in a place or breed.

Their Bayesian outlier criterion judges each marker against the background pattern rather than by a fixed cutoff. A cleaner way to call outliers reduces false leads in livestock and wildlife studies alike. Since selected regions often hold genes for adaptation, the method helps researchers move from a mountain of markers to a short list worth following.
plos-pone-0012013:
Koen Peeters Grietens and co-workers investigated in 2010 why preventive malaria treatment misses pregnant teenagers in rural Burkina Faso. The treatment, given in pregnancy as SP doses, was being scaled up across sub-Saharan Africa, yet coverage with the required doses stayed far below the eighty percent goal. Adolescent pregnancies are among the least reached.

Combining several kinds of evidence, the study mapped the bottlenecks: where the chain from policy to a young woman's clinic visit breaks. Teen mothers-to-be face stigma, distance, and services designed for older women. Naming the exact breaks gives programs fixable targets instead of a general lament about low coverage.
plos-pone-0012113:
Amy Moran and H Arthur Woods studied how oxygen reaches embryos sealed inside jelly-like egg masses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sea slugs lay such masses in both temperate and polar waters, and the growing young inside can only get oxygen as it drifts in from the water around them. The shape and size of the mass can help or choke that supply.

The authors compared egg masses across regions and conditions, weighing flow, form, and the needs of the embryos. Their work shows where the limits of this simple supply line lie, and how cold polar water changes the balance. It explains why these masses take the shapes they do, and what puts embryos at risk when conditions shift.
plos-pone-0012213:
Anna Shen, Kathleen O'Leary, Richard Dubielzig, and co-authors characterized a mutant mouse with an eye disease like a human one, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mouse strain appeared by chance in their colony with an enlarged front chamber of the eye. Its cornea's inner lining had turned into layered, skin-like cells that clog the eye's drain, mirroring a human corneal dystrophy that clouds vision.

Working out the mouse's defect points to a candidate gene for the human condition. A faithful animal model lets researchers watch the disease unfold from birth and test treatments safely. It also gives families affected by this rare dystrophy a concrete lead on its cause.
plos-pone-0012313:
Jesús Gómez-Gardeñes, Gorka Zamora-López, Yamir Moreno, and co-authors modeled synchronization across the cat's cerebral cortex in PLOS ONE in 2010. Conscious perception seems to need far-flung brain assemblies flashing in step for brief moments, yet the cortex's wiring map in mammals is still incomplete. Their model organizes the cortex's functional areas into a network and asks how its sync patterns arise.

They trace a shift from local, modular synchrony toward a coordinated whole as coupling strengthens. That shift mirrors what a brain must do to bind scattered features into one perception. Network models like this guide the reading of brain recordings, where the sync itself, not just the firing, may carry the message.
plos-pone-0012413:
Karin Norrman, Yvonne Fischer, Blandine Bonnamy and colleagues compared always-on gene switches in human embryonic stem cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Researchers use promoters — DNA switches that keep genes on — to tag and track stem cells. A switch that fades or varies ruins long experiments, yet promoters were rarely compared head to head in these cells.

The team tested several common promoters side by side for strength and steadiness. Some held their output far better than others during culture and differentiation. The ranking gives stem cell labs a practical guide, helping them pick switches that keep reporter genes honest from the first dish to the final cell type.
plos-pone-0012513:
Delphine Fradin, Keely Cheslack-Postava, Christine Ladd-Acosta and colleagues searched for parent-of-origin effects in autism, in a 2010 PLOS ONE genome study. Autism is strongly heritable yet genetically tangled, and most scans ignore whether a gene copy came from mother or father. For some genes, origin matters, because only one parent's copy is switched on.

Scanning sixteen thousand DNA markers with linkage methods that track parental origin, the team found regions where origin changed the effect. Such regions would be invisible to standard scans. The results argue for origin-aware analysis in autism genetics, which may recover heritability that past studies missed.
plos-pone-0012613:
Boisson, Kiyombo, Sthreshley and co-authors ran a field trial of a home water filter in the Congo. Cleaning water at home can cut germs and may prevent diarrhoea, a major killer of young children. Yet many past trials were open to bias, because families knew who got the real filter.

Their 2010 trial used a placebo filter and random assignment to keep the test fair. Households used the new device in daily life while the team tracked health and water quality. Careful trials like this one show what home filters can truly deliver in poor rural settings.
plos-pone-0012713:
Govindaraj, Manavalan, Lee and co-authors built a computer model of a little-known human immune sensor, TLR10. Toll-like receptors spot germs by their chemical signatures and raise the alarm. TLR10 sits in a family group with TLR1, 2 and 6, yet its own target stayed unclear.

Their 2010 modelling study predicted the sensor's shape and screened for molecules it might bind. Candidate ligands give lab teams a concrete list to test. Filling in the last blanks of this receptor family sharpens the whole picture of innate immunity.  Models of this kind guide costly lab work well.
plos-pone-0320713: Nyukuri and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a new way to treat HIV in Nairobi, Kenya. Instead of daily pills, patients can get long-acting shots. The team explored how patients at two large hospitals feel about the shots. One patient phrase, quoted in the title, calls the injection freedom. Knowing what patients value helps clinics roll out the shots in ways people accept.
plos-pone-0326013:
Jared Charlton-Webb and six colleagues set out a study protocol, published in 2026, for patients measuring their own vital signs in emergency care. Crowded departments often miss or delay basic checks like pulse and blood pressure. A smartphone tool offers a workaround. Patients record a thirty-second face video, and camera-based software estimates their vital signs. The study will run across three urgent care services in London.

Fifteen hundred patients will be measured both ways, manually and by phone. Surveys afterwards will judge whether the approach is workable and welcome. A small group of triage clinicians will rate staff acceptance. Ten thousand more patients will answer questions about digital health tools generally. As a protocol, this entry describes a plan, not results. Its findings should later show whether self-recorded vitals can safely ease triage pressure.
plos-pone-0329913:
Michaela Taylor-Williams and co-authors piloted a camera that reads oxygen in the tiny vessels at the fingertip nail fold. Standard nailfold imaging shows vessel shape in systemic sclerosis, a disease that deforms small blood vessels. Their 2026 feasibility study asked whether multispectral imaging could add oxygen information to the picture.

A nine-band camera imaged twenty-two people, ten with systemic sclerosis and twelve controls. The team compared oxygen-sensitive measures across nailfold regions using statistical models suited to repeated measures. The study's aim was feasibility, not diagnosis: can the device capture usable functional signals at all? Taylor-Williams and colleagues present the pilot as groundwork for imaging that could one day separate patients from healthy people by vessel function.
plos-pone-0335813:
Hannah Williams and colleagues examined how gun injuries changed in central and southeastern Ohio as the COVID-19 pandemic hit, a pairing sometimes called a dual pandemic. They drew on a regional trauma registry covering twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-one, with nearly four thousand patients hurt by firearms. They modelled how injury counts, patient handling, and related problems shifted when lockdowns began and ended.

Nearly every measure jumped or changed direction at the start of the pandemic period, and shifted again when it closed, while hospital stays stayed about the same length. The authors point to rising substance use and more deliberate, non-accidental shootings as part of the surge, with signs of strain on trauma services as lockdown wore on. They call for region-specific work on what drove the rise.
plos-pone-0338613:
Liang Ge and colleagues explored whether a blood measure called the hemoglobin glycation index tracks with thinking skills in older Americans. The index compares a person's long-term sugar marker against what their recent glucose would predict, capturing how readily someone's blood proteins soak up sugar. Data came from a national health survey of more than fourteen hundred older adults who took three standard thinking tests.

Both extremes fared worse. People with the lowest and highest index values scored below those in the middle on memory and processing speed measures, even after many adjustments. The pattern differed by sex and by whether people took diabetes medicine. The authors suggest the sweet spot sits in the middle, and that this cheap index, already computed from routine blood work, might help flag older adults at risk of decline.
plos-pone-0338813:
Bardel and colleagues fed laying hens hormones and plant extracts to test chick sex outcomes in a 2026 study. One hundred older breeder hens were split into five diet groups for five weeks: plain feed, two hormone additions, fennel extract, and garlic extract. Blood hormones were checked twice, and late eggs were hatched.

Fennel raised a male hormone in the blood across the study. Garlic, fennel, and one hormone each raised the female share among chicks, while the other hormone shifted results the other way. Egg producers value hens over roosters, so a feed-based nudge to sex ratios would carry real economic weight if it holds at farm scale.
plos-pone-0340713:
Bingyang Wu and Yongxi Yi published a 2026 theory paper in PLOS ONE on how governments should write open-source rules for artificial intelligence foundation software. Platforms and small independent projects differ greatly in size and in what compliance costs them, yet rules are usually uniform. Wu and Yi built a three-player dynamic game model to test whether tiered mandates, stricter for platforms and lighter for independents, grow a healthier ecosystem.

In the model, tiered rules beat uniform ones once the players differ enough from each other, with the best settings imposing clearly stricter duties on platforms and real flexibility for independents. Ecosystem health, the authors' composite measure of scale, diversity, and balance, improved substantially, most when platform compliance costs far exceeded those of small projects. They close with boundary conditions and an adaptive framework, arguing calibrated differences best protect innovation in AI infrastructure.
plos-pone-0342713:
Lei Zhengyao led a computer study of blood flow in a narrowed brain artery. Such narrowing is a major cause of stroke. Doctors often judge risk by how tight the narrowing looks. But blood thickness also varies from person to person. The team rebuilt a real artery scan in a model. They made mild and severe versions of the narrowing. Then they ran blood of three grades of thickness through each.

Flow turned on both factors at once. A severe narrowing made fierce stress on the wall inside the tight spot. Past the spot, flow turned slow and swirled. One stress measure even fell at the worst narrowing. The team says risk checks should add blood traits and flow measures.
plos-pone-0344213:
Wubet Tazeb Wondie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of deaths among low birth weight newborns in Ethiopia. Small babies face many times the death risk of normal-weight newborns, and Ethiopian studies disagreed on the scale. The reviewers pooled fifteen studies covering more than seven thousand babies.

Lack of kangaroo mother care, cold stress, extreme smallness, and being born early all predicted death. Wondie urges strict practice of skin-to-skin care, screening, and breastfeeding, plus stronger community newborn care, to cut a toll that better routines can prevent.
plos-pone-0346413:
Malinda Desjarlais examines whom people blame or credit when feedback on their Instagram photos goes well or badly. Likes and comments can sway mood and self-worth, but the explanations users give themselves matter too. In the 2026 study, students were told a photo of theirs had been posted and then received made-up praise or criticism, after which they wrote down what they thought caused it.

Photos of the self, whether self-taken or taken by others, drew explanations pointed inward, often about looks. Meme posts instead drew explanations pointed at the audience. Students knew society judges selfie posters, yet rarely blamed that bias. The pattern shows how posting self-images can turn outside judgment into self-judgment.
plos-pone-0346713:
Xuanhuang Chen and co-workers test a light-based guidance system for placing screws into the small bones of the neck. Neck screws must be exact, since nerves and blood vessels sit close by. Their 2026 study uses cow neck bones as stand-ins, planning screw paths on scans first, then guiding real placement with structured light that maps the surface during the mock procedure.

Every one of the more than one hundred test wires landed in the safest grade of placement. Entry points missed the plan by less than a millimeter on average. The light scan lined the model up with the plan almost exactly. Such guidance could make a delicate operation steadier, though human trials remain ahead.
plos-pone-0346813:
Lukas Waltenberger and colleagues created software that estimates the sex of people whose cremated remains survive only as burnt bone fragments. Archaeologists need this to rebuild ancient funeral customs and populations, yet cremation destroys the pelvis and skull features normally used. Their 2026 tool, called CRISP, was trained on a prehistoric Italian sample where grave goods hinted at each person's sex.

The program uses measurements from up to twenty-one surviving bones inside a Bayesian model, which reached about eighty-nine percent accuracy, beating simpler cut-off rules. A test on Austrian remains confirmed the approach travels across regions. CRISP is released openly, and can even flag deposits mixing more than one person.
plos-pone-0347313:
Zhaonan Ban and colleagues fingered a cell-division protein as an accelerant of rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune disease that inflames and erodes joints. Mining public arthritis datasets showed the protein's gene network glowing with immune activation signals. In lab experiments, the team silenced the gene in joint-like cells and in macrophages, the immune cells whose aggressive form pours out inflammatory messengers in arthritic joints.

Silencing worked on every front: the joint cells grew and migrated less, and the macrophages failed to mature into their inflammatory form, with their surface marker and messenger output both dropping sharply. The authors conclude the protein helps drive the disease by pushing macrophages into attack mode. They nominate it as a drug target in a condition where many patients still lack a treatment that truly works for them.
plos-pone-0348013:
Bicky Yadav and Megha Arakeri design one combined system for sending medical scans safely over weak networks. Hospitals must shrink huge images without losing diagnostic detail, keep them secret in transit, and prove they were not tampered with. Their 2026 paper joins near-lossless squeezing, scrambled encryption, future-proof key exchange, and a shared ledger that logs only harmless proof data.

A fine-tuning layer caps how far any pixel can shift, guarding fine detail. Keys are tied to each image's own identity data rather than managed loosely. The ledger entry lets receivers verify where an image came from. Putting the steps in one design aims to close gaps that appear when each step is bolted on alone.
plos-pone-0348113:
Metogbe Belfrid Djihouessi and colleagues review forty years of work on Benin's Porto-Novo Lagoon. Their review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The city lagoon feeds fishers and local trade. It also suffers nutrient overload and plant blooms. Bouts of low oxygen strike it too. These ills have grown worse since the 1980s.

The review asks if Benin could report the lagoon's health under a UN clean-water goal. It also tests a European-style health grading for gaps. Basic measures are partly tracked now. Acidity, oxygen, and phosphate are among them. Other needed data are missing. The authors map what exists and what is lacking. Managers get a clear place to start.
plos-pone-0348313:
Lily Soto and co-workers take a snapshot of which HIV strains circulated in the Dominican Republic in twenty twenty-four.
