The Caribbean carries a distinct older branch of the commonest strain, and tracking it guides care and vaccine thinking. Their 2026 study sequences parts of the virus from twenty-six patients in two cities and tests which gene regions sort the branches reliably.

Nearly every sample belonged to the usual strain, and most of those sorted to the Caribbean branch. Two gene regions sorted branches dependably, while a third did not. One sample proved to be a mixed form common in Africa and Europe, a first for the country. Even one odd strain shows why ongoing virus watching matters on the island.
plos-pone-0348413:
Anne Elizabeth Glassgow and a large team lay out the design of a five-year study of new mothers in American cities. Maternal deaths and serious complications run far higher in the United States than in other wealthy countries, and long-term stress is a suspected driver. Their 2026 paper is a protocol: it describes the study they will run, following two hundred women after childbirth.

The team will combine neighbourhood data, medical records, and interviews about trauma and support with blood tests that read chemical marks on DNA and measure inflammation and stress hormones. The plan is to trace how hard lives get written into the body. As a protocol, it reports no results yet.
plos-pone-0348713:
Xiao Liang, Andrew F. Teich, and Lenwood S. Heath trace how old human genes active in the brain and immune system really are. Their 2026 study follows more than a thousand such genes across thirty-one primate species and four other mammals, comparing them with random genes and with one gene picked from each family.

Brain genes turned out older on average, reaching back before primates appeared, and they were kept by most species since. Immune genes looked younger by comparison. Genes active in both systems leaned toward the brain pattern, suggesting they served the brain first and took on immune roles later. The history hints that the brain's toolkit is deeply ancient and hard to replace.
plos-pone-0349013:
Miao Zhao led a survey of women students at two Chengdu universities. The topic was the virus called HPV and its vaccine. The team compared health majors with all other majors. They graded what each group knew, basic and deep. They also asked who would take the shot. Near twelve hundred forms were fit to use.

Basic facts were known in part. Deep facts were known by few. Health majors scored higher on most counts. They also showed more will to take the shot. City roots and more cash to live on tracked with will too. The math showed one clear lever: basic facts. Raise them, and will to vaccinate rose. The team backs plain, clear teaching for non-health students.
plos-pone-0349113:
Ivaan Pitua and co-workers set out a plan to review wasting and muscle loss among children with cancer in Africa. Malnutrition is the most common side problem in these wards and worsens survival, yet bedside checks may miss it. Their 2026 protocol describes a review of studies from the year two thousand onward across four major databases.

Two reviewers will screen studies separately and grade their quality with a standard tool. The review will pool how common wasting is, compare measuring methods such as arm tapes against weight charts, and link wasting to harms like infection and treatment dropout. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it targets a hidden burden that better measuring could expose.
plos-pone-0349313:
W. Gregory Hood reports this 2026 PLOS One field study on beavers living in tidal wetlands of the Pacific Northwest coast. Beavers are usually pictured in rivers and lakes, where their dams turn flowing water into ponds. Hood surveyed tidal river deltas and estuaries in coastal British Columbia and in Washington and Oregon, where tides can rise and fall by several meters each day.

He found beaver dams throughout these tidal systems, flooded at high tide and holding water back only at low tide so the animals can move about. Tidal dams were packed more densely than river dams reported elsewhere, though somewhat smaller, and some have lasted at least thirty-five years in aerial photos. The findings argue that beavers likely shape tidal marshes, important habitat for young salmon, as strongly as they shape rivers.
plos-pone-0349413:
Ajay Malhotra and colleagues used United States Medicare payment data from 2017 to 2021 for over thirty three thousand diagnostic radiologists to compare women and men. Women made up about one quarter of the group. Practice setting, subspecialty, service volume, patients served, and payments were compared in detail.

Women clustered more in academic posts, urban areas, large practices, and breast imaging, where they formed nearly two thirds. On average women received about eighty six percent of mens Medicare payments, billed fewer services, and served fewer patients. Gaps persist even in a specialty often seen as flexible, which points leaders to workload and referral patterns, not just pay scales.
plos-pone-0349513:
Xinghai Pu and colleagues tackle hidden faults in the buried metal grids that keep power substations safe. Old search methods miss how grid parts connect, so fault spots stay vague. Their method draws the grid as a map of nodes and links, then trains a graph based learning model on fused data from electric checks, heat images, and field sensors.

Training also bakes in physical connection rules, so answers name the exact faulty wire segment rather than a rough zone. Tests at a large substation showed clear gains in accuracy over older routes. Precise fault maps mean crews dig once, in the right place, and return a risky grid to safe service faster.
plos-pone-0349613:
Moein Yoosefi and colleagues charted how long emergency patients in Newfoundland and Labrador wait to first see a physician, and projected the trend to 2026. Records from 2015 to 2021 covered rural and urban departments and the middle urgency bands of Canada's triage scale. A statistical model separated the effects of place, urgency, and time, and simulations attached uncertainty ranges to the forecast.

The projected average wait grows from about an hour and a half in 2015 to nearly three hours in 2026, close to double. Waits are the pressure gauge of an emergency system, and a credible forecast lets a province argue for staffing and redesign before the gauge hits red. Rural departments, far from backup, are watched especially closely in the analysis.
plos-pone-0350013:
Lingfeng Chen, Fengzhu Guo, and Chunlin Hong used gene data to search for what severe pancreatitis and sudden lung injury share at the molecular level. Severe pancreatitis can trigger lung damage, and the pair together are dangerous. The team combined mouse lung datasets for both conditions with blood data from human pancreatitis patients in a public database.

Ninety-four genes changed in the same direction in both mouse conditions, out of hundreds altered in each. Network analysis grouped these genes into shared pathways and highlighted hub genes that sit at busy crossroads. Checking the human data supported the same pathways across species. The short list of genes gives drug and diagnosis researchers concrete targets to test in the laboratory.
plos-pone-0350513:
Bernadette Walter and colleagues screened newly arrived asylum seekers in Heidelberg, Germany, in late summer and autumn 2024 for diphtheria and resistant wound germs. Europe had seen a rise in diphtheria among asylum seekers in the two prior years. Just over one thousand arrivals gave throat swabs, wound swabs where relevant, and survey answers, with blood tests in a subset.

No toxin making diphtheria germs were found. Among thirty seven people with inflamed wounds, about half carried resistant staph germs, near two percent of all arrivals. Over a third of those blood tested lacked protective diphtheria antibody levels. Screening found little active diphtheria, but thin immunity argues for catch up vaccination on arrival.
plos-pone-0350613:
Numbing the nerves running to the shoulder lets surgeons operate while using less general anesthetic. Hang Su and colleagues tested whether adding butorphanol, a pain drug, lets doctors use a weaker numbing solution, in this 2026 PLOS One trial with shoulder surgery patients.

Fifty patients were split between plain ropivacaine and ropivacaine mixed with butorphanol, guided by ultrasound. Each next patient's dose rose or fell depending on the previous patient's response, a staircase method that homes in on the middle effective strength. Forty patients finished. The mixed solution worked at a clearly lower strength, suggesting the added drug stretches the numbing effect and may spare side effects.
plos-pone-0350813:
María Yehisiri Martín–Báez and Candelaria de la Merced Díaz-González surveyed school teachers on Gran Canaria in 2026 about pupils with type one diabetes. Teachers often give daily help to these children, and negative attitudes can put safety at risk.

Staff at seven public schools for young children answered a tested questionnaire on attitudes and bias. About half of those invited took part, fewer than the study needed for firm claims. A share said they currently teach a child with diabetes. The results give local schools a starting picture of where training and support for teachers should be aimed.
plos-pone-0351113:
Jafar Keighobadi and Farnaz Imani worked on calibrating an atomic gyroscope, a sensor that measures rotation by splitting atoms rather than spinning parts. Such sensors promise very precise navigation, but small biases and unknown settings spoil accuracy. Lacking a physical unit to test, they fed real flight-path data from standard navigation systems into a software model of the gyroscope.

A two-stage Kalman filter, a method that learns while it tracks, estimated the sensor's bias and settings at the same time. Bias uncertainty shrank by orders of magnitude, and orientation accuracy improved by about a third over the uncalibrated model. The approach offers a cheap rehearsal for calibration before costly hardware is built. It also explores which laser wavelengths best drive the sensor, a detail that shapes future designs.
plos-pone-0351213:
Long-acting HIV treatment by injection usually means clinic visits, but trained friends or family could give the shots at home. Beth Bourdeau and colleagues built a selection tool helping patients pick the right treatment buddy, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

The team interviewed clinicians, patients, and candidate buddies to learn what makes a buddy suitable, then drafted questions and piloted them with seven patients. A community panel reviewed wording for clarity and completeness. Picking the right person, one participant said, can make or break the whole deal. The finished tool weighs trust, steadiness, and practical skills so home treatment stays safe.
plos-pone-0351313:
Junhao Li and Yiran Wang built a chip-based test that measures six cancer-related markers at once, all tied to how tumors invade and spread. The usual lab route tests markers one at a time, slowly, with large machines and much blood. Their platform uses a microfluidic chip, channels thinner than hair, with magnetic particles and glowing tags to catch each marker in parallel.

The six targets include enzymes and signals that help cancers break tissue barriers and grow blood vessels. The team checked the basics any test must prove: a straight measuring range, the smallest amount it can detect, repeatability, and freedom from mix-ups between markers. A single small sample yielding six invasion markers at once could speed decisions in clinics without big laboratories, and lets doctors follow several warning signs across a patient's treatment.
plos-pone-0351413:
Jingjing Yan and colleagues set out a plan, not finished results, for comparing types of gardening therapy for older adults. The planned review covers older people whose memory and thinking have weakened and who often feel low in mood as well. Gardening care can differ in setting, soil or other growing base, and how active each person is.

Under the plan, the team will search eight large databases for trials where gardening was added to usual care. Two reviewers will screen studies, pull out the data, and judge bias with a standard tool. They will then rank the gardening types for effects on thinking skills and low mood. No findings are reported yet, because the review is still to be done.
plos-pone-0351713:
Víctor Juan Vera-Ponce and a large team pooled the world's research on the impostor phenomenon among medical students, the nagging feeling of being a fraud despite real achievement. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered thirty-five studies, and combined twenty-six that used the standard Clance scale, covering more than nine thousand students across many countries.

Just over half the students scored in the impostor range, though carefully sampled studies produced a lower figure near a third, warning that the headline number depends on who gets asked. Rates were similar for women and men, and for early and late training. Country differences were wide, from under a third in Peru to nearly nine tenths in the United Arab Emirates. The authors press medical schools to normalize the conversation.
plos-pone-0352813:
Yo Muraki and six colleagues examine how an upgraded cancer cell therapy rallies the patient's own immune system, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mouse study. The therapy engineers T cells with a synthetic receptor plus two helper molecules that summon and grow immune cells. Conventional versions struggle against solid tumours. Four days after treatment of mice bearing such tumours, the team profiled the host immune cells inside them.

Tumours treated with the upgraded cells filled with the host's own killer T cells and macrophages, which conventional therapy did not achieve. Those host cells switched on inflammatory and summoning genes. The engineered cells, it seems, act as recruiters as much as fighters — a mechanism that could matter for human solid-tumour trials.
plos-pone-0353113:
Duc Khanh Nguyen, Thanh Tuan Tran, and Van Sy Hoang compare two admission tools for heart failure in this 2026 PLOS One study. Both aim to predict who will die within a year. One is a blood marker of heart strain. The other is a clinical score called AHEAD, built from age and several conditions. The cohort followed four hundred thirty hospitalized patients. About one in five died during the year.

The blood marker clearly out-did the score. Each doubling of it came with roughly double the risk of death. The score predicted death on its own. But it added nothing once the marker was known. Combining the two did not beat the marker alone. The highest-marker third of patients were high risk, whatever their score said. The authors still recommend testing in other hospitals before practice changes.
plos-pone-0353213:
David Fräulin, Irina Sidorenko, and Renée Lampe propose a radiation-free way to check the tools that monitor curved spines in teenagers, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Scoliosis affects up to three percent of adolescents, but tracking it with X-rays means repeated radiation. Camera systems that read the back's surface offer an alternative, yet proving their accuracy is tricky because surface scans and X-rays are taken at different times, in different postures.

Their fix generates the test data automatically from CT scans, extracting the outer back surface and the inner spine from the very same image. Posture mismatch disappears by construction. Clean verification data of this kind could finally let surface methods graduate from sidekick to trusted diagnostic tool.
plos-pone-0353613:
Mayank Singh, Anuj Singh, and Abhay Kumar Tiwari tackled child mortality counting in India, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Counting deaths of newborns, infants, and children under five is hard where records are patchy. The team developed an indirect estimation technique and applied it to India and its states in a population-based study.

Singh's method gives policymakers credible state-by-state numbers to act on. Child mortality varies hugely across India, so national averages hide the places needing help most. Indirect methods use data that already exist, such as survey reports of births and deaths, and correct them carefully. Better estimates steer health spending toward the states and districts where children are most at risk.
plos-pone-0354013:
Hansa Gul and seven colleagues test compounds from a soil fungus against drug-resistant staph bacteria that infect cow udders, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off antibiotics partly by pumping them out of the cell. The team profiled the fungus's chemistry, tested its extract against the bacteria in dishes, and used computer docking to see whether its molecules could jam four of those pumps.

The crude extract stopped the bacteria in a clear ring on the plate, and two isolated compounds matched that performance. Simulations showed several fungal molecules binding the pumps stably. Blocking the pumps rather than killing the bacterium outright is a promising flank attack on resistance, though animal testing lies ahead.
plos-pone-0354513:
Beilin Dong and colleagues redesigned the height-adjustment mechanism of a machine that torture-tests mining cables by bending them, so the machine can match the different dragging heights of real coal faces. Their 2026 engineering study built a hydraulic rack-and-pinion lifting system, modeled a heavy mining cable's material behavior from strand tests, and simulated the mechanism's moving stresses and fatigue life.

Peak stresses in the gears, guide columns, and sliders stayed within safe bounds, and the team pinpointed the guide column's limiting hole as the fatigue-critical spot. A topology optimization pass then carved away unneeded material for a lighter design. Better test rigs matter because cables that fail underground, under load and constant flexing, are a lethal hazard.
plos-pone-0354713:
Ali Aranizadeh, Behrooz Vahidi, and Amir Khorsandi published this 2026 study of keeping medium-voltage electrical switchgear healthy and safe in power networks. Switchgear wears under heat, strain, and electrical stress until failures black out customers. Their framework sorts readings into four groups covering power flow, moving parts, insulation, and support, then blends scaling, probability, and fuzzy expert logic into health scores and remaining life.

Tested on real data from two substations, the method outscored older techniques in both accuracy and clarity. Aranizadeh offers it to utilities fixing gear when its state demands it, not by the calendar.
plos-pone-0354813:
Caitlin A Hildebrand led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study of family doctors and food. Thirty-two primary care physicians described their training, daily practice, and teamwork around nutrition, a topic central to chronic disease yet thin in medical education. The study used design thinking, learning from users to frame the problem.

Doctors valued nutrition but felt unsure where their role as generalists starts and stops. They asked for clearer expectations, handier resources, and stronger links with dietitians. Hildebrand argues training reform should follow that clarified role, so advice to patients becomes practical instead of vague.
plos-pone-0354913:
Muse Shomre, Dawit Meskele, and Yishak Beyene assess in 2026 water and climate trends on the eastern edge of a lake basin in Ethiopia's Rift Valley. They combined records from several weather stations and a river gauge over many decades. Trend tests, drought indices at different time spans, and checks on river flow patterns gave a joined picture.

Rainfall trends were mostly flat, but hottest monthly temperatures rose at nearly all stations. Drought grew more frequent and severe in recent decades at several places. River flow shifted too, with higher low flows and weaker peaks. Short span drought indices caught repeated dry spells best, guiding local water planning.
plos-pone-0355113:
Doris van der Smissen and colleagues interviewed twenty-two cancer survivors. They also ran focus groups with twenty-five health workers in the Netherlands. The question was what good support after cancer treatment actually looks like. Their 2026 study spanned survivors of different ages, sexes, and times since diagnosis. The workers ranged from hospital doctors to job physicians and informal caregivers.

Both sides converged on person-centered care, cut to fit each person. It should reach beyond medicine into work and peer contact. It should help survivors steer their own recovery. The workers added hard truths. Many doctors do not know what support exists, roles blur, and referral options lack any shared map. The study names delivery, not intent, as the failing point in survivorship care.
plos-pone-0355313:
Kassandra Giragosian, Marina Davila-Ross, and Derry Taylor listen for dialects in young chimpanzees at two sites, a wildlife orphanage and a national park in Africa. Human speech differs by community, and chimp calls also carry site signatures, but whether those signatures grow with age was unclear. The team measured thousands of laughs, grunts, and whimpers from infants and juveniles and tested whether a computer could tell the two homes apart.

Calls from both ages carried site signatures, with one exception: infant whimpers did not. Juvenile calls were easier to sort by site than infant calls, so the dialect signal strengthens as young chimps grow. Giragosian and colleagues argue that social life and local surroundings help shape the voice, not genes alone.
plos-pone-0355413:
Qinxingzi Li and co-authors chart in 2026 how common bacterial and fungal infections differ by sex, age, and season at a large Chinese hospital. Six years of test records covered the species found most often, making up nearly all positive samples. Each species was checked for patterns across the three factors and by a staining group used in microbiology.

Most species showed sex differences, almost always peaking in males, and nearly all varied by age. Summer brought the peak for many species. One staining group reacted more strongly to sex and season than the other. Prevention and testing plans should build in these patterns, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0355613:
Ali Raza and four colleagues redesign a small but crucial component of neural networks in this 2026 paper: the activation function, the curve that decides how strongly each artificial neuron fires. Standard curves are fixed, which limits how well a network can adapt to varied data. Their proposal lets the function's slope, range, and curvature adjust, in three flavors: preset by hand, learned globally by the network, or learned separately by each layer.

Across handwritten digits, fashion images, skin lesion photos, and COVID-19 scans, the adaptive versions generally converged faster and classified better than fixed functions. A compact network using the layer-wise version beat two famous deep architectures on the fashion benchmark and handled imbalanced medical classes more robustly. The authors argue that letting each layer tune its own nonlinearity is a cheap upgrade for image models that must transfer across domains.
plos-pone-0355713:
Hale Cotuk Yucel, Ali Kaya, and Merve Arslan interview trainee special education teachers in Türkiye about what artificial intelligence could mean for their future classrooms. Fourteen trainees spoke at length. All had already taken part in AI courses or projects. Their accounts were sorted into themes. The themes covered the teacher, the child and family, schooling itself, and AI's future.

Trainees saw AI as more than a tailoring tool: some pictured it reshaping the teacher's role itself. They credited it with promise for independence skills, social practice, and daily decisions for learners with special needs. At the same time they worried about isolation, privacy, dependence, and murky ethics. Yucel and colleagues call for ethics-first AI literacy in teacher training.
plos-pone-0356013:
Hirotaka Eguchi and colleagues asked whether the thickness of the temple muscle, visible on routine head scans, predicts immunotherapy success. Muscle loss can weaken response to immune checkpoint drugs in returning head and neck cancer. Their 2026 study measured the muscle in just over a hundred patients treated with two such drugs.

Patients with thicker temple muscles responded to treatment more often than those with thinner muscles. One year on, both freedom from progression and survival were clearly better in the thicker-muscle group. The link held after adjusting for chemotherapy use. Eguchi and colleagues propose the measurement, free on scans patients already receive, as a simple marker for sorting patients by likely outcome.
plos-pone-0356813:
Lee Hill and her team set out the plan for a new Canadian registry. It will track kids born with one of two bowel flaws that need team care for life. In one flaw, the bowel lacks nerve cells. In the other, the outlet forms in the wrong way. No long-term record for these kids yet exists in Canada. The registry sits at a Montreal children's hospital. It takes in patients up to age seventeen, and tracks them till they are grown.

Clinic facts come from a standard team form used at each visit. Families fill in six tested surveys. The surveys cover life quality, toilet control, family strain, and bowel care at home. Hill and her team will search the data for what drives good results. They hope to ease the move to adult care, and to let Canadian data join world studies of these rare flaws.
plos-pone-0357013:
Hong-Nhu Nguyen, Quang Sang Nguyen, and Tan N Nguyen analyzed a hybrid network where a satellite and ground stations serve many users at once. The network uses a signal-splitting scheme called rate-splitting multiple access. Their 2026 paper derives exact formulas for the system's total data rate and error rate. The formulas assume the flickering signal conditions typical of satellite links. The team then checks the math against simulations.

Rate-splitting beat the conventional non-orthogonal scheme on efficiency and interference control. The authors trace how dividing transmit power tunes the result. The split runs between the shared and private parts of each message. Such networks are candidates for bringing broadband to remote regions in the coming generation of mobile systems. These formulas help engineers design them without endless trial simulations.
plos-pone-0357213:
Sadikul Haque Sadi, Md Arman Hossain, and Md Nurul Ahad Tawhid add family background to brainwave analysis in a screening system for attention deficit disorder risk in children. Diagnosis today leans on behavior reports, which are subjective. Brainwave models exist, yet they ignore income and home context, which shape brain development strongly. The team's network reads brainwaves two ways, as time traces and as time-frequency pictures, then fuses both with background data.

On a public dataset built for exactly this question, the combined system beat brainwave-only rivals on every one of four thinking tasks, with the biggest gains in catching true cases. Scores held up under a strict test that holds out whole children. Sadi and colleagues argue screening tools should use context, not pretend brains grow in a vacuum.
plos-pone-0357313:
Tan Arda Gedik, Vania De la Garza, and Ewa Dabrowska ask whether learning to read helps adults understand that others can believe things that are false. This skill, called false-belief understanding, is usually studied in children from literate homes. The team tested native Turkish adults, some literate and some not, on a tricky belief task plus measures of nonverbal reasoning, self-control, and timed word reading.

Reading speed stood out as the strongest predictor by far, explaining about half of the gap between people. Reasoning and self-control mattered less once reading was counted. Gedik and colleagues suggest that reading itself trains skills the belief task needs, such as handling sentences about thoughts and following written stories. The finding matters for adult literacy teaching and for psychology's literate bias.
plos-pone-0357413:
Nuo Ya Li and colleagues mine a global survey of several thousand doctoral students to ask what kind of supervisor support actually tracks with a satisfying PhD. Students in more than one hundred countries rated how often they met supervisors and how good the relationship, research guidance, and career help felt. The team then modeled overall satisfaction against each support type, checking the results several ways.

Meeting frequency looked helpful at first glance, but its link faded once support quality entered the model. Relationship quality, research guidance, and career support stayed strong and steady throughout, and also tracked whether students felt the degree met their hopes. Li and colleagues advise universities to train supervisors for depth of support, not just regular meetings.
plos-pone-0357713:
Toshio Narimatsu and four colleagues show that eyes pronounced perfectly corrected can still see poorly in dim contrast, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They studied forty-three healthy adults at a Tokyo checkup center. All scored normally on the standard eye chart and had no eye disease history. The question was whether ordinary, non pathological short sight quietly degrades low contrast vision, the kind used to read grey print or drive at dusk.

Low contrast scores worsened as short sight grew. Eyes with milder prescriptions saw the faint chart clearly better than more myopic eyes, a gap that reached firm significance, and age chipped away at the scores too. Axial length of the eye and uncorrected vision also entered the picture. A perfect standard score, the authors conclude, does not guarantee full visual ability. Myopia care should be judged on more than the bright chart.
plos-pone-0357813:
Yuting Zhang, Hantao Li, and Jiye Li published a tracking methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their problem was keeping a lock on a moving target when sensor readings are noisy and clutter hides the path. Systems from radar to sonar face that same problem when a lost track can mean a missed threat or a failed rescue.

Zhang and her colleagues extended a tracking method by feeding the target's past path back into the process, using it to limit where the target can plausibly be. That feedback steadies the track when fresh readings jump around. The gain is practical: steadier tracks mean fewer false alarms and fewer moments when operators lose the object they most need to follow.
plos-pone-0359213: Wang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on chemicals floating in the air of Qingyang, China. VOCs are gases given off by fuels, paints, and industry that can harm health. The team described which ones are present and judged the risk they pose. City air data of this kind help officials decide which sources to control first.
plos-pone-0359413: Huang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on surgery for a stubborn eye disease. Mooren's ulcer is a painful sore at the edge of the cornea that resists standard care. The team reviewed past cases treated with a strategy based on how severe each case was. Follow-up ran for a long term. Their series may help eye surgeons choose steps when drugs alone fail.
plos-pone-0359513:
Gayathri Ashok and co-authors described in 2026 their work on a peptide designed to do two jobs at once against human papillomavirus linked head and neck cancer. Some cancers of the head and neck are driven by this virus, whose proteins interfere with the host cell's controls. The team set out to build a short protein chain, a peptide, that targets the interacting proteins where virus and host meet.

Their peptide is meant to act as both an antiviral and an anticancer agent, striking the viral machinery and the cancer it sustains. Work of this kind is early stage and computational and laboratory based. It reflects a broader search for precise treatments for virus driven cancers, which differ from other head and neck cancers in cause and behavior.
plos-pone-0360513:
Nicolas Tugui, Shahinur Islam, and Daniel Heath developed in 2026 high throughput tests for how salmon and their relatives respond to salt stress at the gene level. Salmonids move between fresh and salt water, and their bodies must remodel to handle each, a process called osmoregulation. When that adjustment is stressed, by farming conditions or warming rivers, gene activity reveals the strain early.

The authors built assays that read those gene responses across several species at once and assessed how well the tests perform. Hatcheries and conservation programs could use such tools to check fish welfare and readiness for sea transfer without waiting for visible harm. The work also supports comparisons of how different salmonid species cope with changing waters.
pmc-13237113:
Gmelin and colleagues run a genome-wide study of short repeating DNA stretches in Alzheimer's disease. Most such studies scan single letter changes and skip these repeats, called short tandem repeats, though repeats can switch genes on or off. The team tested repeats across the genomes of about a third of a million people in the UK Biobank.

Their group included a few thousand Alzheimer's cases, many more people classed by family history as likely cases, and a large control group. Repeats were read both from gene-chip guesses and from full genome sequencing. Hits from this overlooked layer of DNA could reveal fresh mechanisms behind a disease that still lacks a clear genetic story.
pmc-13241413:
Ng's team at Flinders University compared telehealth use between Australians with and without cancer. National Patient Experience Surveys from 2022 to 2024 supplied the data. Respondents numbered over two thousand with cancer and 45 thousand without. Logistic models mapped who used telehealth and what followed.

Thirty-eight percent of cancer respondents had used telehealth, against 26 percent of others. Mental health conditions raised use in both groups, while being uninsured or less educated lowered it. Cancer patients using telehealth reported the poorest health and most hospital contact, reflecting greater need. Over ninety percent of users rated the service positively.
pmc-13241513:
Elkhoriby and colleagues at Mansoura University fed plant additives to two strains of Japanese quail and tracked growth and gene activity. Three hundred young female quails entered the trial, split evenly between brown and white strains. Each strain received a plain control diet or drinking water dosed with frankincense or lemon balm extract. The feeding period lasted twenty-eight days.

Responses depended strongly on strain, a clear interaction between genetics and treatment. Frankincense at both tested levels suited the brown strain best. For white quails, the lower frankincense level and the stronger lemon balm dose worked best. Treated birds gained weight more efficiently and switched on growth and antioxidant genes while quieting a muscle-limiting gene.
pmc-13242113:
Neven and colleagues in Antwerp correct their systematic review of recessive congenital methemoglobinemia, a rare inherited blood disorder. The review catalogued reported cases and their CYB5R3 gene variants. Two production errors slipped into the printed version. An author's name was also printed incorrectly.

Tables 2 and 3 had been switched, sending readers to the wrong tables from three spots. Table 2 covers diagnostic tests and therapy; Table 3 lists the unique gene variants. The garbled byline is fixed to Marije Meuwissen. Treatment details in the review stand: most documented patients got vitamin C, some with methylene blue. The original article has been updated accordingly.
pmc-13242513:
Mona Hegazy and co-authors tested a diabetes drug as a partner for the standard treatment of schistosomiasis in mice. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Praziquantel kills the Schistosoma mansoni worms, but liver damage from the infection often persists, so helpers are needed. Infected mice received dapagliflozin alone or combined with praziquantel, and the team counted worms and eggs and examined liver tissue under the microscope.

The combination clearly outperformed the untreated course of infection. Worm burden and liver egg load fell, more of the remaining eggs were mature or dead, and the granulomas that scar the liver grew fewer and smaller. Protective liver chemicals rose, and a marker of programmed cell death increased as well. Used alone, dapagliflozin also showed benefit, though the pairing looked strongest. The authors propose it as a convenient add-on that targets inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death together.
pmc-13244513:
Yue Xi and colleagues built a prediction model for metabolic syndrome in women around menopause, centered on a simple body shape measure. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. The body roundness index, computed from height and waist, estimates visceral fat better than weight alone. Models were trained on United States survey data from 2007 to 2020, checked in a Chinese hospital cohort, and extended with a ten-year follow-up.

A neural network won the cross-sectional contest, scoring about 0.85 on internal testing and 0.88 externally, with sound calibration. Importance ranking put body roundness at the very top of sixteen predictors, ahead of liver enzymes and blood cell measures. Adding how roundness and lab values drift over years sharpened the long-term forecasts further. The authors offer the tool for screening in clinics where a tape measure is always available. Catching the syndrome early is the prize.
pmc-13247313:
Yaikhan and co-authors analyzed the genomes of a notorious hospital pathogen at global scale in this 2026 Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal study. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many antibiotics, and its resistance genes often travel on mobile DNA such as plasmids and insertion sequences. The team assembled ten and a half thousand quality genomes and asked whether resistance load tracks the mobile element load within each bacterial lineage.

A few lineages dominated the collection. Genome-wide, resistance burden correlated only modestly with insertion-sequence counts and plasmid variety, and a stricter count of genuinely acquired resistance told a similar story. Mobile-element features differed sharply between lineages, while virulence gene profiles stayed comparatively uniform. The authors argue resistance in this pathogen must be understood lineage by lineage, not as one global pattern.
pmc-13247913:
Havers, Fazel, and Smuk mapped how childhood maltreatment and teenage emotional problems intersect across social positions in England, in this 2026 Epidemiology and Psychiatric Sciences study. Average group comparisons hide combined disadvantage. So the team used a multilevel intersectional method on the OxWell 2023 survey. Nearly twenty thousand students aged eleven to sixteen were sorted into one hundred eighty strata. The strata combined gender, ethnicity, poverty, school year, and school deprivation.

Maltreatment's damage was pervasive yet uneven across those strata. Most inequality in emotional problems reflected simply additive social patterning, each disadvantage stacking. But non-additive intersectional effects appeared too, and they were stronger among maltreated adolescents. The authors argue for trauma-informed, equity-focused policy that looks at combinations of disadvantage. Teenagers carrying several disadvantages at once bear distinctive, not merely summed, psychological costs.
pmc-13248113:
Cezar and colleagues built a scoring system for pig diseases in the United States, reported in 2026. Veterinary labs confirm many infections in tissue samples, yet no single ranking showed which causes were most active. The team combined years of records from the Iowa State University diagnostic laboratory into one index.

They analyzed nearly sixty thousand tissue cases covering eighty-one causes, from bacteria and viruses to parasites. The index stayed stable across years, with PRRS virus and Streptococcus suis scoring highest most often. Two less familiar viruses rose over time. The authors offer the index, shown on an interactive dashboard, as a planning tool for disease control.
pmc-13249113:
Roh, Yoon, and Oh tested a sleep chatbot built around questions rather than instructions, reported in 2026. Digital therapy for insomnia teaches proven habits, yet users often drop out because the programs lecture instead of listening. Their SleepPathfinder chatbot asks Socratic questions, then lets users decide their own next step, in a four-stage conversation.

A one-session pilot with forty-five users rated the system usable and credible. In a five-day comparison with thirty users, the questioning style softened how threatening users found their sleep problems and nudged feelings of choice upward. Deeper personal storytelling, not the sheer number of questions, tracked with changed thinking. The authors propose the layer as a companion to standard digital therapy.
pmc-13249713:
Alperen Aksakal and colleagues report a 2026 lung study of young smokers who feel perfectly healthy. Standard breathing tests can look normal early in smoking, even while the smallest airways are already changing, so the team used a gentler sound-wave test that is more sensitive to those airways.

University students who smoked were compared with never-smokers before and after a six-minute walk test. Both groups had similar standard test results, but smokers showed higher airway resistance and stiffer small airways. Smokers also walked less far and had lower oxygen levels in their leg muscles. The authors say the sound-wave test could flag early smoking harm sooner.
pmc-13250213:
Tuyisenge and colleagues reflect on a six-year partnership that worked to improve care for mothers and newborns in Rwanda. Their 2026 BMJ Paediatrics Open paper describes work by British and Rwandan pediatric bodies with UNICEF and Rwanda's health ministry. From 2017 to 2023, the program ran across many hospitals and selected health centers.

The authors report measurable gains in care quality and patient outcomes over the program years. Even so, preventable newborn deaths persisted, which they link to deeper system limits and community-level health factors. They argue that the numbers are only part of the program's value. Working side by side for years also revealed the structural reasons good clinical steps sometimes fail to become reliable care.
pmc-13253713:
Lasse Bohlen and colleagues test machine learning for intensive care in a 2026 study across two health systems. Models were built with data from a German university hospital and the MIMIC-IV database from the United States. The tasks were to predict death, length of stay, and return to hospital for ICU patients.

Models trained on local data beat models brought in from outside when enough local data existed. Simpler and mid-level models, such as additive models, traveled better across hospitals than complex ones. They also needed far less local data, and tools that explain model choices helped show where data gaps hurt results.
pmc-13253813:
Shakila Umer and a large team study plant DNA barcodes in a 2026 paper on the western Himalayas. The region holds many plants found nowhere else, yet its local flora is little studied at the DNA level. The team tested eight barcode regions in 32 endemic and threatened species from Pakistan's western Himalayas.

One marker, rbcL, worked best, with full copying success and 96% sequencing success. Another marker reached full copying but 80% sequencing, while ITS2 lagged at 52%. Database matches were at least 97% alike for most species, supporting barcodes as a tool to name and group these plants.
pmc-13254113:
Sadia Munawar and colleagues build an AI tool for lung tissue diagnosis in a 2026 study. The system uses CLIP, a model that links images with text, to sort lung samples into benign tissue, adenocarcinoma, or squamous cell carcinoma. Tailored text prompts and a loss method that handles uneven class sizes guided training.

Training used thousands of images per class, split for training, checking, and testing. The best check accuracy reached 95.20 percent, with strong curve scores near 0.987. Training stopped early at epoch 23, a full pass through the data, after steady gains. The authors see promise for digital pathology systems.
pmc-13255213:
Jan Stein and colleagues track body temperature in major trauma in a 2026 registry study. Low body temperature is part of a deadly triad in severe injury, but how it changes during early care is less known. The team analyzed 34,877 patients from a German trauma registry between 2015 and 2023.

Low temperature affected 10.7 percent of patients on arrival and 9.7 percent at intensive care transfer. Staying cold throughout carried the highest death rate at 43.5 percent, plus the most clotting problems and transfusions. New cold at transfer also fared badly, with 31.9 percent deaths. The authors urge active temperature tracking and control.
pmc-13256613:
Shevchenko and a local team surveyed drug residues in beef, pork, and animal feed across Kazakhstan's Kostanay region, and tested meat bacteria for drug resistance. Traces were common in all three materials, though every level stayed below legal maximum limits. Levels differed sharply by feed type.

Meat samples carried E. coli and S. aureus, with samples showing moderate to high resistance, strongest in pork. Resistance was highest against tetracycline, streptomycin, and thiamphenicol. The authors warn that even trace residues moving through the feed-to-food chain may sustain selective pressure and spread resistant microbes. They call for thorough checks of feed and animal products.
pmc-13260213:
Zhenbing Ma and colleagues compare starch from zhiqu wheat, grown for liquor starter, with bread wheat starch. The two wheats feed very different crafts, yet their starch architecture was barely contrasted. Their 2026 analysis measures granules, crystals, and cooking behavior side by side.

Zhiqu starch carried slightly less amylose and somewhat larger mid-sized granules. Its crystals packed more orderly, and its pastes thickened higher at peak, trough, and finish. Branching ran lower in the liquor wheat's starch chains. Statistical mapping showed zhiqu quality traits holding unusually steady across samples. Growers choosing varieties for fermentation now have firmer guidance.
pmc-13260813:
Mohamed M Shabib and colleagues present a 2026 numerical study of tuned mass dampers for earthquake protection in twelve-story steel buildings. A tuned mass damper is a heavy mass that sways against a building's motion to cut shaking, without external power. Using nonlinear time-history simulations under scaled earthquake records, the team compared a single damper with multi-damper layouts spread vertically, horizontally, and around the perimeter, in regular and irregular building plans.

For the regular building, a four-corner horizontal layout was tested for mistuning, and a frequency deviation of plus or minus four percent gave the lowest top displacement. For irregular plans shaped like T, C, L, and a stadium, a perimeter multi-damper layout cut maximum top displacement by between 18.3 percent and 52.3 percent, depending on the plan. Torsional rotation fell by between 25.4 percent and 68.0 percent, a large drop in twist, with base shear and acceleration also reduced.
pmc-13262613:
Xiaoxiao Sun and colleagues present a shared resource for studying cancer cells that survive targeted drugs in a 2026 journal article. These persister cells lack stable genetic resistance yet can seed relapse. The resource, called ResMap, offers a standard test setup and a data set so results from different labs can be compared fairly.

The team tested 94 compounds against 57 candidate targets in four lung cancer models, under normal and low oxygen. A first screen found 12 targets with activity across cancer types and oxygen levels, and follow-up work confirmed 9 of them. Some targets worked only in certain settings, including combinations tied to KRAS-driven cancer. Mouse and human cell data added a safety check for ranking targets.
pmc-13262713:
Cornelia M Weyand and Jörg J Goronzy review how ageing reshapes the immune system in a 2026 journal article. The immune network defends against infection and cancer, but stress over a lifetime wears down its structure. The authors trace changes in blood stem cells and in T and B cells, the white blood cells that learn to target specific threats.

Ageing stem cells renew themselves less well and produce skewed mixes of cells, they explain. Learner immune cells lose their fresh, untrained pool, their variety shrinks, and their internal power and stress systems falter. The result is a paradox: weaker defense alongside more chronic inflammation and self-attack. They illustrate this with rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis, two diseases of older adults.
pmc-13263013:
Annie Reid and co-authors evaluate action planning inside a digital program to cut sugary drink intake in Appalachian adults in a 2026 journal article. The program, iSIPsmarter, pairs online lessons with text-message drink tracking and a connected scale. In most modules, users set goals, name barriers, and pick strategies, then update plans as feedback arrives.

The 119 participants completed most of their drink action plans, and 80 percent finished all five. About half rated carrying out their plans as hard or impossible, a share that stayed steady. At the program's end, 57 percent of remaining users met their drink goal, and 46 percent met the recommended daily limit. Top barriers were caffeine, taste, and habit.
pmc-13263213:
Shejil Kumar and co-authors evaluate a risk-targeted bone fracture service in Sydney in a 2026 journal article.
