The team took ideas proven at a recent international prediction contest and built a neural network that handles protein information in three tracks at once, covering sequence, residue pairs, and coordinates.

Information flows back and forth between those tracks as the network refines its guess of the folded structure. The authors show the method also handles proteins that work together in complexes. Freely released methods of this kind changed daily practice in biology, letting researchers start from a reliable predicted shape instead of a blank page.
pmc-8287113:
Connor Shorten, Taghi Khoshgoftaar, and Borko Furht surveyed in 2021 how data augmentation, artificially expanding training data, can strengthen deep learning for language. Working with text is among the most striking uses of deep learning, yet models often hunger for more labeled examples than projects can supply. Augmentation answers by creating varied new examples from existing ones.

The survey gathers the main strategies, from swapping and editing words to generating fresh sentences, and groups them by the ideas behind them. The authors weigh the gains reported for tasks such as classification and translation. For practitioners facing small datasets, the survey is a practical menu of tricks that can lift a model without collecting new data.
pmc-8662613:
Carlos Cantalapiedra and colleagues released eggNOG-mapper version two in 2021, a major upgrade of a tool that labels genes with their functions. Annotating genes automatically is a basic step in nearly every genome and metagenome study, yet doing it well at large scale stays hard. The tool works from precomputed groups of related genes, called orthology groups, so each new gene inherits carefully built functional information.

The upgrade speeds and widens that process, adding domain prediction alongside functional labels and family assignments. The authors show it handling metagenomic data, where millions of genes from mixed species need labels. Reliable annotation is the bridge between raw sequence and biological meaning, and this tool is one of its main carriers.
pmc-9252913:
Joseph Khoury and a large editorial team summarized in 2022 the fifth edition of the World Health Organization classification for myeloid and related blood cancers. The classification is part of a wider effort to catalog all human cancers in one consistent, layered system. This companion article covers the cancers of myeloid cells, the family that gives rise to most blood cells, plus related histiocytic and dendritic cell tumors.

The authors explain the new edition's structure and the entities it recognizes, noting where genetic findings have redrawn boundaries between diseases. Leukemia diagnosis and treatment planning around the world key off these definitions. The update therefore shapes which tests patients receive and which trials they can join.
pmc-9825413:
Elliot Sollis and co-authors described the GWAS Catalog in 2022, a knowledgebase of genome-wide association studies run jointly by institutes in the United States and Europe. Association studies scan genomes for variants linked to traits and diseases, and their results are a basic resource for genetics. The catalog stores those results in a detailed, standardized form that computers and people can both use.

It serves hundreds of thousands of users a year from universities, health care, and industry. The article covers how studies and results are deposited, curated, and kept interoperable with other resources. A single trusted catalog prevents the field's findings from scattering across thousands of incompatible journal supplements.
poincare-foundations-of-science-1913:
Henri Poincare, a French sage of maths and deep thought, wrote three books on the nature of science. George Halsted turned all three into English, and this set came out in 1913. The parts are Science and Hypothesis, The Value of Science, and Science and Method.

Poincare asks what a law of nature is, and how much of it men make by choice. He states a rule of relativity much like the one Einstein would make famed soon after. The set is science at thought on its own base, by one of its great minds.
potts-wonderfull-discoverie-lancaster-16:
Thomas Potts served as clerk of the court when twelve people faced witchcraft charges at Lancaster in 1612. His Wonderfull Discoverie of Witches in the Countie of Lancaster came out in 1613. It is the court's own account of the Pendle trials, England's best-known witch case.

Potts records the charges, the proof, and the words of the accused as the assizes heard them. Ten of the twelve were hanged, among them women from the Pendle Hill country. A child witness helped doom her own kin. The book still gives the fullest sense of how such a trial ran, step by step.
pound-canzoni-ripostes-1913:
Ezra Pound published Canzoni in 1911 and Ripostes a year later; the two were combined in this 1913 volume. The Ripostes part carries a famous appendix: the complete poems of T. E. Hulme, the young philosopher-poet who helped seed Imagism. Together the parts show Pound changing direction in public.

Canzoni still glows with troubadours, Renaissance Italy, and formal songs. Ripostes turns harder and plainer, with short, dry poems that point toward the Imagist rules Pound was about to announce. Hulme's five small poems, including The Embankment, close the book like a manifesto in miniature. The combined volume is the book that launched Imagism as a movement.
praetorius-von-zauberey-german-1613:
Anton Praetorius, a Reformed preacher, published his thorough German report on sorcery and sorcerers in 1613. The full title promises a ground-level account, and Praetorius delivers argument meant for ordinary readers and rulers alike. He opposes torture and persecution outright, pleading for the accused in plain German.

His stand grew from witness. Praetorius had seen a witch trial's machinery at close range and turned against it. The report is the first German clerical voice raised against the trials. He argues from Scripture, law, and simple mercy. Later ages nearly forgot him, then honored his courage. His book marks the point where a German pulpit said stop.
principia-mathematica-vol-3-1913:
The third volume of Principia Mathematica, from 1913, completes Whitehead and Russell's great project. Relations, the links between things, receive full treatment in this closing part. Measurement also comes under their logical rebuilding. With those topics secured, the logicist program stands complete in print.

The authors aimed to show that mathematics grows from logic alone. Their three volumes argue the case by doing the work, proof after proof. Later results would limit the dream, but the effort reshaped the field. Foundations research still starts from questions this set posed. The final volume rewards readers who followed the long climb. It ends an era in logic.
proust-swanns-way-1913:
Marcel Proust published Swann's Way in 1913, the first volume of his long novel In Search of Lost Time. The narrator recalls his childhood in the town of Combray. A taste of cake dipped in tea brings back a flood of memories. Family habits, walks, and church visits shape the early chapters.

A long middle section tells of Charles Swann and his love for Odette. Swann's jealousy and pain mirror themes that return later in the work. The translation here is by C. K. Scott Moncrieff. Readers meet Proust's slow, exact style here first. Few novels study memory and time with such care.
psalms-solomon-gray-1913: The Psalms of Solomon, eighteen Jewish poems from the first century BCE, translated by George Buchanan Gray. They lament Roman conquest and hope for a messiah. This edition preserves those ancient songs. The paper lived through the years.
rasaratnakara-rasayanakhanda-1913-1913: Rasaratnakara Rasayanakhanda, 1913. The Sanskrit rasa text. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol3-1913:
Journey's End closes Romain Rolland's Jean-Christophe in Gilbert Cannan's third volume, published in 1913. It holds the last three books of the cycle: Love and Friendship, The Burning Bush, and The New Dawn. Christophe is now older, famous in spite of exile, and worn by struggle.

Love, loss, and the approach of war fill these final books. Christophe learns to let go of striving and to accept life as it comes. Rolland ends the long story on a note of hard-won peace. The ten books together trace one man's growth from cradle to grave. Few novels of the age attempt so wide a span with such warmth.
royce-problem-christianity-vol-1-1913:
The Problem of Christianity, published in 1913 in two volumes, is Royce's mature statement on the Christian faith. This first volume sets out his philosophy of the Beloved Community, the idea toward which his whole career had been moving.

Royce argues that Christianity's essence is not doctrine but loyalty: the community of interpretation bound by memory, hope, and love. Sin, atonement, and the church are reinterpreted through this social lens. The lectures addressed educated believers unsettled by science and criticism. Volume one lays the philosophical ground; its partner volume, treated beside it, turns to history and doctrine.
royce-problem-christianity-vol-2-1913:
The second volume of The Problem of Christianity, published in 1913, completes Royce's two-volume statement. Where the first volume built his philosophy of the Beloved Community, this one faces history: the actual record of Jesus, Paul, and the early church.

Royce treats the historical and doctrinal questions with the candor of a scholar and the sympathy of a believer in community. Paul emerges as the founder of the community idea at Christianity's heart. The lectures close his argument that loyalty to the community of interpretation is faith's living core. Together the volumes form his testament.
russell-principia-mathematica-vol-3-1913:
The third volume of Principia Mathematica, published in 1913, completes the great attempt to derive all of mathematics from logic. It takes up series and measurement, the parts of mathematics closest to the physical world.

Here the theory of order reaches its full growth, and quantity and measurement get their logical base. A planned fourth volume on geometry, to be written by Whitehead alone, never appeared. With this book the logicist program stood complete, its influence assured even where later thinkers trimmed its claims. Few works of the century match its ambition or its austere labor.
rutherford-radioactive-substances-1913:
Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who found the atomic nucleus, wrote Radioactive Substances and Their Radiations in 1913. The book sums up fifteen years of fast discovery by his labs in Montreal, Manchester, and Cambridge. It served as the Cambridge school's bible on the subject.

Rutherford sorts the alpha, beta, and gamma rays by how they bend, pierce matter, and ionize air. He sets out the decay series by which one element changes into another down a fixed chain. Few books catch a science mid-revolution with such authority. Its tables of rays and decay rates served working physicists as a daily tool.
santayana-winds-doctrine-1913:
George Santayana published Winds of Doctrine in 1913, a set of essays on modern thought. The title echoes the winds that blow opinion from age to age. Santayana criticizes William James, Josiah Royce, and other former colleagues with polite sharpness. He also writes on Shelley, modernism, and German philosophy.

The essays mark his break with pragmatism and with Harvard. Santayana defends a cool, classical view of reason and tradition. His judgments are severe yet beautifully phrased. The book helped define his public voice as a critic of modern culture. Readers still enjoy its blend of philosophy and literary portraiture.
scott-last-expedition-vol1-1913:
Robert Falcon Scott led the Terra Nova expedition to Antarctica in 1910, aiming for the South Pole. Volume One of Scott's Last Expedition, published in 1913, prints his journals. Scott never came back; the book is his voice from the ice.

He tells of the landing at Cape Evans, the winter of science and sledging, and the polar march itself. His party reached the Pole in January 1912 to find Amundsen's flag already there. The return journey, through storm and frostbite, ends with the famous last entries. Searchers found the journals beside the bodies, and the world read them as a testament.
shaker-millennial-praises-1813:
Hancock, Massachusetts gave the Shakers their first hymnbook, Millennial Praises, in the year 1813. More than 140 hymns fill its pages, songs shaped for a people who worshipped in motion together. Shaker services joined singing to marching and sacred dance, and these texts carried doctrine into the body itself.

The hymns praise Mother Ann, the millennial dawn, and the pure life of the gathered community. Simple meters made them easy for new converts, many of them unlettered, to hold in memory and sing. As the movement's liturgical core, the little book lets later readers hear Shaker worship from inside the meeting itself.
shaw-pygmalion-1913:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Pygmalion in 1913, naming it after the Greek myth of a sculptor who fell in love with his statue. Shaw had studied phonetics, the science of speech sounds, with real passion. The play opened in London in 1914 after a first production in Vienna.

Professor Henry Higgins bets he can pass off Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl, as a duchess. He retrains her voice and manners in a few months of drills. Eliza succeeds, then asks the question Higgins never expected: what becomes of her now? Shaw uses the story to attack class snobbery and to argue that speech, not birth, builds the walls between people.
shelley-queen-mab-1813: Queen Mab, a philosophical poem by Shelley, 1813. The fairy queen's vision. This book preserves that radical poem. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
sombart-jews-modern-capitalism-epstein-1:
Werner Sombart's study of Jewish economic history appeared in German in 1911, and M. Epstein translated it in 1913. The book asks what part Jewish communities played in the rise of modern capitalism. Many readers pair it with Weber's Protestant Ethic as a counterpart thesis. Sombart traces trade, finance, and the spirit of enterprise across centuries.

His claims about Jewish economic life are contested, and scholars have disputed them ever since. The work is preserved as economic history and as a record of its era's social thought. It should be read as a period document, not as a settled account. Its influence on debate is itself a fact of history.
some-english-alchemical-books-being-an-a: Some English Alchemical Books, 1913. The English alchemy. This book preserves that address. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
spr-proceedings-vol25-1911-1913:
Volume twenty five gathers parts sixty two through sixty four and an appendix, for 1911 to 1913. On the eve of war, the Society for Psychical Research keeps its ledger of wonders. Telepathy trials, by now a veteran genre, run with strict scoring. Fresh surveys echo the old census of hallucinations.

Trance sittings supply the human center, with mediums tested by strangers and sealed questions. Apparition cases arrive from soldiers, nurses, and families at home. The society prints doubts from its own council in the same volume. Volume twenty five is a late, full sample of the archive. It preserves the debate as a generation inherited it.
spr-proceedings-vol26-1913:
Parts sixty five, sixty six, and sixty seven make volume twenty six, dated 1913. The Society for Psychical Research stands here at the edge of the Great War. Its journal mixes telepathy experiments with reports gathered over thirty years. Trance mediumship, with the Piper sittings as the touchstone, fills long reports.

Apparition cases continue to meet the census standards of evidence. Physical phenomena get the brief, wary handling the society had learned. Volume twenty six carries the central archive into its war years. The debate of 1882 to 1930 would resume after the guns stopped. These pages show its prewar state, careful and unresolved. The record invites fresh judgment.
tagore-crescent-moon-1913:
Tagore's Crescent Moon, published in 1913, gathers short prose-poems about childhood, motherhood, and wonder. Many began as Bengali child-songs, which Tagore himself recast in English. The book came west in the same year as his Nobel fame.

The pieces speak in a child's voice, asking why the moon smiles, where babies come from, and what the clouds are doing. Others give the mother's answers, tender and a little sad at how fast children grow. Bengali devotional feeling runs through the songs, softening their play with prayer. Adults often keep the book for the ache beneath its sweetness. It remains one of his most loved books in English.
tagore-gardener-1913:
The Gardener, published in 1913, is Tagore's volume of lyrics on love and devotion cast as prose-poetry. It followed Gitanjali westward and carried his Nobel fame to a wide English readership. Tagore translated and reshaped the Bengali songs himself.

Servant and queen, lover and beloved, trade short speeches full of gardens, rivers, and evening lamps. Human love keeps turning into praise of a divine beloved, and back again, without a hard line between them. The volume shows why readers on several continents took Tagore to their hearts at once. Its themes of parting and return give the love songs a quiet ache.
tagore-sadhana-1913:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize in 1913, gave the lectures printed that year as Sadhana: The Realisation of Life. He delivered them at Harvard for Western hearers new to Indian thought. The book serves as the philosophical companion to his poetry collection Gitanjali.

Tagore presents the Upanishadic vision of man's relation to the universe, in which the self finds truth by union, not by grasping. He treats evil, beauty, love, and action as steps toward that wider life of the soul. American readers met a major Eastern thinker here in his own English voice.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i: Volume thirteen of the Mirror of Literature, an 1829 weekly. Its pages brim with news, tales, and facts. Regency readers found amusement and instruction alike. The living past, week by week, the past in print, lively pages.
the-pit-prop-syndicate-pg2013: Crofts’s 1922 mystery follows shiploads of timber that hide a smuggling ring. Inspector French plods from clue to clue with methodical care. The first great police procedural, exact and gripping to the end. Crofts never wastes a clue or a page.
theragatha-rhys-davids-1913: Psalms of the Brethren, the Theragatha translated by Caroline Rhys Davids in 1913. These verses record early Buddhist monks' verses on liberation. This edition preserves those ancient poems. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
tob-0039-d13:
Roll 36, a late reel of the set, preserves part of the closing mass of the Doctors' Trial transcript from Nuremberg. The trial ran from late 1946 into 1947, before an American military tribunal. Its defendants were doctors and officials charged over camp experiments.

By the late rolls the record holds the weight of months of testimony and exhibits, the full paper trail of the medical case. Nothing here is retold or shortened; it is the tribunal's own file, kept entire. The proceedings ended in prison terms and death sentences, and helped give the world the Nuremberg Code. This roll completes one more stretch of that verbatim history.
tob-0213:
G. K. Chesterton subtitled The Man Who Was Thursday A Nightmare, and his metaphysical thriller earns the label. Gabriel Syme, a poet recruited as a detective, infiltrates the supreme anarchist Council of Days, whose seven members take weekday names. Elected as Thursday, Syme discovers each fellow conspirator stranger than the last, and the chase turns philosophical.

London becomes a dreamscape of duels, disguises, and pursuits that keep reversing hunter and hunted. Beneath the comedy runs an argument about order, evil, and the nature of God, delivered at a run. V1 evidence calls it the most philosophical detective story ever written; readers can decide after the final unmasking, which reframes everything before it.
tob-10813:
John Henry Newman wrote An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845 while leaving Anglicanism for Rome. The essay asks an uncomfortable question: if doctrine changes over centuries, how can later teaching claim to be the same faith? Newman's answer reshaped modern theology on both sides of the Tiber.

Development, he argues, is not corruption but life: a living idea grows, and tests can distinguish healthy growth from decay. He applies those tests to Roman Catholic claims against his former church. Dense and brilliant, the essay is among the most consequential religious books of the nineteenth century, and Newman converted as he finished it.
tob-12913:
Annie Besant, president of the Theosophical Society, wrote The Ancient Wisdom as a plain account of theosophical teaching. Besant was a famed speaker who could make hard systems clear. Generations of students learned the movement's doctrines from her books.

She lays out planes of nature, the rounds of worlds, karma, rebirth, and the path by which a disciple grows toward mastery. Man is presented as a spirit working through body, feeling, and mind toward full self-knowledge. As the movement's textbook for a generation, it states what theosophists taught in ordered, confident form.
tob-4113:
Volume one of the whole Sacred Books of the East series is Muller's Upanishads, part one. Max Muller edited the series and translated these Sanskrit dialogues himself. The Chandogya Upanishad leads, with its teaching that the self within is the ground of all: thou art that.

Other early texts in the volume ask what breath is, what the eye sees by, and what survives death. Teachers answer in stories and bold claims rather than proofs. The series opened the East to the West in fifty volumes, and it started here. Verified from the 1919 edition, part one still anchors the set.
tob-9047-61113:
Volume four of Bostock's Pliny opens the great storehouse of ancient medicine. Remedies drawn from plants fill book after book, arranged by ailment from head to foot. Pliny records what healers used, what patients feared, and what cures cost.

Charms and spoken spells stand beside herbal drugs without embarrassment, since Roman medicine drew no firm line between them. Pliny scolds Greek doctors even while copying their lore. Half the cures strike modern readers as pure magic, yet every page teaches how the ancient world faced sickness. The volume is a full medicine cabinet from the age of the Caesars.
toy-introduction-history-religions-1913:
Crawford Howell Toy was a Harvard Semitist who lost one post for his liberal views and gained another at Harvard's divinity school. His Introduction to the History of Religions, published in 1913, surveys faith from animism to the higher religions. Toy writes a comparative history in a single, steady volume.

He begins with spirits in nature, taboo, and magic, then rises through national gods to the universal faiths. His judgments are calm and humane, shaped by wide reading in texts he could read in their own tongues. The book served American students as a learned doorway into the whole field.
trithemius-de-septem-secundeis-1613:
Johannes Trithemius, a German abbot and scholar of hidden arts, wrote De Septem Secundeis, shown here in a 1613 printing. The title means on the seven secondary beings. Trithemius taught that seven planetary angels rule the ages of the world in turn.

Each angel's reign, lasting a few hundred years, shaped empires, faiths, and the fate of peoples, he argued. Trithemius worked through history from creation to his own day, matching events to the angel then in charge. The scheme blends astrology, Bible history, and prophecy. It influenced later occult writers who sought a hidden clock behind world events, and it shows how Renaissance scholars mixed faith with star lore.
un-ga-res-13:
Eight great offices formed the spine of the first UN Secretariat, under Resolution 13 of the General Assembly, from February 1946. The office setup, the text holds, must let the work run with the greatest speed and thrift. The Secretary-General must build that setup at once. It must let him meet his duties under the Charter and serve the needs of all the UN's arms.

The chief units are named: arms for Security Council affairs, trade and wealth, social work, and lands not yet free. Public facts, law, meetings and services, and the money office round out the list. Assistant chiefs may be named to run them. The chart drawn here still shapes the UN's vast staff today.
un-ga-res-a-69-13: Joint work with a Black Sea trade bloc fills Resolution A/69/13, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Black Sea Economic Cooperation Organization has held observer status at the Assembly since 1999. The text recalls past votes on the tie, the last in 2012, and the Assembly's 1994 call for stronger UN work with regional groups. Any strife in the region, it warns, holds back joint work of this kind.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 13, from the first session in 1946, organized the United Nations Secretariat. The Assembly directed the Secretary-General to build an office setup that could serve all the organs well. It listed eight main units. They included departments for Security Council affairs, economic affairs, and social affairs. They also included trusteeship, public information, legal work, and finance.

Further parts approved the public information plan kept in annex I. They adopted the provisional staff regulations kept in annex II. The text also set pay for senior posts. It backed tax relief for staff salaries. It ordered work on a job grading plan, a provident fund, and a lasting retirement scheme.

General Assembly resolution 69/13 (2014) surveys cooperation between the United Nations and the Black Sea Economic Cooperation Organization, the regional body holding observer status since 1999. The Assembly values its members' work across energy, transport, trade, environment, and crime control. It singles out joint transport projects such as the Black Sea Ring Highway. It urges international financial institutions to help fund project studies. It invites stronger dialogue between the secretariats and cooperation from United Nations agencies. A report is due at the seventy-first session.
un-sc-res-113:
By April 1956, the steps the Security Council had ordered to ease tension along the armistice lines in Palestine had still not been carried out. Resolution 113, adopted without dissent on 4 April 1956, says the situation between the parties is now likely to endanger peace and security.

Instead of issuing new orders, the Council turns to fact-finding. It asks the Secretary-General, as a matter of urgent concern, to survey how the four General Armistice Agreements are being enforced and how its own past resolutions are being obeyed. He is also to arrange with the parties, after talks with them and with the Chief of Staff, any measures that could cut the tension.
un-sc-res-1313:
Sierra Leone's peacekeeping mission faced a rebel onslaught when the Security Council acted on 4 August 2000. The Revolutionary United Front had attacked and detained staff of the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, since May. The Council condemned those attacks in the strongest terms. It praised the force commander for the firm response that freed the mission's position.

The Council extended UNAMSIL only to 8 September 2000 while it rebuilt the mission. It held that the RUF's breaches of the Lomé Peace Agreement had destroyed the cooperative setting the mission was built for. The Council stated its intent to strengthen the mandate: hold the Lungi and Freetown peninsulas, answer any RUF threat with robust force, and deploy in strength at key towns. The Secretary-General was asked to report after talks with the troop contributors. The short renewal bought time for a bigger, harder mission.
un-sc-res-1413:
Afghanistan's new security force needed more time in the spring of 2002. On 23 May 2002 the Security Council extended the International Security Assistance Force. The force, known as ISAF, guarded Kabul under resolution 1386. The Council restated its support for a sovereign and united Afghanistan. It also backed the world campaign against terrorism after the 2001 attacks.

The extension added six months beyond 20 June 2002. Member states in the force could take all needed measures to do the job. The Council asked states to give troops, equipment, and money. It also sought gifts to the trust fund for the force. ISAF's leaders owed monthly reports through the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1513:
One more short renewal kept the Western Sahara mission alive in late 2003. On 28 October 2003 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 31 January 2004. The Council recalled its support for the peace plan adopted that July. Nothing else in the dispute had moved. Morocco and the Polisario Front still held opposed positions on the territory's future.

The Secretary-General had to report on the situation before the term ended. The Council stayed seized of the matter. These brief extensions became the pattern for the mission. Each one kept the ceasefire machinery in place. Each one also marked the lack of a political breakthrough.
un-sc-res-1613:
Short-term judges for the Yugoslavia war crimes court were being selected in the summer of 2005. Governments had sent nominations for these judges, called ad litem judges, to the Secretary-General. Under the court's statute, the Council passes the nominations to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects the judges from the list. Resolution 1613 was adopted on 26 July 2005.

The Council forwarded the nominations it had received to the General Assembly. The text lists more than twenty names, from countries in every part of the world. The step is a staffing decision, not a ruling on any case. Even so, it mattered to the court's work. Ad litem judges let the tribunal run several trials at the same time. That speed was vital in 2005, when the court was under orders to finish its trials and appeals on a fixed timetable.
un-sc-res-1713:
Sudan's sanctions panel gained a year and an extra member in 2006. On 29 September 2006 the Security Council extended the panel until 29 September 2007. The panel watches the arms embargo and the travel and money measures on Sudan. It was first set up under resolution 1591 in 2005. Two earlier extensions had kept it alive. The Council told the Secretary-General to add a fifth expert.

The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was due by 29 March 2007. A final report would close the term. The Council pressed states, United Nations bodies, and the African Union to cooperate. The Darfur Peace Agreement and the southern peace deal frame the text.
un-sc-res-1813:
Resolution 1813 addressed Western Sahara when the Council adopted it unanimously on 30 April 2008. Talks between Morocco and the Polisario Front had run through four rounds. Each side had tabled its own plan in April 2007. No breakthrough was in sight, and the ceasefire mission still had to be kept in place.

The Council extends the mission, called MINURSO, until 30 April 2009. Both sides are urged to move into deeper talks without prior conditions. A fair, lasting deal must give the Sahrawi people a say in their future. The text backs realism and a spirit of compromise. Family visits by land, added to the air program, are welcomed.
un-sc-res-1913: Resolution 1913 is a formal Security Council decision held in this collection through a transcription of the UN's official record. Its opening clauses establish the members' shared view of the matter; its numbered clauses establish their shared command. The entry preserves both establishments whole, which is what makes it a primary source rather than a reference note.
un-sc-res-413: The Socialist Republic of Viet Nam applied to join the United Nations in 1977. On 20 July 1977 the Security Council examined the application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Viet Nam be admitted to membership. The decision was taken by consensus. Earlier bids had failed during the postwar dispute over Vietnam's status. The unified state took its seat that September, two years after the war ended.
un-sc-res-713: The record catalogued as Resolution 713, dated 1991, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 113, adopted unanimously on 4 April 1956, finds that tension along the armistice lines in Palestine could endanger international peace. The steps earlier resolutions required had still not been carried out. It asks the Secretary-General, as a matter of urgency, to survey how the four General Armistice Agreements are being enforced. He is to arrange measures with the parties. Those include withdrawal of forces from the lines and full freedom of movement for United Nations observers. He is to report back within one month.

Siam, the country now called Thailand, applied to join the newborn United Nations in 1946. It had never been colonized, but the war had left its status tangled. A dispute with France over border territory had to be settled first. The Council noted that its members unanimously approved the application.

Resolution 13 then recommends Siam's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly admitted Siam in December 1946. It was among the UN's earliest new members. The country's later name change to Thailand did not affect the seat. This short text preserves the formal step by which a Southeast Asian kingdom joined the postwar order at its very start.

Resolution 1313, adopted on 4 August 2000, extends the UN mission in Sierra Leone while admitting the peace there has broken down. Rebels of the Revolutionary United Front had attacked and detained UNAMSIL peacekeepers that spring, breaking the Lomé Peace Agreement. The Council praised the mission and its commander for pushing back against the threat.

The mandate was extended only until 8 September 2000. The Council judged that the rebels' widespread and serious breaches since May had destroyed the cooperative climate the agreement assumed. Until security allowed progress toward a settlement, it said, the mission's structure, strength, resources, and mandate all needed beefing up, and it signaled its intent to order that strengthening next.

Resolution 1413 is a UN Security Council extension of the Afghanistan security force, adopted unanimously on 23 May 2002 under Chapter VII. The International Security Assistance Force, created after the Taliban's fall to protect Kabul and the interim Afghan government, had been led by Britain, and Turkey had offered to take command.

The resolution extends the force's authorization for six months beyond 20 June 2002 and authorizes participating states to take all necessary measures to fulfill its mandate. It thanks Britain for organizing and leading the force and welcomes Turkey's offer to assume the lead. The force it kept in being later expanded nationwide under NATO.

Three months of cover for the Sahara mission came from this spare text of 2003. On 28 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1513 without dissent. It recalls the Council's past Sahara texts. One stands out: Resolution 1495 of July 2003. That text backed the envoy's peace plan as the best path for the territory.

One step does the work here. MINURSO's mandate runs to 31 January 2004. A report from the Secretary-General is due before that term ends. The bridge kept the mission in place while replies to the plan hung fire. The Polisario Front had accepted the plan by then. Morocco had not, and the gap stayed open.

Names, not laws, fill this Council text on the Yugoslavia court. On 26 July 2005, it adopted Resolution 1613. The court, built by Resolution 827 in 1993, used stand-in judges to widen its trial capacity. Candidates reached the Council through the Secretary-General. The Assembly then elects the judges from the Council's list.

The text sends thirty-five names to the Assembly. The nominees come from many states, from Pakistan and Nigeria to Canada. Latvia and Jamaica are on the list as well. Such staffing steps were routine work for the Council. They kept the court's rooms staffed through its busiest trial years. Each name had to pass the Assembly vote to serve.

Another year of scrutiny for Sudan's sanctions began with Resolution 1713. It was adopted on 29 September 2006. A Darfur peace deal existed, but key rebel groups had refused to sign. Violence and impunity were getting worse. Aid workers faced growing danger. The expert panel's final report had landed that August.

Members extended the panel until 29 September 2007. A fifth expert was added to strengthen it. The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was set for 29 March 2007. Non-signers were urged to join the Darfur agreement at once. Signers were told to honor it. All parties had to halt attacks on civilians.

Negotiations over Western Sahara gained rare momentum in 2007 and 2008. Morocco offered an autonomy plan in April 2007. The Polisario Front tabled its own proposal a day earlier. Four rounds of direct talks followed. Resolution 1813, adopted on 30 April 2008, tried to keep that process alive after the Secretary-General's latest report.

MINURSO, the UN mission in the territory, was extended until 30 April 2009. Members demanded respect for the ceasefire agreements. They told both parties to negotiate in good faith, without preconditions. Realism and compromise were called essential. The text also backed family visits between separated relatives, by air and possibly by land. Money from member states was sought for such confidence-building steps.

In March 2010 the future of the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, known as MINURCAT, was still unsettled. Chad's government and the United Nations were still discussing what should happen to the mission. Resolution 1913 simply extended the mandate until 15 May 2010, on the same terms as before. The Council said the situation in the region remained a threat to international peace and security. The short extension kept the mission in place while the talks went on.

Cast out by Malaysia in August 1965, Singapore stood alone. The rich port city had not sought the split. It had to build a state from scratch, fast. A bid for a UN seat came at once. Resolution 213 passed with no dissent on 20 September 1965.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Singapore. The Assembly did so the next day. Lee Kuan Yew led the new state. Few gave the small isle much hope then. It had no farms, no oil, and a port as its chief wealth. Time proved the doubters wrong. The seat was a first shield for a weak new state. This one-line text is the legal start of Singapore's life among nations.

Few Council demands are as short, or as blunt, as this one of 1972. On 28 February, it adopted Resolution 313 without dissent. Israel had struck into Lebanon by ground and air. The raids answered guerrilla attacks from across the border. Lebanon brought the matter before the Council.

One sentence carries the whole text. Israel must halt and shun all ground and air action against Lebanon at once. All its forces must leave Lebanese soil. The brevity is itself the message. Most Middle East texts balance calls on both sides. This one speaks to a single party, in command voice, with no softening clauses at all.

Vietnam had been shut out of the UN for years by vetoes. The war ended in 1975 with the land made one. Saigon fell, and a single state took shape. Its bid for a seat had been blocked in 1976 by the United States. In 1977 the mood had changed. Resolution 413 passed by common consent on 20 July 1977.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam. The Assembly did so that fall. Hanoi took the seat with no foe at the gate this time. The vote closed a long tale. The UN had split the land's fate in the 1950s. War and cold rivalry kept a seat out of reach for a full age. Now the one state took its place.

Yugoslavia was breaking apart in fighting in the autumn of 1991. The federal army faced forces in Croatia and Slovenia. Cease-fire deals signed that September were already breaking down, and the loss of life was heavy. Yugoslavia itself had welcomed a meeting of the Council. Resolution 713 was adopted on 25 September 1991.

The Council praised the peace efforts of the European Community and of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Then, acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, it ordered a general and complete arms embargo. All states had to stop deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Yugoslavia at once. The embargo would last until the Council decided otherwise. It was meant to help establish peace and stability in the country. The Council kept the matter on its agenda until a peaceful solution was achieved.
un-un-res-second-report-of-the-secretary:
Early 2000 finds the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone still finding its feet, and the second report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/13, takes stock. UNAMSIL had taken over from the observer team under the Lomé peace deal. Its troops were spread thin across a tense country.

The report covers deployment, disarmament of fighters, and talks with rebel leaders. It notes slow progress and lists the risks that could wreck the peace. Read with the later reports, it shows a mission walking a narrow line before the crisis that nearly destroyed it.
us-amendment-13:
The Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified in December 1865, eight months after the Civil War ended. Congress had passed it in January, and Abraham Lincoln signed the proposal before his death. Emancipation had come by war proclamation; the amendment wrote abolition into the nation's supreme law.

Its first section declares that neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall exist in the United States, except as punishment for a crime. The second gives Congress power to enforce the ban by law. Four million enslaved people gained legal freedom by its words, though the fight for real freedom had only begun. The charter of freedom for those four million souls was bought at the cost of over six hundred thousand war dead. It remains the first of the three Reconstruction amendments.
vidyabhusana-nyaya-sutras-1913:
Logic in India begins with the Nyaya Sutras of Gotama, translated complete into English by Satis Chandra Vidyabhusana in 1913. The volume, eighth in the Sacred Books of the Hindus series, holds the founding text of the Nyaya school. Its subject is right reasoning: how we know, how we prove, and how we argue fairly.

Short sutras lay out kinds of proof, the parts of a syllogism, and the traps of bad debate. Every later Indian school of thought had to answer Nyaya's standards. For students of logic beyond the West, no shelf starts earlier than this one.
webster-unabridged-dictionary-1913:
The 1913 edition of Webster's Unabridged Dictionary was the standard desk dictionary of the English-speaking world for a century. It descends from Noah Webster's great American dictionary, expanded by generations of editors. Every headword, definition, root, and pronunciation is given in full.

Entries run from common words to rare scientific and literary terms, with examples of use. The book's size was its promise: nothing a reader met in print should be missing. Libraries, schools, and newspaper offices kept it close at hand. As a snapshot of English in 1913, it remains a rich quarry for writers and historians.
wharton-custom-of-the-country-1913:
Edith Wharton published The Custom of the Country in 1913, her most savage look at American money and marriage. Wharton wrote it while her own marriage was collapsing. Her heroine, Undine Spragg, came from a small midwestern town with rich parents and unlimited ambition.

Undine climbs through a string of husbands: a gentle New York heir, a French marquis, and a railroad magnate. Each marriage buys her a higher social floor, and each bores her once she owns it. Divorce, in Wharton's account, is simply the custom of the country for women like Undine. The novel is funny, cold, and prophetic about celebrity culture. Many readers rank it as Wharton's finest satire.
witches-apprehended-examined-executed-16:
Bedford gives this 1613 pamphlet its case: witches taken, questioned, and put to death. Witches Apprehended, Examined and Executed pairs the trial report with a guide to finding witches. The two parts sit side by side, court record first and plain advice after.

The guide tells readers what marks, acts, and signs should raise alarm in their own towns. That pairing is the point of the print, and it was a shrewd one. Trial news taught fear, and the guide taught readers how to act on it. The pamphlet shows charge and belief feeding each other in Jacobean England.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol13:
Liverpool printed Volume XIII of the Journal of Discourses in 1871, well into the set's second decade of publication. The stenographic pages hold sermons by Brigham Young, his counsellors, the Twelve Apostles, and other leading speakers. By now the Journal was a fixture: the way spoken teaching became lasting print for the Saints everywhere.

Readers find doctrine taught with the confidence of a church no longer fighting for its ground. Daily counsel still threads through the talks, since the speakers governed towns as well as souls. Volume XIII adds its full share to the year-by-year record of nineteenth-century Mormon teaching.
